human-body-and-movement.title: The Skeleton: Structure and Functions
human-body-and-movement.description: Bones of the skeleton, joint types and the six functions the skeletal system provides for movement.
human-body-and-movement.content_html:
The Framework of Movement

The human skeleton is a living structure made of 206 bones that provides the framework for every movement you make in sport. Without it, muscles would have nothing to pull against. The skeleton works in partnership with the muscular system: muscles contract and pull on bones, which act as levers, creating movement at joints. Understanding which bones are where — and what they do — underpins everything else in PE.

Bones of the Skeleton: Head to Toe

Working from the top of the body downwards, the cranium sits at the very top of the head, curving down around the brain. Below it, the vertebrae form a column of 33 bones running from the base of the skull to the pelvis — protecting the spinal cord and giving the trunk both stability and a controlled range of movement.

At the shoulder, two bones are key. The scapula (shoulder blade) is a flat, triangular bone that sits across the upper back, providing attachment points for the muscles that control the shoulder. The humerus is the long bone of the upper arm, running from the shoulder joint down to the elbow. Together, the scapula and humerus form the shoulder joint — a ball-and-socket joint that allows the greatest range of movement in the body.

At the elbow, three bones meet. The humerus comes down from the shoulder. The radius runs along the thumb side of the forearm, and the ulna runs along the little-finger side. The elbow joint between the humerus and the ulna is a hinge joint allowing flexion and extension. The radius also rotates around the ulna to allow the forearm to turn palm-up or palm-down, a movement essential in racket sports.

Key Fact

Ball-and-socket joints are found at the hip (pelvis and femur) and shoulder (scapula and humerus). Hinge joints are found at the elbow (humerus, radius, ulna), knee (femur and tibia) and ankle (tibia, fibula and talus).

Moving to the lower body, the pelvis is a large basin-shaped structure of fused bones at the base of the spine. It forms the hip joint with the head of the femur — a ball-and-socket joint that allows the greatest range of movement in the lower limb. At the knee, the femur articulates with the tibia (the large shin bone), forming a hinge joint. The patella sits in front of the knee joint, protecting it and improving the mechanical advantage of the quadriceps muscle. The fibula runs alongside the tibia on the outer side of the lower leg, providing a point of attachment for muscles but bearing very little weight. Finally, the talus links the lower leg to the foot, sitting between the tibia and fibula above to form the ankle joint.

The Six Functions of the Skeleton

The skeleton does far more than hold the body upright. It serves six distinct functions, each of which can be applied directly to sport and physical activity.

Support — the skeleton holds the body upright against gravity. A sprinter’s lower limbs support their entire body weight as they drive off the blocks. Without a rigid skeletal frame, the muscular system would have nothing to act on.

Protection — flat bones protect vital organs. The cranium shields the brain; the ribs and sternum form a cage around the heart and lungs. In contact sports such as rugby, the ribcage absorbs impact forces that would otherwise damage the heart and lungs directly.

Movement — bones act as levers. When the biceps contracts during a bicep curl, the forearm bones (radius and ulna) pivot at the elbow to lift the load. In kicking a football, the femur swings at the hip and the tibia swings at the knee, producing explosive leg extension.

The spec distinguishes between long bones and short bones in terms of movement. Long bones such as the femur, tibia, humerus, radius and ulna enable gross movements — the large, powerful movements used in sprinting, jumping and throwing. Short bones, such as those in the wrist and ankle, enable finer, more controlled movements. Flat bones such as the cranium, ribs and scapula serve a protective function and provide broad surfaces for muscle attachment.

The shape and design of each bone directly determines how much movement it allows. The rounded head of the femur fits into the cup-shaped socket of the pelvis, allowing movement in all directions at the hip. The pulley-shaped end of the humerus fits into the groove of the ulna at the elbow, restricting movement to a single plane (flexion and extension only).

Attachment for muscles — the skeleton provides attachment points for muscles. Tendons connect muscles to bones at these points. When a muscle contracts, it pulls on its attachment point and the bone moves. Without firm attachment points, muscular contractions would produce no movement at all.

Mineral storage — bones store calcium and phosphorus. These minerals are released into the bloodstream when the body needs them, and exercise that loads the skeleton — such as weight training or running — stimulates the bones to increase their mineral density, making them stronger over time.

Blood cell production — red bone marrow inside flat and irregular bones produces red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Red blood cells carry oxygen to the working muscles during exercise via haemoglobin. This function links directly to cardiovascular performance: a well-functioning skeletal system supports oxygen delivery to muscles.

Key Fact

The six functions of the skeleton are: support, protection, movement, attachment for muscles, mineral storage and blood cell production. Each one can be applied to sport — for example, the femur acts as a lever during kicking (movement) and the ribs protect the lungs during a tackle (protection).

A common mistake is to write only about support and movement when asked for skeletal functions. The mark scheme rewards all six, so always aim for a wider range. Remember that flat bones protect organs (ribs protect the heart and lungs) and that the skeleton is a living structure involved in mineral storage and blood cell production. In a 6-mark analyse question, linking blood cell production to oxygen delivery for aerobic exercise would place you in the top band.
human-body-and-movement.exam_tip_html: On a 3-mark ‘Describe’ question about skeletal functions, name a function, explain what it means, and apply it to a sport — that’s the three marks. On a 6-mark ‘Analyse’ question, avoid listing functions as bullet points. Instead, write in continuous prose: state the function, explain how it works physiologically, and link it to a named sporting movement. A common error is to confuse the role of bones in ‘attachment’ with the role of muscles themselves — remember it is the tendons that attach muscles to bones, not muscles attaching directly. If asked to name bones at a joint, state both bones: for example, the knee joint involves the femur and tibia (and the patella sits in front).
human-body-and-movement.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ball-and-socket joints (shoulder and hip) allow the greatest range of movement; hinge joints (elbow, knee, ankle) allow flexion and extension in a single plane. Knowing the bones at each joint is essential for movement analysis questions.
  • The six functions of the skeleton are support, protection, movement, attachment for muscles, mineral storage and blood cell production — each one links to sporting performance and can earn marks when applied to a named sport.
  • Long bones act as levers for gross movement (running, throwing); flat bones protect vital organs (cranium protects the brain, ribcage protects heart and lungs); short bones allow finer, controlled movements.

practice_questions.text: A county-level hockey player relies on her skeleton for a range of functions during a match. Analyse how two functions of the skeleton contribute to her performance during the game.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two functions are clearly identified and developed with accurate physiological explanation, each applied specifically to hockey performance. The candidate links structure to function (e.g. how the femur acts as a lever at the hip during a reverse hit) and demonstrates understanding of how skeletal function supports overall performance.

Secure: Two functions are identified with mostly accurate explanation and applied to a general sporting context. Some links between structure and performance may be undeveloped.

Developing: One or two functions are mentioned with limited development. Application to sport is vague or missing from one function.

Emerging: Basic naming of functions with little or no explanation or sporting application.

Acceptable content includes: movement (long bones act as levers; femur pivots at the hip to produce the sweeping action of a reverse hit); protection (ribcage protects the heart and lungs from stick or ball impact); attachment for muscles (the scapula and pelvis provide attachment points for muscles that control the swing of the arms and legs); mineral storage (calcium stored in the skeleton maintains bone density under the repeated loading of running on hard surfaces); blood cell production (red blood cells produced in bone marrow carry oxygen to working muscles during aerobic play).

practice_questions.text: A Year-11 student says: 'The skeleton is only important for holding you upright — it doesn’t do anything else useful in sport.' How far do you agree with this statement? Evaluate the functions of the skeleton in the context of sporting performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of skeletal functions discussed with accurate physiological detail; both the role in structural support AND wider functions (protection, movement/levers, muscle attachment, mineral storage, blood cell production) are evaluated; consistent sporting examples applied throughout; candidate reaches a clear, justified conclusion that goes beyond simple support.

Secure: Most functions are covered with reasonable accuracy; sporting examples present but may not always be specific; conclusion present.

Developing: Support and one or two other functions discussed; limited sporting application; argument may be one-sided (only agreeing or disagreeing).

Emerging: Basic statement that the skeleton does more than support, but little development or sporting application.

Agreeing content: the skeleton does hold the body upright, which is essential for balance in static positions (yoga pose, balance beam, penalty kick stance); without skeletal support, the body would collapse under gravity.

Disagreeing content: the skeleton also provides protection (flat bones shield the brain and heart and lungs); movement through levers (the femur acts as a lever in running; the humerus and forearm bones produce the throwing action in cricket); attachment points for muscles (no attachment = no movement); mineral storage (calcium maintains bone strength for impact sports); blood cell production (red blood cells carry oxygen to muscles during aerobic exercise). A well-rounded athlete benefits from all six functions simultaneously.

human-body-and-movement.title: Muscles and Antagonistic Pairs
human-body-and-movement.description: Major muscles, agonist and antagonist roles, and isotonic and isometric contractions in sporting actions.
human-body-and-movement.content_html:
Why Muscles Work in Pairs

Muscles can only pull — they cannot push. Because of this, every joint in the body is controlled by at least two muscles that work in opposite directions. When one muscle contracts and shortens to produce movement, the opposing muscle relaxes and lengthens to allow that movement. This arrangement is called an antagonistic muscle pair. Understanding these pairs — and always naming them in the context of a specific joint and a specific direction of movement — is essential for exam answers.

Major Muscles of the Body

At the shoulder, the deltoid forms the rounded cap of the shoulder. It is the prime mover for abduction of the arm (lifting it out to the side) and also contributes to flexion and extension. The rotator cuffs are a group of four muscles that wrap around the shoulder joint, stabilising the ball-and-socket joint and assisting rotation — critical in throwing sports such as cricket bowling and javelin. The pectorals (chest muscles) lie across the front of the thorax and act as prime movers in horizontal adduction, such as in the push-up or front crawl pull phase. The latissimus dorsi (‘lats’) is the large fan-shaped muscle of the back, responsible for extension and adduction of the arm at the shoulder, powerful in swimming and rowing movements.

At the elbow, the biceps sits on the front of the upper arm. During elbow flexion (the upward phase of a bicep curl), the biceps is the agonist (prime mover), contracting concentrically to shorten and pull the forearm up. On the back of the upper arm sits the triceps. During elbow flexion, the triceps acts as the antagonist, relaxing and lengthening to allow movement. The roles reverse completely during elbow extension (the downward phase of a press-up): the triceps becomes the agonist and the biceps becomes the antagonist.

At the hip and knee, two large muscle groups dominate. The quadriceps group (four muscles on the front of the thigh) is the prime mover for knee extension — straightening the knee. The hamstrings lie on the back of the thigh and are the prime mover for knee flexion (bending the knee). At the knee, the quadriceps and hamstrings form the classic antagonistic pair: quadriceps agonist during extension, hamstrings agonist during flexion. The gluteals are the large buttock muscles that drive hip extension — critical in sprinting and jumping. The hip flexors are the antagonists to the gluteals, acting as agonists during hip flexion (lifting the knee forwards in running).

At the ankle, the gastrocnemius runs from behind the knee down to the heel via the Achilles tendon. It is the prime mover for plantar flexion — pointing the toes down, as in sprinting push-off or jumping. The tibialis anterior on the front of the lower leg is the prime mover for dorsiflexion (pulling the toes upward), and the two muscles form an antagonistic pair at the ankle.

The abdominals are the core muscles on the front of the trunk. They flex the spine, stabilise the pelvis during running and throwing, and are active in almost every sporting movement as a postural stabiliser.

Key Fact

In a bicep curl upward phase: biceps = agonist (concentric contraction), triceps = antagonist. In kicking (knee extension): quadriceps = agonist, hamstrings = antagonist. In a sprinting push-off (plantar flexion): gastrocnemius = agonist, tibialis anterior = antagonist.

A very common error in exams is to name a single muscle as ‘the agonist’ without specifying the joint, the direction of movement, or the antagonist. Mark schemes award marks for the complete picture: agonist named (1), antagonist named (1), action described at the correct joint (1). Writing ‘the biceps is the agonist’ alone will not earn full marks. Always frame answers as: “During elbow flexion, the biceps acts as the agonist (prime mover) while the triceps acts as the antagonist at the elbow joint.”

Types of Muscle Contraction

Muscles do not always contract in the same way. The spec identifies three types of contraction: isotonic concentric, isotonic eccentric and isometric.

Isotonic concentric contraction occurs when a muscle shortens while it contracts, producing movement. The biceps during the upward phase of a bicep curl contracts concentrically — it shortens, and the elbow flexes. This is the most obvious form of contraction in sport: the quadriceps contracts concentrically to extend the knee when kicking a ball.

Isotonic eccentric contraction occurs when a muscle produces tension while it lengthens. This happens when the muscle is acting as a brake. During the downward phase of a bicep curl, the biceps contracts eccentrically — it is still producing tension to control the lowering of the weight, but it is getting longer as the elbow extends. Eccentric contractions are responsible for DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness) because the lengthening under load causes tiny tears in muscle fibres.

Isometric contraction occurs when a muscle is active but the joint does not move. A gymnast holding a crucifix position on the rings keeps the arms outstretched perfectly still — the deltoids and pectorals are working hard isometrically. A rugby player locked in a scrum uses isometric contractions to maintain position against an opposing force.

Key Fact

Concentric = muscle shortens (produces movement). Eccentric = muscle lengthens under tension (controls or brakes movement). Isometric = muscle produces tension but no joint movement occurs. All three can happen in the same exercise: a squat involves concentric quadriceps on the way up, eccentric on the way down, and isometric if you pause at the bottom.

Tendons are strong, inelastic connective tissues that attach muscles to bones. Without tendons, a muscle contraction would not move the skeleton. The Achilles tendon, for example, attaches the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles to the calcaneus (heel bone). When the calf muscles contract concentrically, the Achilles tendon transmits the force to the heel, producing plantar flexion for sprinting. Tendons are denser and less elastic than muscles, which is why they take longer to strengthen with training. Overloading tendons without adequate rest is a common cause of injury in growing athletes.
human-body-and-movement.exam_tip_html: For any question asking about agonist and antagonist muscles, always include three elements: (1) the name of the agonist (prime mover), (2) the name of the antagonist, and (3) the specific joint and direction of movement. Missing any of these costs marks. On a 4-mark ‘Explain’ question, the mark scheme typically awards 1 mark for each element plus 1 for an accurate description of the type of contraction (concentric or eccentric). For contraction-type questions, the trick is to ask yourself: ‘Is the muscle getting shorter (concentric) or longer (eccentric) while it is working?’ A common error is to say the antagonist ‘contracts’ — the antagonist actually relaxes and lengthens to allow the movement to occur.
human-body-and-movement.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Muscles work in antagonistic pairs: the agonist (prime mover) contracts to produce movement at a joint while the antagonist relaxes and lengthens. Always name both muscles and the joint when answering exam questions.
  • Concentric contraction = muscle shortens (producing movement); eccentric contraction = muscle lengthens under tension (controlling or braking movement); isometric contraction = muscle produces tension with no change in length and no joint movement.
  • Key sporting pairs: biceps/triceps at the elbow, quadriceps/hamstrings at the knee, gastrocnemius/tibialis anterior at the ankle, deltoid acting with the lats at the shoulder. Tendons connect each muscle to its bone attachment point.

practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the quadriceps as the agonist during knee extension; 1 mark for stating the quadriceps contracts concentrically (shortens under tension) to produce knee extension; 1 mark for stating the hamstrings act as the antagonist, relaxing and lengthening to allow the movement to occur.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between concentric and eccentric contraction, using the biceps muscle as an example in both cases.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining concentric contraction: the biceps shortens under tension during elbow flexion (upward phase of bicep curl); 1 mark for explaining eccentric contraction: the biceps lengthens under tension during elbow extension (lowering phase of bicep curl) to control the movement; 1 mark for correctly linking concentric to movement production; 1 mark for correctly linking eccentric to movement control or braking (and noting this is why DOMS can occur).

practice_questions.text: A club-level badminton player notices that her forehand smash relies on coordinated muscle action at the shoulder and elbow. Analyse the role of antagonistic muscle pairs in producing this movement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear identification of at least two antagonistic pairs relevant to the movement (e.g. deltoid/latissimus dorsi at the shoulder; triceps/biceps at the elbow); each pair discussed in terms of agonist and antagonist roles with correct contraction types (concentric/eccentric) applied to specific phases of the smash; consistent sporting application throughout; technically accurate language throughout.

Secure: Two pairs identified; mostly correct agonist/antagonist assignment; contraction types mentioned but may not be consistently linked to specific phases; generally applied to the smash.

Developing: One pair discussed with development; or two pairs identified but with limited contraction type analysis; sporting context present but superficial.

Emerging: Basic mention of agonist/antagonist with little development; incorrect assignment possible; limited sporting application.

Acceptable content: at the shoulder, the deltoid (agonist) contracts concentrically during abduction/flexion to raise the arm; the latissimus dorsi (antagonist) relaxes; at the elbow, the triceps (agonist) contracts concentrically during extension to produce the smashing action; the biceps (antagonist) relaxes and lengthens; on the follow-through, the roles reverse as the biceps contracts eccentrically to decelerate the arm.

practice_questions.text: A sprint coach claims that eccentric muscle contractions are just as important as concentric contractions for athletic performance. Evaluate this claim, referring to specific muscles and sporting actions in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full evaluation of both concentric and eccentric contractions; multiple sporting examples applied accurately; candidate demonstrates understanding of eccentric loading (DOMS, injury risk, deceleration, landing mechanics) alongside the more obvious role of concentric power production; balanced argument with a justified conclusion.

Secure: Both types discussed with relevant examples; most points accurate; conclusion present; some sporting application.

Developing: One type discussed more fully than the other; limited sporting examples; argument is one-sided.

Emerging: Basic description of contractions with little evaluation or sporting application.

Agreeing (eccentric is equally important): eccentric contractions of the hamstrings decelerate the leg after a kick, preventing knee injury; the biceps contracts eccentrically to control the lowering phase of a pull-up, building strength through a full range; the quadriceps contracts eccentrically during landing from a jump to absorb force and protect the knee; eccentric loading in plyometric training (depth jumps) maximises the stretch-shortening cycle for explosive power.

Disagreeing / partial challenge: concentric power is what drives the explosive movements in sprinting, jumping and throwing; most spectators and coaches focus on concentric strength as it directly produces performance outcomes; without concentric quadriceps power, there would be no sprint speed to decelerate.

human-body-and-movement.title: Synovial Joints and Types of Movement
human-body-and-movement.description: Hinge and ball-and-socket joints, joint structures that prevent injury, and movement at major joints.
human-body-and-movement.content_html:
What Is a Synovial Joint?

Every freely movable joint in the body — at the shoulder, elbow, hip, knee and ankle — is a synovial joint. Synovial joints are the most common type of joint in the body, and they all share the same basic structure: a capsule surrounding the joint, fluid inside to reduce friction, and a range of soft-tissue structures that hold the joint together and prevent injury. Understanding these structures is important not just for anatomy, but for explaining how joints withstand the demands of sport.

Structures of a Synovial Joint

The outer shell of a synovial joint is the joint capsule. It is made of tough, fibrous connective tissue that wraps completely around the joint, forming a sealed envelope. The joint capsule holds the bones in position and contains the joint fluid.

Inside the capsule, the synovial membrane lines the inner surface of the capsule. Its job is to produce synovial fluid — a viscous, egg-white-like substance that coats the ends of the bones inside the joint. This fluid dramatically reduces friction, allowing bones to glide smoothly past each other. Without synovial fluid, the grinding of bone on bone would cause rapid joint damage. During the warm-up phase of exercise, synovial fluid becomes less viscous and spreads more effectively, which is one reason why warming up reduces injury risk.

Covering the ends of the bones inside the joint is articular cartilage, a smooth, bluish-white tissue that absorbs compressive forces and provides an almost frictionless surface. Cartilage has no blood supply of its own — it relies on synovial fluid for nourishment. Once damaged, cartilage heals very slowly, which is why cartilage injuries (such as a torn meniscus in the knee) can end sporting careers.

Ligaments are short, tough bands of fibrous tissue that connect bone to bone across the joint. They are the primary restraints against excessive movement — without them, joints would be unstable. The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) inside the knee, for example, prevents the tibia from sliding forward relative to the femur during landing from a jump. A ruptured ACL is one of the most serious injuries in contact sport.

Tendons do not form part of the synovial joint structure itself, but they pass close to most joints and contribute to stability. The Achilles tendon at the ankle and the patellar tendon at the knee are essential force transmitters from muscle to bone.

Bursae (singular: bursa) are small cushioning sacs filled with fluid. They sit at points where tendons or ligaments would otherwise rub against bone, such as at the front of the knee (the prepatellar bursa). Inflammation of a bursa, known as bursitis, is a common overuse injury in sports that involve repeated kneeling or shoulder work.

Key Fact

The six key structures of a synovial joint are: synovial membrane (produces fluid), synovial fluid (reduces friction), joint capsule (encloses and seals the joint), bursae (cushion tendons against bone), cartilage (absorbs compression and provides frictionless surface), and ligaments (connect bone to bone for stability).

Types of Synovial Joint

The spec identifies two types of synovial joint relevant to GCSE PE. A hinge joint permits movement in one plane only — flexion and extension. The elbow (humerus articulating with the ulna and radius), the knee (femur articulating with the tibia) and the ankle (tibia and fibula articulating with the talus) are all hinge joints. A ball-and-socket joint permits movement in multiple planes. The shoulder (head of the humerus fitting into the glenoid cavity of the scapula) and the hip (head of the femur fitting into the acetabulum of the pelvis) are ball-and-socket joints.

Types of Movement at Synovial Joints

Flexion is a decrease in the angle at a joint — bending. Extension is an increase in the angle — straightening. Both occur at the shoulder, elbow, hip and knee. At the elbow, flexion and extension are the only movements possible because it is a hinge joint. At the shoulder and hip (ball-and-socket), a much wider range of movements is available.

Abduction is movement of a limb away from the midline of the body — lifting the arm out to the side in a star jump. Adduction is movement towards the midline — bringing the arm back down. Both abduction and adduction are available at the shoulder and hip (ball-and-socket joints) but not at the elbow or knee (hinge joints).

Rotation of the shoulder is turning the arm in or out along its long axis. A cricket bowler’s bowling arm rotates at the shoulder during delivery. Circumduction of the shoulder is a circular movement combining flexion, abduction, extension and adduction in sequence — the arm traces a full cone shape. Throwing a javelin involves circumduction of the shoulder.

At the ankle, the movements are named differently. Plantar flexion is pointing the foot downward (pressing the toes away from the body). A sprinter’s powerful push-off at the end of each stride is driven by plantar flexion at the ankle. Dorsiflexion is pulling the toes upward towards the shin — the ankle bends when a gymnast lands from a vault. Both plantar flexion and dorsiflexion are hinge movements at the ankle joint.

Key Fact

Shoulder (ball-and-socket): flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation, circumduction. Knee (hinge): flexion and extension only. Ankle (hinge): plantar flexion and dorsiflexion only. The more movements a joint allows, the greater the sporting versatility — but often at the cost of stability.

A 4-mark exam question might ask how the structures of a synovial joint help prevent injury during sport. A well-developed answer links each structure to its protective role: ligaments prevent bones from moving too far out of alignment (stabilising the knee in a tackle); bursae prevent tendons from rubbing on bone during repeated movements (protecting the knee during cycling); cartilage absorbs impact forces when landing from a jump; synovial fluid lubricates the joint and reduces the wear on cartilage surfaces during sustained aerobic exercise. Always name the structure, state what it does, and give a sporting example.

As body temperature rises during a warm-up, synovial fluid becomes less viscous and distributes more evenly across the joint surfaces. This increases the range of movement available and reduces friction, meaning joints can work more efficiently. Ligaments and tendons also become more pliable at higher temperatures, reducing the risk of tears. This is the physiological reason why a warm-up includes a pulse raiser and stretching before high-intensity work.
human-body-and-movement.exam_tip_html: On a ‘State Two’ question about synovial joint structures, give two different structures — do not write ‘synovial fluid’ and ‘synovial membrane’ as your only two answers without an explanation, as these are closely related. Spread your answers: one structural component (e.g. ligaments) and one lubricating component (e.g. synovial fluid) will demonstrate wider knowledge. On a 4-mark ‘Explain’ question about movement types, state the movement, define it (angle increasing/decreasing, towards/away from midline), name the joint where it occurs, and give a sporting example — that covers all four marks. For plantar flexion and dorsiflexion, a very common mistake is to mix them up: remember plantar flexion = pointing the toes (like a sprinter’s push-off), dorsiflexion = toes up (like landing from a jump).
human-body-and-movement.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Synovial joints contain six key structures: synovial membrane, synovial fluid, joint capsule, bursae, cartilage and ligaments — each helping to reduce friction, absorb impact and prevent excessive movement that could cause injury.
  • Ball-and-socket joints (shoulder and hip) allow flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation and circumduction. Hinge joints (elbow, knee, ankle) only allow flexion and extension (plus plantar flexion and dorsiflexion at the ankle).
  • Plantar flexion (toe pointing down) drives the push-off in sprinting; dorsiflexion (toes pulling up) occurs during landing. Abduction moves a limb away from the midline; adduction moves it towards the midline.

human-body-and-movement.title: The Cardiovascular System and Exercise
human-body-and-movement.description: Heart structure, the pathway of blood, blood vessels and how the cardiovascular system responds to exercise.
human-body-and-movement.content_html:
The Heart: Structure and Function

The heart is a hollow, muscular organ roughly the size of a fist, located in the chest slightly left of centre behind the sternum. It is divided into four chambers by a central wall called the septum. The two upper chambers are called atria (singular: atrium) — the right atrium receives deoxygenated blood returning from the body, and the left atrium receives oxygenated blood returning from the lungs. The two lower chambers are called ventricles — the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs, and the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. The left ventricle has a thicker, more muscular wall than the right because it must generate much higher pressure to push blood all the way around the body.

Valves inside the heart open due to changes in blood pressure and close automatically to prevent backflow of blood. The right side of the heart and the left side each have valves between the atrium and the ventricle (atrioventricular valves) and between the ventricle and the outgoing vessel (semilunar valves). You do not need to name individual valves, but you must know they prevent backflow.

The Cardiac Cycle: How the Heart Beats

The heart works through a two-phase cycle. During diastole, the chambers relax and fill with blood — the atria fill with incoming blood and then push it through to the ventricles. During systole, the ventricles contract and eject blood out of the heart: the right ventricle forces blood into the pulmonary artery (to the lungs) and the left ventricle forces blood into the aorta (to the body). This cycle repeats every beat, which at rest typically occurs 60–80 times per minute.

The Pathway of Blood Through the Heart and Lungs

Following the pathway of blood precisely is a common exam demand. Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium via the vena cava. From the right atrium it passes through a valve into the right ventricle. The right ventricle then contracts and forces the blood through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. In the lungs, carbon dioxide is released and oxygen is picked up by haemoglobin in the red blood cells to form oxyhaemoglobin. The now-oxygenated blood returns to the heart via the pulmonary vein, entering the left atrium. It passes through a valve into the left ventricle, which contracts powerfully and ejects the oxygenated blood into the aorta — from which it is distributed to every organ and muscle in the body.

Key Fact

Blood pathway: vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs (gas exchange) → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body. Note that the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood — this is the opposite of most arteries.

Blood Vessels: Arteries, Veins and Capillaries

Arteries carry blood away from the heart. They have thick, muscular walls because they must withstand the high pressure generated by the ventricular contraction. The walls are elastic, allowing them to stretch and recoil with each heartbeat, smoothing out the pulsed blood flow. All arteries (except the pulmonary artery) carry oxygenated blood.

Veins carry blood back towards the heart. They have thinner walls than arteries because blood pressure is much lower by the time it reaches the venous system. Veins contain valves that prevent backflow, which is especially important in the legs where blood must travel upward against gravity. All veins (except the pulmonary vein) carry deoxygenated blood.

Capillaries are the microscopic vessels that form the link between arteries and veins in the tissues. Their walls are just one cell thick, allowing oxygen and nutrients to diffuse into the muscle cells and carbon dioxide and waste products to diffuse back into the blood. Every working muscle is surrounded by a dense network of capillaries. Long-term aerobic training increases capillary density in muscles, improving oxygen delivery.

During exercise, the working muscles need much more oxygen and glucose than at rest. The body redirects blood flow using two mechanisms. Vasoconstriction reduces the diameter of blood vessels supplying areas that are not active during exercise (e.g. the digestive system), reducing blood flow to those areas. Vasodilation increases the diameter of the blood vessels supplying the active muscles, dramatically increasing blood flow to where it is needed most. The redistribution of blood during exercise through vasoconstriction and vasodilation is called the ‘vascular shunt’. This is why it is inadvisable to exercise vigorously immediately after a large meal — the digestive system is competing with muscles for blood supply.

Cardiac Output, Stroke Volume and Heart Rate

Three linked measurements describe how efficiently the heart pumps blood. Stroke volume is the amount of blood pumped out of the heart with each beat. At rest, stroke volume is approximately 70 ml. Heart rate is the number of beats per minute (bpm). A typical resting heart rate is 60–80 bpm (trained endurance athletes may have a resting heart rate as low as 40 bpm — a long-term adaptation called bradycardia). Cardiac output (Q) is the product of the two:

$$Q = \text{stroke volume} \times \text{heart rate}$$

At rest: Q = 70 ml × 72 bpm = 5,040 ml/min (approximately 5 litres per minute). During intense exercise, heart rate can rise to 200 bpm or more and stroke volume increases to around 110–130 ml, so cardiac output can reach 20–25 litres per minute in a trained athlete.

Key Fact

Cardiac output (Q) = stroke volume × heart rate. Always show the formula, substitute the values, and include the unit (ml/min or L/min). Example: Q = 70 ml × 72 bpm = 5,040 ml/min. At maximum exercise this can rise to over 20,000 ml/min in a trained athlete.

A heart rate graph during exercise typically shows four phases. First, an anticipatory rise — heart rate climbs before exercise even begins, driven by the release of adrenaline as the performer prepares mentally and physically. This is why athletes’ hearts are already beating faster as they stand in the starting blocks. Second, heart rate rises steeply at the onset of exercise as oxygen demand increases. Third, a plateau occurs at a steady exercise intensity as supply and demand equalise. Fourth, a recovery curve drops steeply at first then more gradually after exercise stops, as the body repays its oxygen debt. A trained performer recovers faster (steeper drop) because their cardiovascular system is more efficient.
human-body-and-movement.exam_tip_html: The cardiac output calculation is one of the most predictable questions in this unit — always worth attempting. Show three things: (1) the formula (Q = stroke volume × heart rate), (2) the substitution with figures from the question, and (3) the answer with the correct unit (ml/min or L/min). Missing the unit is a frequent error that costs the final mark. On a ‘Describe the pathway of blood’ question, a common mistake is to say the pulmonary artery carries oxygenated blood — it is the one artery in the body that carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs. For extended-response questions on the cardiovascular system, link vasoconstriction and vasodilation explicitly to the redistribution of blood to working muscles, and give a sport-specific example of why this matters.
human-body-and-movement.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Blood pathway through the heart: vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood — this is the exception to the rule that arteries carry oxygenated blood.
  • Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate (Q = SV × HR). At rest this is approximately 5 litres per minute; during maximal exercise it can exceed 20 litres per minute in a trained athlete.
  • Vasodilation increases blood flow to working muscles during exercise; vasoconstriction reduces blood flow to inactive areas. Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure; veins return blood to the heart under low pressure; capillaries allow gas and nutrient exchange with tissues.

human-body-and-movement.title: The Respiratory System and Gas Exchange
human-body-and-movement.description: The pathway of air, breathing mechanics, and gas exchange in the alveoli during exercise.
human-body-and-movement.content_html:
The Journey Air Takes Into Your Body

Every time you inhale, air travels along a precisely ordered pathway before oxygen reaches your working muscles. Understanding this route is essential for explaining how the body meets the increased demand for oxygen during exercise. Air enters through the mouth or nose, where it is warmed, moistened and filtered. It then passes into the trachea — the windpipe — which is kept open by C-shaped rings of cartilage. From the trachea, air divides into the left and right bronchi (singular: bronchus), one entering each lung. Inside the lungs, the bronchi branch repeatedly into smaller and smaller tubes called bronchioles. The bronchioles finally open out into tiny air sacs called alveoli (singular: alveolus), and it is here that the vital process of gas exchange occurs.

Key Fact

The pathway of air follows five stages in sequence: mouth/nose → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. Commit this order to memory — it appears regularly in short-answer questions.

Gaseous Exchange at the Alveoli

Gaseous exchange is the movement of gases between the lungs and the bloodstream. It relies on diffusion — molecules naturally move from areas of high concentration to areas of low concentration. In the alveoli, the concentration of oxygen is high (freshly inhaled air) while the blood arriving from the body has a low oxygen concentration and a high concentration of carbon dioxide. As a result, oxygen diffuses across the alveolar wall into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses in the opposite direction, out of the blood and into the alveolus to be exhaled.

Six structural features of the alveoli are specifically designed to maximise the speed and efficiency of this exchange. First, the alveoli have a very large surface area in total — hundreds of millions of tiny sacs create an enormous surface for diffusion to occur across. Second, the alveolar walls are moist and only one cell thick, meaning the distance gases must travel is as short as possible. Third, the alveoli are surrounded by a rich network of capillaries, ensuring a continuous and large blood supply. Fourth, blood flowing through these capillaries is constantly replenished (deoxygenated blood arrives and oxygenated blood leaves), which maintains the concentration gradient that drives diffusion.

Once oxygen crosses into the blood, it binds with haemoglobin in the red blood cells to form oxyhaemoglobin. This oxygenated blood then travels via the pulmonary veins to the left side of the heart and is pumped out to the working muscles. Haemoglobin can also carry carbon dioxide on the return journey to the lungs.

A common misunderstanding is that oxygen delivery to muscles is purely about breathing harder. In fact, the rate of diffusion at the alveoli is limited by concentration gradients and surface area — you cannot increase the surface area of your alveoli by trying harder. What exercise does achieve is an increased breathing rate and deeper breaths (greater tidal volume), which refreshes the air in the alveoli more frequently, maintaining a strong concentration gradient. Additionally, more capillaries open up around active alveoli during exercise, increasing the effective surface area available for gas exchange. The structural adaptations of the alveoli — thin walls, large surface area, rich blood supply — are what make rapid exchange possible, not effort alone.

The Mechanics of Breathing

Breathing is an active mechanical process driven by muscles changing the volume and pressure inside the chest cavity. During inhalation at rest, the diaphragm contracts and moves downward, while the intercostal muscles contract to raise the rib cage upward and outward. These combined actions increase the volume of the chest cavity, which lowers the air pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric pressure. Air rushes in from outside to equalise the pressure — this is inhalation. During exhalation at rest, the diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax. The rib cage falls inward and downward under gravity, reducing the chest volume and increasing pressure in the lungs. Air is pushed out passively. Breathing at rest is therefore largely passive on the exhale.

During intense exercise, the body must move air much more forcefully and rapidly. On the inhale, accessory muscles come into play: the pectorals (chest muscles) and the sternocleidomastoid (a neck muscle) help to elevate the rib cage further and faster than the intercostals alone can manage. On the exhale, the abdominal muscles actively contract, pulling the rib cage down more quickly and forcefully expelling air. This ensures that stale air (rich in carbon dioxide) is cleared from the lungs faster, making room for fresh, oxygen-rich air.

Tidal Volume and Minute Ventilation

Tidal volume is the amount of air moved in or out with each breath. At rest, tidal volume is approximately 0.5 litres. During maximal exercise it can rise to 3 litres or more as the body draws on inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes. On a spirometer trace, tidal volume appears as the regular rhythmic wave; the peaks and troughs become taller and more frequent as exercise intensity increases.

Minute ventilation is the total volume of air moved per minute and equals tidal volume multiplied by breathing rate. For example, a resting athlete breathing at 15 breaths per minute with a tidal volume of 0.5 litres has a minute ventilation of 7.5 litres per minute. During hard exercise, both tidal volume and breathing rate increase, so minute ventilation can rise to 100–150 litres per minute in trained performers. This enormous increase ensures the concentration gradient at the alveoli is maintained even as muscles consume oxygen at a high rate.

Key Fact

Six features make alveolar gas exchange efficient: large surface area, moist thin walls (one cell thick), short diffusion distance, large capillary network, large blood supply, and a maintained concentration gradient (high O⊂2; low CO⊂2; arriving from the body).

A spirometer trace records lung volumes over time. At rest, the trace shows a regular shallow wave — this is the tidal volume. Above the resting inhale is the inspiratory reserve volume (the extra air you could breathe in above a normal breath). Below the resting exhale is the expiratory reserve volume (the extra air you could push out). Below that is the residual volume — the air that always remains in the lungs and can never be exhaled. When exercise begins, the trace changes: the tidal volume wave gets taller (deeper breaths) and the waves appear more frequently (faster breathing rate). The residual volume remains unchanged throughout.
human-body-and-movement.exam_tip_html: For “describe” questions on gaseous exchange, students often say oxygen “moves into the blood” without explaining why — the mark scheme almost always requires the word “diffusion” and a reference to the concentration gradient (high to low). For “analyse” questions worth 6 marks, go beyond description: link each structural feature to a specific sporting implication. For example, “the large surface area of the alveoli means a marathon runner can exchange sufficient oxygen even at race pace, sustaining aerobic energy production.” Bullet-point responses rarely score above the Developing band — extended-response questions reward connected prose where each point is developed with a sporting example.
human-body-and-movement.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Air travels in a fixed sequence — mouth/nose, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli — and gaseous exchange occurs at the alveoli by diffusion, driven by concentration gradients.
  • Six structural features of the alveoli (large surface area, thin moist walls, short diffusion pathway, rich capillary network, large blood supply, maintained concentration gradient) maximise the speed of oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange.
  • During exercise, tidal volume and breathing rate both increase, raising minute ventilation dramatically so the alveolar concentration gradient is maintained even under heavy muscular demand.

human-body-and-movement.title: Aerobic and Anaerobic Exercise
human-body-and-movement.description: Energy equations, EPOC, and how cool down and recovery methods help the body return to rest.
human-body-and-movement.content_html:
Two Ways Your Body Produces Energy

All physical activity requires energy, and the body produces that energy by breaking down glucose. The critical difference between the two energy pathways is whether sufficient oxygen is available. Aerobic exercise occurs when there is enough oxygen to fully break down glucose. The chemical summary is: glucose + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water. This process is efficient, releasing large amounts of energy, and can be sustained for a long time — making it the dominant pathway for moderate-intensity, longer-duration activities such as a 10 km run, a long swim or a cycling time trial.

Anaerobic exercise occurs when the intensity of effort is so high that the cardiovascular system cannot deliver oxygen to the muscles fast enough. The body bypasses oxygen entirely and breaks down glucose without it: glucose → energy + lactic acid. This pathway is fast but inefficient — it produces far less energy per glucose molecule and cannot be sustained for long because lactic acid accumulates in the muscles, causing fatigue and the familiar burning sensation. Sprinting 100 m, an explosive plyometric jump or a short all-out rowing effort are classic examples of anaerobic activity.

Key Fact

Aerobic: glucose + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water. Anaerobic: glucose → energy + lactic acid. The key distinction is the presence or absence of oxygen, not simply whether the sport involves running or swimming.

Identifying Aerobic and Anaerobic Activity: Duration and Intensity

A common error is simply labelling a sport as “aerobic” or “anaerobic” without justifying the classification. The correct approach is to consider both the duration and the intensity of the effort. High-intensity activity lasting fewer than roughly ten seconds is almost entirely anaerobic because the demand for energy outpaces oxygen delivery. Activities lasting several minutes at moderate intensity are primarily aerobic. Many sports — such as football, netball and rugby — involve both pathways at different moments: a striker’s burst of speed to latch onto a through ball is anaerobic, but the sustained movement across the pitch throughout the match is predominantly aerobic.

Students often believe “aerobic” simply means easy or low-intensity exercise. This is incorrect. A trained 5,000 m runner racing at full competitive pace is still working aerobically — the intensity is high, but oxygen delivery keeps pace with demand throughout the race (approximately 13 minutes in duration). The correct justification is always intensity-and-duration together: “This activity is aerobic because the intensity, although high, can be maintained with sufficient oxygen delivery over the multi-minute duration.” Similarly, a short, explosive effort is anaerobic because the intensity is so extreme that oxygen cannot be delivered quickly enough — not because the activity is “hard” in some vague sense. Always frame your answer with both criteria.

EPOC: Repaying the Oxygen Debt

After intense anaerobic exercise, the body must process the accumulated lactic acid and restore normal physiological conditions. This requires additional oxygen above the resting level, a process known as EPOC (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption), sometimes called the oxygen debt. EPOC is why you continue to breathe hard even after you stop exercising: your respiratory and cardiovascular systems remain elevated to deliver the extra oxygen needed to convert lactic acid back into glucose in the liver, and to restore oxygen stores in the muscles and blood.

The greater the intensity and duration of the anaerobic effort, the larger the EPOC and the longer it takes to recover fully. Elite sprinters, for example, may experience measurable EPOC for an hour or more after a 400 m race. Understanding EPOC is important for planning training and competition schedules — athletes need sufficient recovery time to allow the body to return to homeostasis before the next hard effort.

Key Fact

EPOC (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption) is the elevated oxygen uptake after exercise that repays the oxygen debt caused by anaerobic activity. The extra oxygen is used to remove lactic acid and restore oxygen stores in the muscles and blood.

Recovery Methods After Vigorous Exercise

The body can be helped back to its resting state through several evidence-based recovery strategies. Each has a specific physiological rationale that you must be able to explain, not just name.

The cool down is the most immediately useful recovery tool. By continuing light activity (such as a slow jog or brisk walk) after stopping vigorous exercise, the athlete maintains an elevated heart rate and breathing rate, which keeps blood flowing through the muscles. This sustained blood flow continues to deliver oxygen to the muscles, accelerating the removal and processing of lactic acid. The cool down also typically includes static stretching, which helps maintain the range of movement gained during the warm-up period and reduces the risk of muscle tightness.

Rehydration replaces the fluids lost through sweating. Dehydration thickens the blood, reducing its ability to carry oxygen efficiently, so rehydrating restores blood viscosity and helps the cardiovascular system return to normal function. Consuming carbohydrates after exercise replenishes glycogen stores in the muscles and liver, replacing the glucose fuel that was broken down during activity.

Ice baths (cold-water immersion) and massage both target the prevention of DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness). Ice baths are thought to reduce inflammation and micro-damage in the muscle fibres by constricting blood vessels, limiting the swelling that contributes to soreness. Massage helps by improving circulation to the muscles and reducing tension and adhesions in the muscle tissue. Both methods are widely used by elite athletes in the days following heavy training or competition.

Different sports benefit from different recovery strategies. A 100 m sprinter who has generated a large oxygen debt in a very short time needs the cool down and rehydration immediately, but may rely heavily on ice baths to manage DOMS between competition rounds in the same championship. A marathon runner, by contrast, has run aerobically for hours and generates less lactic acid, but needs substantial carbohydrate replenishment and hydration as the priority recovery tools. Massage is valuable for both, but particularly for endurance athletes who use the same muscle groups repetitively over long durations, creating chronic tightness in the hamstring group, gastrocnemius and hip flexors. When evaluating recovery for a given athlete, always link the method to the specific physiological challenge of that activity.
human-body-and-movement.exam_tip_html: For “identify” and shorter questions on aerobic vs anaerobic, a common error is giving the activity name without any justification. Even a 1-mark question may expect you to say why: “anaerobic, because the high intensity means oxygen cannot be delivered fast enough.” For 9-mark “evaluate” questions on recovery methods, students often produce one-sided answers — praising cool down or ice baths without considering limitations (not all athletes can access ice baths; a cool down is time-consuming between competition rounds). Build your response using a “For X… However Y…” structure, anchor each point to a named sport or athlete type, and end with a justified conclusion about which method is most important for the stated context.
human-body-and-movement.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Aerobic exercise uses oxygen to break down glucose fully (producing CO⊂2; and water); anaerobic exercise occurs without sufficient oxygen and produces lactic acid. Justify each classification with both intensity and duration evidence.
  • EPOC (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption) is the elevated breathing after anaerobic exercise that repays the oxygen debt — the extra oxygen removes lactic acid and restores muscle oxygen stores.
  • Recovery methods include cool down (lactic acid removal via sustained blood flow), rehydration and carbohydrate intake (restoring fluids and fuel), and ice baths or massage (preventing DOMS). Each has a specific physiological rationale that must be explained, not just named.

practice_questions.text: A Year-11 sprinter completes a 200 m time trial. Analyse why this activity is primarily anaerobic and explain the physiological consequences she is likely to experience in the minutes immediately after finishing.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Clear identification that a 200 m sprint involves very high intensity over approximately 20-25 seconds, meaning oxygen cannot be delivered fast enough for aerobic respiration alone. Glucose → energy + lactic acid explained. Lactic acid accumulation linked to fatigue and the burning sensation during the effort. Post-exercise: EPOC defined and linked to sustained elevated breathing, with the purpose of removing lactic acid and restoring oxygen stores explained. Sporting context (the sprint distance and intensity) woven throughout.

Secure (3-4 marks): Anaerobic identification with brief justification; lactic acid named; EPOC described with at least one purpose. Most points accurate but may lack development or sporting application.

Developing (2 marks): Identifies the activity as anaerobic; mentions lactic acid or EPOC but does not explain the mechanism. Limited or no sporting application.

Emerging (1 mark): A basic correct point, such as identifying the activity as anaerobic or naming lactic acid, with no developed explanation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of ice baths and cool down as recovery methods for a competitive swimmer who trains twice a day during a major competition block.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9 marks): Balanced, well-developed evaluation of both methods with clear sporting application to the twice-daily training context. Cool down: advantages (maintains blood flow, removes lactic acid, reduces muscle tightness); limitations (time-consuming between sessions; reduces available recovery window when training is twice daily). Ice baths: advantages (reduces inflammation and DOMS between sessions, particularly valuable when recovery time is short); limitations (discomfort, access in pool environments, some evidence suggests they may blunt training adaptations if used too frequently). Candidate reaches a justified conclusion about which method is most valuable for this specific context.

Secure (5-7 marks): Both methods addressed with relevant advantages and disadvantages. Sporting application to swimming competition context mostly present. Minor gaps in development or balance.

Developing (3-4 marks): One method covered well, or both methods described with limited evaluation. Sporting application present but limited. One-sided or descriptive rather than analytical.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about one or both methods. Little or no evaluation. Minimal sporting application.

human-body-and-movement.title: Short and Long Term Effects of Exercise
human-body-and-movement.description: Immediate, short-term and long-term physiological changes, including hypertrophy and bradycardia.
human-body-and-movement.content_html:
Three Timescales of Change

Exercise affects the body across three distinct timescales, and your ability to distinguish between them is frequently tested. Immediate effects occur during the exercise session itself. Short-term effects appear in the hours following exercise, typically lasting up to 36 hours. Long-term effects emerge only after months or years of consistent training and represent genuine physiological adaptation. Mixing these up in an exam will cost marks, so developing a clear mental map of which changes belong to which category is essential.

Immediate Effects: What Happens While You Exercise

As soon as exercise begins, several changes are immediately visible or measurable. The skin becomes hot, sweaty and flushed (red): core body temperature rises as the working muscles generate heat, and the body responds by directing blood to the skin capillaries, where heat can radiate away. Sweating further cools the skin through evaporation. The increase in depth and frequency of breathing is driven by rising carbon dioxide levels in the blood: chemoreceptors detect this and signal the respiratory centre to increase breathing rate and tidal volume, delivering more oxygen and removing CO⊂2; more rapidly. Finally, heart rate rises to pump more oxygenated blood to the working muscles — this increase begins even before exercise with an anticipatory rise, driven by adrenaline release, and climbs further as exercise intensity increases.

Key Fact

The three immediate effects of exercise are: (1) hot, sweaty and red skin; (2) increased depth and frequency of breathing; (3) increased heart rate. These all begin during the exercise session and return to normal within minutes of stopping.

Short-Term Effects: The Hours After Exercise

In the period immediately after exercise and for up to 36 hours, the body experiences a range of short-term effects as it recovers. Tiredness and fatigue result from the depletion of glycogen (stored glucose) in the muscles and the accumulation of waste products. Light-headedness can occur as blood redistributes away from the brain toward the muscles during exercise, or when exercise stops suddenly and blood pools in the lower limbs before circulation fully adjusts. Nausea may follow high-intensity efforts, particularly in the stomach, as blood flow to the digestive system is significantly reduced during exercise. Aching, cramp and most importantly DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness) develop as the micro-damage to muscle fibres — especially after eccentric contractions or unfamiliar movements — triggers an inflammatory response that peaks 24–48 hours post-exercise.

DOMS is caused by micro-tears in the muscle fibres, particularly following eccentric (lengthening) contractions — for example, lowering a weight under control, running downhill or landing from a jump. These micro-tears are repaired by the body, and during that repair process the muscle fibres are rebuilt slightly thicker and stronger than before. This is the fundamental mechanism of muscle hypertrophy. Experienced athletes experience less DOMS because their muscles have already adapted to a given level of stress. When DOMS does appear, it is typically a signal that a new training stimulus has been applied and adaptation is underway — but the soreness itself should not be severe enough to limit movement significantly.

Long-Term Effects: Adaptations From Months of Training

Consistent exercise over months and years causes permanent physiological adaptations in multiple body systems. These long-term effects represent the body becoming structurally and functionally more efficient at the demands placed on it.

Body shape may change: regular resistance training increases muscle size and reduces relative body fat, while prolonged endurance training may produce a leaner physique with visible muscular definition. Specific components of fitness improve: muscular endurance, speed, suppleness, muscular strength, cardiovascular endurance and stamina all increase with appropriately designed training programmes. For example, a sprinter who trains over many months will improve their speed and explosive strength; a cross-country runner will develop greater cardiovascular endurance and muscular endurance in their legs.

Two of the most significant long-term cardiovascular adaptations are cardiac hypertrophy and bradycardia. Cardiac hypertrophy refers to the heart growing larger and stronger as a muscle in response to the repeated demands of training. A larger, stronger heart can pump more blood per beat — a greater stroke volume. Because stroke volume is higher, the heart does not need to beat as many times per minute to deliver the same cardiac output. This produces bradycardia: a lowered resting heart rate. While the average untrained person has a resting heart rate of around 60–80 beats per minute, elite endurance athletes such as cyclists or distance runners may have resting heart rates of 35–50 bpm. Mo Farah, for example, is reported to have had a resting heart rate in the low 40s during the peak of his marathon career.

Key Fact

The chain: regular training → cardiac hypertrophy (the heart grows larger) → greater stroke volume per beat → bradycardia (lower resting heart rate needed to maintain cardiac output). These are all long-term adaptations — they take months or years of consistent training to develop.

Hypertrophy as a general term refers to the growth in size of a muscle caused by an increase in the size of individual muscle fibres. When applied to skeletal muscles (e.g. the biceps or quadriceps group), it is the result of progressive resistance training: repeated eccentric and concentric contractions under load cause micro-tears, which repair larger and stronger over time. When the term is used specifically as “cardiac hypertrophy,” it refers to the same growth process applied to the heart muscle itself, driven by the sustained cardiovascular demands of endurance training. In both cases, the underlying stimulus is the same — the body adapts to repeated stress by growing the muscle tissue — but the practical outcomes differ: skeletal muscle hypertrophy increases strength and power for movement, while cardiac hypertrophy increases stroke volume and reduces resting heart rate.
human-body-and-movement.exam_tip_html: The most common error on questions about effects of exercise is confusing the three timescales. A short-term effect such as DOMS appears hours to days after exercise — it is not the same as the immediate effects (hot skin, increased heart rate) that occur during exercise. In “describe” and “explain” questions, always state the timescale explicitly: “in the long term, after months of training, the heart undergoes hypertrophy, which leads to bradycardia.” For 6-mark “analyse” questions, go beyond listing: connect the adaptation to a named component of fitness and then to a sporting performance benefit. For example: “Cardiac hypertrophy increases stroke volume, improving cardiovascular endurance, which allows a club cyclist to sustain a higher pace over a 40 km time trial without fatigue.”
human-body-and-movement.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Immediate effects (during exercise) include hot/sweaty/red skin, increased breathing rate and depth, and increased heart rate — these reverse within minutes of stopping.
  • Short-term effects (up to 36 hours after) include fatigue, light-headedness, nausea, and DOMS — caused by glycogen depletion, lactic acid, and micro-tears in muscle fibres.
  • Long-term effects (months to years of training) include improved fitness components, cardiac hypertrophy and, as a result, bradycardia — a permanently lower resting heart rate due to greater stroke volume.

practice_questions.text: Identify one immediate effect of exercise on the body.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: increased heart rate; increased breathing rate/depth; hot, sweaty or red skin. Accept equivalent physiological descriptions.

practice_questions.text: State two short-term effects of exercise that may appear within 36 hours of a training session.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two distinct short-term effects from: tiredness/fatigue; light-headedness; nausea; aching muscles; DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness); cramp. Do not accept 'increased heart rate' (immediate effect). Award once for the same point expressed differently.

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows the resting heart rates of three athletes before and after a 6-month endurance training programme.

Athlete | Resting HR before (bpm) | Resting HR after (bpm)
Alex   | 74                      | 61
Beth   | 68                      | 55
Carlos | 72                      | 58

Calculate the mean reduction in resting heart rate across all three athletes. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly calculating each individual reduction (Alex: 13 bpm; Beth: 13 bpm; Carlos: 14 bpm); 1 mark for summing correctly (13 + 13 + 14 = 40 bpm) and dividing by 3; 1 mark for the correct final answer: 13.3 bpm (accept 13 or 13.3). Units required (bpm) for the final answer mark.

practice_questions.text: Explain how cardiac hypertrophy leads to bradycardia in a trained endurance athlete.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining cardiac hypertrophy as the long-term increase in the size of the heart muscle due to training; 1 mark for explaining that this means the heart can pump a greater stroke volume per beat; 1 mark for explaining that a higher stroke volume means the heart beats fewer times to deliver the same cardiac output; 1 mark for naming or defining bradycardia as a lower resting heart rate (below normal, typically below 60 bpm in trained athletes). Full marks require the logical chain to be clear.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old county-level basketball player has been following a structured fitness programme for eight months. Analyse the long-term physiological effects this programme is likely to have had on her body, and how these effects might improve her performance on court.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Detailed, well-developed response identifying multiple long-term effects (cardiac hypertrophy, bradycardia, muscular hypertrophy, improved muscular endurance/strength/speed, possible changes to body composition). Each adaptation is linked to a mechanism (e.g. cardiac hypertrophy increases stroke volume, lowering resting HR) and then to a specific basketball performance benefit (e.g. sustained cardiovascular output across four quarters; greater explosive power for jumping). Technically accurate language used throughout.

Secure (3-4 marks): Most key long-term effects identified with generally accurate explanations. At least one adaptation linked to a basketball context. May lack development on mechanisms.

Developing (2 marks): One or two long-term effects mentioned but not fully explained. Limited sporting application to basketball.

Emerging (1 mark): A basic correct point about a long-term effect (e.g. the heart gets bigger) with little or no explanation or sporting application.

practice_questions.text: A club runner claims that feeling sore the day after a hard run means she has overtrained and should rest completely. Evaluate whether this claim is accurate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Clear identification of DOMS and its mechanism (micro-tears in muscle fibres, especially from eccentric contractions). Explains that DOMS is a normal, expected short-term effect rather than a sign of overtraining. Discusses when DOMS is benign (manageable soreness, peaks 24-48 hours) vs when it signals overtraining (severe, persistent, affecting movement). Considers both sides: complete rest is not always necessary — light activity, massage or ice baths can manage DOMS while allowing recovery; but if soreness is extreme or persistent, rest is warranted. Justified conclusion reached.

Secure (3-4 marks): DOMS explained correctly; the claim is challenged with some justification. Some appreciation of both sides (DOMS is normal; severe cases need rest). Sporting context present.

Developing (2 marks): DOMS mentioned but not well explained. Limited evaluation — may agree or disagree with the statement without full justification.

Emerging (1 mark): Identifies DOMS or muscle soreness as the relevant concept but provides little analysis.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is a LONG-TERM effect of regular endurance training?
What is the correct definition of cardiac hypertrophy?
options: A lower resting heart rate caused by training
The long-term increase in the size of the heart muscle through training

Match each effect of exercise to the correct timescale:
right: Immediate (during exercise)
Short-term (up to 36 hours after)
Long-term (months/years of training)

glossary_terms.definition: The rise in heart rate that occurs before the start of exercise, triggered by adrenaline release and anticipation of physical effort.
