human-body-and-movement.title: Lever Systems and Mechanical Advantage
human-body-and-movement.description: First, second and third class levers in sport, mechanical advantage calculations and sporting examples.
human-body-and-movement.content_html:
What Is a Lever System?

The human body is a machine built from levers. Every time you kick a ball, perform a push-up or rise onto your toes, you are using a lever system to transmit force. Understanding how levers work allows coaches and athletes to explain why some movements generate great force, and why others allow great speed but require more effort. A lever consists of three components arranged around a pivot point. The fulcrum is the fixed pivot point — in the body, a joint. The load (also called the resistance) is the weight or force being moved. The effort is the force applied to move that load — in the body, this is the force produced by the contracting muscle. The three classes of lever differ in the relative positions of these three components: fulcrum (F), load (L) and effort (E).

Key Fact

The three lever classes by component order along the lever bar: First class — Fulcrum between Load and Effort (FLE / EFL). Second class — Load between Fulcrum and Effort (FLE with load in the middle). Third class — Effort between Fulcrum and Load (FEL). A reliable mnemonic: first class has F in the middle; second class has L in the middle; third class has E in the middle.

First Class Levers

In a first class lever, the fulcrum sits between the load and the effort. Think of a seesaw: the pivot is in the middle, with weight on one side and the pushing force on the other. In the body, the clearest example is the nodding action of the head at the atlantooccipital joint: the skull (load) rests at one end of the vertebral column, the neck muscles (effort) pull from behind, and the joint itself (fulcrum) sits between them. Another example is elbow extension during a push-up: the triceps apply effort at the olecranon behind the elbow joint (fulcrum), moving the weight of the forearm and body (load) on the other side. First class levers can produce both force and speed depending on where the effort and load arms fall.

Second Class Levers

In a second class lever, the load sits between the fulcrum and the effort. The classic everyday example is a wheelbarrow: the wheel is the fulcrum at one end, the load sits in the middle, and your hands apply effort at the handles. In the body, plantar flexion at the ankle — rising onto the toes — is the textbook second class lever: the ball of the foot acts as the fulcrum, the body weight (load) acts through the ankle joint in the middle, and the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles (effort) pull via the Achilles tendon at the heel, which is behind and above the load. Second class levers always produce a mechanical advantage greater than 1, meaning the effort arm is longer than the load arm, so a relatively small muscular effort can move a larger load. This makes them excellent for force production but not for speed.

Third Class Levers

In a third class lever, the effort is applied between the fulcrum and the load. This is the most common lever arrangement in the human body. The classic example is elbow flexion during a bicep curl: the elbow joint is the fulcrum, the biceps apply effort just below the elbow joint, and the load (the forearm, hand and any weight held) is at the far end. The effort arm (joint to biceps insertion) is shorter than the load arm (joint to hand), which means more muscular effort is needed to move the load. However, a small movement of the biceps produces a large movement of the hand — trading mechanical disadvantage for speed and range of movement. Third class levers therefore favour speed and range over force, which is why most striking and throwing actions in sport use them.

A very common exam error is mis-labelling the positions of the fulcrum, load and effort on a lever drawing, or confusing which class a sporting example belongs to. The mark scheme specifically requires the correct LFE arrangement to be visible on any diagram question. A reliable approach is to identify the joint first (that is always the fulcrum), then identify what is being moved (the load, usually the body part or weight), and finally identify where the muscle pulls (the effort). Once you have these three pinned, the class follows logically: if the joint (F) is between the other two, it is first class; if the weight (L) is in the middle, it is second class; if the muscle pull (E) is in the middle, it is third class. Double-check by asking: “Where is the pivot?” — then label outward from there.

Mechanical Advantage

Mechanical advantage (MA) is a number that tells you whether a lever amplifies force (MA > 1) or amplifies speed and range of movement (MA < 1). The formula is: Mechanical advantage = effort arm ÷ load (resistance) arm. The effort arm is the distance from the fulcrum to the point where effort is applied. The load arm (resistance arm) is the distance from the fulcrum to the point where the load acts.

A mechanical advantage greater than 1 means the effort arm is longer than the load arm — a small effort produces a large force at the load point. This is the case in second class levers, and is why rising onto your toes lifts your entire body weight with relatively modest calf muscle effort. A mechanical advantage less than 1 means the load arm is longer than the effort arm — more muscular effort is required, but the trade-off is greater speed and range. Third class levers have MA < 1. First class levers can have MA either above or below 1, depending on the position of the fulcrum relative to the load and effort arms.

Imagine a simplified model of the elbow during plantar flexion (second class lever). The effort arm (heel to Achilles insertion) measures 6 cm. The load arm (heel to ankle joint) measures 4 cm. Mechanical advantage = effort arm ÷ load arm = 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5. Because MA is greater than 1, the calf muscles need to produce less force than the body weight they are lifting — the lever system amplifies force. Now consider elbow flexion (third class lever). Effort arm (elbow joint to biceps insertion) = 4 cm. Load arm (elbow joint to hand holding a dumbbell) = 30 cm. MA = 4 ÷ 30 = 0.13. The biceps must produce around 7.5 times the load to lift the weight — a significant mechanical disadvantage — but the hand moves through a much greater arc than the biceps shortens, generating the high speed needed for throwing and striking actions.

Key Fact

Mechanical advantage = effort arm ÷ load arm. MA > 1 means force is amplified (second class lever). MA < 1 means speed and range are amplified (most third class levers). In the exam, always show the formula, the substitution, and the units (dimensionless, but arm lengths in cm).
human-body-and-movement.exam_tip_html: For calculation questions on mechanical advantage, the mark scheme typically awards marks for: writing the formula, correctly substituting the values, and giving the numerical answer. Do not just write the number — the examiner needs to see your working. For “describe” questions asking you to describe a lever system in a sporting example, always name all three components (fulcrum, load and effort) and identify which body part acts as each. A common error is labelling the muscle itself as the fulcrum — the fulcrum is always the joint. When drawing lever diagrams, practise placing F, L and E in the correct order for each class: first class (F between L and E), second class (L between F and E), third class (E between F and L). Getting this order wrong costs straightforward marks on short-answer questions.
human-body-and-movement.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The three lever classes differ by the position of the fulcrum (F), load (L) and effort (E): first class has F in the middle; second class has L in the middle; third class has E in the middle. Third class levers are the most common in the human body.
  • Mechanical advantage = effort arm ÷ load arm. MA > 1 favours force (second class, e.g. rising onto toes); MA < 1 favours speed and range (most third class levers, e.g. bicep curl, throwing action).
  • In exam questions, always identify the joint (fulcrum), what is being moved (load) and where the muscle pulls (effort) before classifying the lever. Label all three components precisely on any diagram.

practice_questions.text:
Which class of lever is used when a gymnast rises onto the tips of her toes (plantar flexion at the ankle)?
A) First class lever — the fulcrum is between the load and the effort
B) Second class lever — the load is between the fulcrum and the effort
C) Third class lever — the effort is between the fulcrum and the load
D) Second class lever — the effort is between the fulcrum and the load
practice_questions.marks: B) Second class lever — the load is between the fulcrum and the effort [1 mark]. The ball of the foot = fulcrum, body weight at the ankle = load, gastrocnemius pulling at the heel = effort.

practice_questions.text: A rugby player's forearm acts as a lever during elbow flexion. The effort arm (elbow joint to biceps insertion) measures 4 cm and the load arm (elbow joint to ball being caught) measures 36 cm. Calculate the mechanical advantage of this lever.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct substitution into the formula: mechanical advantage = effort arm ÷ load arm = 4 ÷ 36; 1 mark for the correct answer: 0.11 (accept 0.1 or 1/9). Units: the answer is dimensionless (no unit needed, but lengths must be in the same unit). The arm lengths must be in the same unit — if a student uses different units (cm vs m) without converting, award method mark only if the formula is correctly applied.

practice_questions.text: Describe the first class lever used when a swimmer performs a push-back stroke, focusing on elbow extension. Name all three components and their positions.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the fulcrum as the elbow joint; 1 mark for identifying the effort as the triceps muscle force (pulling on the olecranon behind the elbow); 1 mark for identifying the load as the weight of the forearm/hand/water resistance (in front of the elbow joint), with the fulcrum correctly placed between load and effort. Award full credit only if the positions confirm a first class arrangement (fulcrum between load and effort).

practice_questions.text: A sports coach tells a group of young athletes: 'Most of your throwing and striking actions are inefficient because the effort arm is shorter than the load arm.' Explain why this is not necessarily a limitation, and how the lever arrangement in throwing actually benefits performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the throwing action uses a third class lever (effort between fulcrum and load); 1 mark for explaining that when the effort arm is shorter than the load arm, mechanical advantage is less than 1; 1 mark for explaining that this mechanical disadvantage is compensated by an amplification of speed — a small muscular shortening produces a large movement of the hand; 1 mark for applying to throwing: the high speed of hand movement produced by the third class lever allows the athlete to throw the object with greater velocity than a lever with MA > 1 would generate. Accept equivalent reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the three classes of lever are each used in sport, explaining how the mechanical advantage of each influences the type of movement it is best suited to.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): All three lever classes correctly identified with accurate sporting examples. The mechanism and position of F, L and E described for each. Mechanical advantage for each class linked to a clear explanation of the movement advantage it provides: first class (variable MA, can favour force or speed depending on positions — e.g. head nodding); second class (MA > 1, force amplified — plantar flexion, good for lifting body weight); third class (MA < 1, speed amplified — elbow flexion, throwing, good for striking/catching). Explanations developed and clearly connected to sporting performance.

Secure (3-4 marks): At least two lever classes correctly described with sporting examples and a link to mechanical advantage. Minor inaccuracies or missing development on one class.

Developing (2 marks): One or two lever classes described; limited understanding of mechanical advantage or sporting application.

Emerging (1 mark): Names one lever class or provides a basic description without full component labelling or sporting application.

practice_questions.text: A sprinter's ankle joint acts as a lever during the push-off phase of a running stride. The effort arm measures 7 cm and the load arm measures 4 cm. Calculate the mechanical advantage and state what this tells you about the type of force this lever produces.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct calculation: MA = 7 ÷ 4 = 1.75; 1 mark for correct interpretation: MA > 1 means force is amplified (this lever has a mechanical advantage — the calf muscles can lift the body weight with less effort than the weight itself). Accept: this is a second class lever that favours force production.

knowledge_checks.q: In which class of lever is the EFFORT positioned between the fulcrum and the load?
What does a mechanical advantage of less than 1 tell you about a lever system?
options: The load arm is shorter than the effort arm
The lever amplifies speed and range of movement
The fulcrum is between the load and the effort

During elbow flexion (a bicep curl), the elbow joint acts as the _____ of the lever system.

right: Fulcrum between load and effort

Effort between fulcrum and load

glossary_terms.definition: The pivot point around which a lever rotates; in the body, this is usually a joint.
The resistance that the lever system must move; in the body, this is usually the weight of the body part plus any load being moved.
The force applied to the lever to move the load; in the body, this is the muscular force generated by the contracting muscle.
A lever in which the fulcrum lies between the load and the effort; the most common everyday lever (e.g. a seesaw or a pair of scissors).
A lever in which the load lies between the fulcrum and the effort; generates high mechanical advantage, favouring force production over speed.

human-body-and-movement.title: Planes and Axes of Movement
human-body-and-movement.description: Frontal, transverse and sagittal planes and axes applied to gymnastic and athletic movements.
human-body-and-movement.content_html:
Imagining the Body in Three Dimensions

When a gymnast performs a forward roll, a discus thrower spins in a full circle, or a dancer executes a cartwheel, their body is moving through space in a precise, describable way. Movement analysts use a system of planes and axes to describe exactly which direction that movement occurs and around which line the body rotates. Mastering this system is essential for analysing sport performance.

Imagine the body standing upright in the anatomical position — feet together, palms facing forwards. Now picture three flat sheets of glass slicing through the body, each at right angles to the others. These are the three planes of movement. For every plane there is a matching axis: a rod passing through the body at right angles to that plane, forming the pivot point for rotation.

Key Fact

There are three planes of movement — sagittal, frontal and transverse — each with a matching axis around which rotation occurs. Every body movement can be described using one of these plane-and-axis pairs.

The Sagittal Plane and Transverse Axis

The sagittal plane runs from front to back, dividing the body into a left half and a right half. Movement in this plane involves the body moving forwards or backwards. The matching axis is the transverse axis, which runs from side to side like a rod passing through both hips.

Classic sporting actions in the sagittal plane include a forward somersault (gymnastics or trampolining) and a forward roll. In both cases the body rotates in a forwards direction around the transverse axis. Running also takes place primarily in the sagittal plane, as the arms and legs swing forwards and backwards. A back somersault is also in the sagittal plane, but the rotation is in the opposite direction around the same transverse axis.

A common misconception is that any “big” movement must involve multiple planes. In running, the limbs swing forward and backward — that is purely sagittal-plane motion. A cartwheel, however, takes the body to the side rather than forward: the legs move apart in the frontal plane and the body tips sideways over a sagittal axis. The key question is always “which direction does the body travel, and around which axis does it rotate?” Always answer both before you identify the plane and axis.

The Frontal Plane and Sagittal Axis

The frontal plane runs from side to side, dividing the body into a front half and a back half. Movements in this plane take the body out to the side or bring it back in. The matching axis is the sagittal axis, which runs from front to back like a rod passing through the navel and the spine.

The cartwheel is the clearest sporting example of the frontal plane. The gymnast tips their entire body sideways over their hands, rotating around the sagittal axis. Abduction and adduction movements at the shoulder and hip also occur in the frontal plane — for instance, a star jump (jumping jack) sees the arms and legs moving away from and back to the midline of the body in the frontal plane around the sagittal axis.

The Transverse Plane and Longitudinal Axis

The transverse plane runs horizontally, dividing the body into an upper half and a lower half. Think of it as a table top cutting through the body at waist height. Movements in this plane involve twisting or spinning. The matching axis is the longitudinal axis, which runs from the top of the head straight down through the spine to the feet.

Sporting examples of transverse-plane movement around the longitudinal axis include a 360° twist in ice skating (an ice spin), a discus thrower rotating in a circle before release, and a figure skater pulling in their arms to spin faster. In all of these, the performer is rotating horizontally around a vertical axis running through the middle of their body.

Key Fact

Sagittal plane — transverse axis — forward roll/somersault. Frontal plane — sagittal axis — cartwheel. Transverse plane — longitudinal axis — 360° twist/ice spin. Learn these three triplets as a set.

Applying Planes and Axes to Joint Movements

The plane-and-axis framework also maps directly onto the joint movements covered in the musculoskeletal system. Flexion and extension occur in the sagittal plane around a transverse axis. Abduction and adduction occur in the frontal plane around a sagittal axis. Rotation at the shoulder or hip occurs in the transverse plane around a longitudinal axis. This connection means that when you analyse a sporting action, you can describe both the joint movement and the plane and axis in which it occurs, giving a much richer technical account.

During the pull phase of front crawl swimming, the shoulder moves from a position in front of the body backwards and then past the hip. This is shoulder extension, occurring in the sagittal plane around the transverse axis. The latissimus dorsi is the prime mover (agonist), with the pectorals assisting. The posterior deltoid acts as a stabiliser. When the hand enters the water in front of the body, the shoulder is in flexion (again, sagittal plane, transverse axis) — the anterior deltoid now acts as agonist. This kind of layered analysis — naming the joint, action, plane, axis and muscle — is precisely what high-mark analytical questions reward.

A Summary Table in Words

Rather than relying on a diagram, build the framework in your memory by anchoring each plane to a vivid spatial image. The sagittal plane is like the lens of a camera filming you from the side as you walk forward — you can only see forward-and-back motion. The frontal plane is like filming you from the front — you see side-to-side motion. The transverse plane is like a bird’s-eye view from above — you see spinning or twisting. Each plane’s axis is simply the rod your body spins around when moving in that plane: side-to-side for sagittal-plane movements, front-to-back for frontal-plane movements, and top-to-bottom for transverse-plane movements.
human-body-and-movement.exam_tip_html: Questions on planes and axes typically ask you to “identify the plane and axis of movement” for a named sporting action, or to “describe” the plane and axis used in a given skill. Always give both the plane and the axis — a common error is naming only one. Remember the three sporting triplets: forward roll/somersault (sagittal plane, transverse axis), cartwheel (frontal plane, sagittal axis), ice spin or discus spin (transverse plane, longitudinal axis). On “explain” questions, add one sentence linking the rotation to the direction of movement — for example: “A forward somersault occurs in the sagittal plane because the body rotates forwards and backwards around the transverse axis, which runs from side to side through the hips.” For extended-response questions, connect the plane-and-axis description to the joint action (flexion/extension) and the muscles involved; this is what separates Secure from Mastering answers.
human-body-and-movement.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Three planes divide the body into halves — sagittal (left/right), frontal (front/back) and transverse (upper/lower) — and each has a matching axis at right angles to it.
  • The three classic sporting triplets are: forward somersault (sagittal plane, transverse axis), cartwheel (frontal plane, sagittal axis) and 360° twist/ice spin (transverse plane, longitudinal axis).
  • Joint movements map onto planes: flexion and extension are in the sagittal plane, abduction and adduction in the frontal plane, and rotation in the transverse plane.

practice_questions.text: Identify the plane of movement used during a forward somersault.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: sagittal plane.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'longitudinal axis'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a vertical axis; 1 mark for stating it runs from the top of the head to the feet (or through the spine/centre of the body vertically) and that the body rotates around it during spinning or twisting actions.

practice_questions.text: Describe the plane and axis of movement used when a gymnast performs a cartwheel. Include the direction of movement in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the frontal plane; 1 mark for identifying the sagittal axis; 1 mark for describing the direction of movement as side-to-side (the body tips laterally over the hands, moving away from the midline).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a discus thrower spinning in a full circle before release uses the transverse plane and longitudinal axis rather than any other plane-and-axis combination.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating the movement is a horizontal rotation/spin; 1 mark for identifying the transverse plane (which divides the body into upper and lower halves); 1 mark for identifying the longitudinal axis (which runs vertically from head to feet); 1 mark for explaining that because the thrower rotates around a vertical axis — not forwards/backwards or side-to-side — neither the sagittal nor frontal planes apply.

practice_questions.text: A sports science student is asked to analyse the movement of a figure skater performing a spin entry and a subsequent jump that involves a forward somersault rotation. Analyse how the planes and axes of movement change between the spin and the somersault, and explain how understanding these differences helps a coach improve the athlete's technique.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): clearly identifies the transverse plane and longitudinal axis for the spin, with explanation that the body rotates horizontally around a vertical axis; clearly identifies the sagittal plane and transverse axis for the forward somersault, with explanation that the body rotates forward/backward around a side-to-side axis; analyses what changes between the two movements (from vertical to horizontal rotation, from longitudinal to transverse axis); links both to how coaching cues could reinforce these axes (e.g. a coach teaching the spin would cue the athlete to keep their longitudinal axis straight and centred; for the somersault they would cue tucking to increase rotation speed around the transverse axis). Sustained sporting application throughout.

Secure (3-4 marks): correctly identifies both plane-axis pairs; some explanation of direction of rotation; limited or inconsistent application to coaching.

Developing (2 marks): one plane-axis pair correctly identified; basic description of direction of movement; little or no coaching application.

Emerging (1 mark): one relevant term used (plane or axis) with minimal explanation.

practice_questions.text: A trampoline club coach argues that teaching athletes to understand planes and axes improves technical performance more than simply repeating skills. Evaluate this claim, considering both the benefits of applying planes-and-axes analysis to trampoline coaching and the limitations of this approach for beginner and intermediate performers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9 marks): evaluates benefits of planes-and-axes knowledge for coaching (e.g. understanding the sagittal plane and transverse axis helps a coach identify why a performer's somersault is losing height — they are not tucking to accelerate rotation around the transverse axis; understanding the longitudinal axis helps diagnose twisting technique); evaluates benefits for the athlete (mental model of movement helps self-correct; links plane-and-axis to joint actions covered in anatomy, deepening overall understanding of performance); evaluates limitations (beginners may lack the cognitive capacity to apply abstract spatial concepts during actual performance; practical skill repetition may be more effective in the early stages of learning; analysis can lead to over-thinking and disrupted automatic execution); provides a balanced conclusion (analysis is most valuable in the feedback phase with intermediate to advanced performers; beginners benefit more from demonstration and repetition); consistent sporting examples from trampolining throughout.

Secure (6-7 marks): identifies several benefits and at least one limitation; applies planes-and-axes knowledge to trampolining with reasonable accuracy; some balance in the argument.

Developing (3-5 marks): identifies benefits with limited limitation analysis; partially applied to trampoline context.

Emerging (1-2 marks): one relevant point about planes/axes in sport with minimal evaluation.

human-body-and-movement.title: Health, Fitness and the Components of Fitness
human-body-and-movement.description: Definitions of health and fitness and the ten components needed for sporting performance.
human-body-and-movement.content_html:
Health and Fitness: Not the Same Thing

Most people use the words “healthy” and “fit” interchangeably, but in sports science they have precise, separate definitions. Health is defined as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being — not simply the absence of illness. This definition, taken from the World Health Organization, emphasises that a person can feel ill or stressed and still have no diagnosable disease, meaning their health is compromised even if a doctor would not prescribe anything.

Fitness, in contrast, is defined as the ability to meet the demands of the environment. This means that fitness is specific to purpose: a sprinter needs explosive power and speed; a marathon runner needs cardiovascular endurance and muscular endurance; a goalkeeper needs agility, reaction time and explosive strength. A person who is highly fit for one sport may be relatively unfit for another.

Crucially, health and fitness do not always go together. Someone with a serious injury (poor health) can still maintain cardiovascular fitness through swimming. Equally, an elite athlete may be very fit but show signs of overtraining — sleep disruption, hormonal imbalance, low mood — which are all health issues. Understanding this relationship is essential when evaluating the role exercise plays in an individual’s life.

Key Fact

Health = a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being (not merely the absence of disease). Fitness = the ability to meet the demands of the environment. These are two distinct definitions — learn both precisely.

Decreased fitness because of ill health: a footballer recovering from a knee injury cannot train at full intensity, so their cardiovascular fitness and muscular strength decline even though they are otherwise healthy. Increased fitness despite ill health: a competitive cyclist with a managed long-term condition such as asthma can still train rigorously and maintain high cardiovascular endurance, even though their health is not “complete.” These two scenarios show that fitness and health influence each other but are not the same variable — an important distinction in exam questions.

The Ten Components of Fitness

The specification identifies ten components of fitness. No single sport requires all ten in equal measure, so a key skill is identifying which components are most relevant to a given activity and justifying why. The ten components are:

Agility — the ability to change body position quickly and accurately while moving. Essential in team sports such as rugby, basketball and hockey, where players must dodge opponents and change direction at speed.

Balance — the ability to retain the body’s centre of mass over its base of support. Can be static (holding a handstand) or dynamic (a gymnast on a balance beam). Important in gymnastics, surfing, skiing and judo.

Cardiovascular endurance (also called aerobic power) — the ability of the heart and lungs to supply oxygen to working muscles during sustained exercise. This is the foundation of performance in long-distance running, rowing, cycling, football and many other activities.

Coordination — the ability to use two or more body parts together smoothly and efficiently. Vital in cricket (eye-hand coordination for batting), tennis (eye-hand for racket sports) and swimming (synchronising arms and legs).

Flexibility — the range of movement possible at a joint. Crucial in gymnastics, dance, swimming (stroke efficiency) and martial arts. Poor flexibility can limit performance and increase injury risk.

Muscular endurance — the ability of a muscle to undergo repeated contractions over a long period without tiring. Important in rowing, cycling and long-distance swimming, where the same muscle groups perform thousands of repeated actions.

Power (also called explosive strength or anaerobic power) — the ability to exert maximum force in as short a time as possible; it combines strength and speed. Power is critical in sprinting, shot-put, jumping events and boxing.

Reaction time — the time taken to initiate a response to a stimulus. A sprinter reacting to the starting gun, a goalkeeper responding to a shot, and a batsman reading a delivery all depend on a fast reaction time.

Strength — the maximum force a muscle or muscle group can exert in a single effort. The specification identifies four types: maximal strength (the greatest force in a single effort), static strength (force exerted against an immovable object), dynamic strength (force produced through a full range of movement repeatedly) and explosive strength (maximum force in the shortest time, which overlaps with power).

Speed — the maximum rate at which an individual is able to perform a movement or cover a distance in a period of time. Speed is relevant not just in sprinting but in any sport where rapid movement is an advantage — a winger in football breaking past a defender, for example.

Key Fact

The ten components: agility, balance, cardiovascular endurance, coordination, flexibility, muscular endurance, power, reaction time, strength, speed. Questions often ask you to select components and justify their importance for a specific sport — always name the component AND give a sporting reason.

A 100m sprinter needs: (1) reaction time — to leave the blocks the instant the starter’s pistol fires, reducing overall race time; (2) power — to accelerate explosively from the blocks during the drive phase; (3) speed — to maintain maximum velocity during the top-speed phase; and (4) muscular endurance — to sustain near-maximal effort for the full 10–12 seconds before significant lactic acid accumulation. Cardiovascular endurance is less important than in a marathon because the race duration is too short for the aerobic system to be the limiting factor. In the exam, always justify why the component matters for that specific sport — not just list its name.
human-body-and-movement.exam_tip_html: On questions asking you to “define” health or fitness, quote the specification definitions precisely — “complete physical, mental and social well-being” for health, and “ability to meet the demands of the environment” for fitness. Both words are needed for full marks on a definition question. On “explain” or “analyse” questions about components, you must name the component AND justify its relevance with a sporting example. Simply listing components without explanation is a very common error that loses marks. If asked to justify which components are most important for a sport, avoid saying “all components are important” — the question is asking you to discriminate and prioritise with reasons.
human-body-and-movement.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Health is complete physical, mental and social well-being; fitness is the ability to meet the demands of the environment — these are separate concepts and a person can be fit but unhealthy, or healthy but unfit.
  • There are ten components of fitness: agility, balance, cardiovascular endurance, coordination, flexibility, muscular endurance, power, reaction time, strength and speed.
  • Different sports require different combinations of fitness components; exam questions always require you to name a component and justify its relevance with a specific sporting example.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the correct definition of fitness?
A) A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being
B) The ability to meet the demands of the environment
C) The absence of disease or infirmity
D) The ability to perform aerobic exercise for long periods
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: B — the ability to meet the demands of the environment.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'cardiovascular endurance'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as the ability of the heart and lungs (cardio-respiratory system) to supply oxygen; 1 mark for stating this is during sustained/prolonged exercise (to working muscles).

practice_questions.text: Describe why a rugby union forward needs both strength and cardiovascular endurance to perform effectively.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for describing strength as needed for scrummaging/tackling/carrying the ball through contact (max force against opposition); 1 mark for describing cardiovascular endurance as needed to sustain effort across an 80-minute match (heart and lungs supplying oxygen to working muscles); 1 mark for describing how the demands switch between high-intensity bursts (strength/power) and sustained running phases (cardiovascular endurance) in a single game.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a gymnast competing on the balance beam requires balance and flexibility as two of their most important fitness components.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining balance: the gymnast must maintain their centre of mass over a 10cm-wide beam throughout routines — without static and dynamic balance, they would fall; 1 mark for explaining flexibility: the range of movement at joints must be extreme to perform splits, walkovers and leaps to the required technical standard; 1 mark for applying balance to a named movement (e.g. holding a scale on one leg requires static balance); 1 mark for applying flexibility to a named movement (e.g. a backbend walkover demands extreme spinal and hip flexibility to complete safely).

practice_questions.text: A county-level badminton player wants to improve their game. Analyse which three components of fitness are most important for elite badminton performance and explain how developing each would improve their results.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): identifies three appropriate components (e.g. agility, reaction time, coordination, muscular endurance) with a precise definition or understanding of each; for each component, provides a specific analysis of how it influences badminton performance (e.g. agility allows rapid direction changes to reach shots in the back-court corners; reaction time determines how quickly the player responds to a smash; coordination ensures the racket meets the shuttlecock cleanly); explains how developing each would improve results with sporting specificity; sustained analytical writing rather than bullet-listing.

Secure (3-4 marks): identifies three appropriate components with generally accurate descriptions; some application to badminton; explanation of development benefits present but may lack depth.

Developing (2 marks): identifies two appropriate components; limited application to badminton; development link present for at least one.

Emerging (1 mark): names one relevant component with minimal explanation.

practice_questions.text: A physical education teacher claims that a person must be both healthy and fit to achieve their best sporting performance. Evaluate this claim, using examples from sport to consider whether health and fitness are equally important, and whether it is possible to perform well when one is present but the other is not.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9 marks): clearly defines both health (complete physical, mental and social well-being) and fitness (ability to meet the demands of the environment) and treats them as separate variables; evaluates the claim in favour (high-level sport demands both — a footballer with an anxiety disorder affecting sleep and concentration may find their decision-making and reaction time impaired even if their cardiovascular fitness is excellent; an injured sprinter whose physical health is compromised cannot train specifically and therefore fitness declines); evaluates against the claim (elite athletes regularly perform at very high levels while managing chronic conditions that affect their health — e.g. athletes with managed asthma or diabetes who maintain world-class fitness; a performer may experience poor mental health but still maintain physical fitness through regular training); considers the relationship between them (poor health often leads to decreased fitness through an inability to train; high fitness can coexist with some health impairment); a balanced conclusion with examples from named sports or specific contexts; consistent sporting application throughout.

Secure (6-7 marks): defines health and fitness; covers both sides of the argument with sporting examples; some balance; generally accurate.

Developing (3-5 marks): distinguishes health from fitness; one-sided argument or limited examples.

Emerging (1-2 marks): basic reference to health or fitness with minimal evaluation.

human-body-and-movement.title: Fitness Testing: Procedures and Validity
human-body-and-movement.description: Standard fitness tests, what they measure, and why test data has real limitations for sport.
human-body-and-movement.content_html:
Why We Test Fitness

Fitness testing gives coaches and athletes a window into an individual’s current physical condition. Without measurement, training decisions rely on guesswork. With structured testing, a coach can identify which components of fitness are strengths and which need attention, set a baseline from which improvement is tracked, compare results against national norms, and motivate athletes by giving them concrete targets.

The specification identifies six reasons for conducting fitness tests: to identify strengths and weaknesses in performance or a training programme; to monitor improvement over time; to show a starting level of fitness; to inform training requirements; to compare against norms of a group or national averages; and to motivate athletes and help them set realistic goals. A seventh reason is to provide variety in a training programme, as testing sessions can break up routine and maintain engagement.

Key Fact

Seven reasons for fitness testing: (1) identify strengths/weaknesses, (2) monitor improvement, (3) establish a baseline, (4) inform training needs, (5) compare to norms, (6) motivate/set goals, (7) provide variety. In a question, give the reason and a brief example to show you understand it.

The Standard Tests and Their Procedures

For each component of fitness there is a named standard test. You must know the component it measures, the equipment needed and the basic procedure.

Illinois Agility Test — measures agility. The performer lies face down at the start. On a signal they sprint to a set of cones arranged in a specific pattern, weaving in and out, before sprinting back. Time is recorded in seconds. A shorter time means better agility.

Stork Stand Test — measures balance. The performer stands on their dominant leg, places the non-dominant foot against the inside of the dominant knee and raises the heel. They hold this position for as long as possible with eyes open. Time in seconds is recorded.

Multi-Stage Fitness Test (bleep test) — measures cardiovascular endurance. The performer runs back and forth between two lines 20 metres apart in time with an audio signal (bleep). The signal speeds up progressively. The level reached when the performer fails to reach the line twice in a row is their score.

Wall Toss Test — measures coordination. The performer stands at a set distance from a wall and throws a ball with one hand at the wall, catching it with the opposite hand. The number of successful catches in 30 seconds is the score.

Sit and Reach Test — measures flexibility. The performer sits on the floor with legs straight, feet flat against a box with a measuring scale. They reach forward as far as possible and hold the position; the distance reached (in cm) is recorded. A greater distance indicates greater flexibility.

Vertical Jump Test — measures power (explosive strength). The performer stands next to a wall, reaches as high as possible to mark a standing-reach height, then jumps and marks the highest point reached. The difference between the two marks (in cm) is the score.

Ruler Drop Test — measures reaction time. A ruler is held by a partner at 0 cm and the performer places their dominant hand around the ruler without touching it. When the ruler is released without warning, the performer catches it as quickly as possible. The distance the ruler falls before it is caught indicates reaction time — a shorter drop = faster reaction time.

30 Metre Sprint Test — measures speed. The performer sprints 30 metres from a standing start. Time in seconds is recorded using a stopwatch or timing gate. Shorter time = greater speed.

Handgrip Dynamometer Test — measures strength. The performer squeezes a handgrip dynamometer as hard as possible (dominant hand), holding for 5 seconds. The force recorded in kilograms (kg) is the score. Three trials are typically taken and the highest is used.

The Sit-Up Bleep Test measures muscular endurance, and the One Rep Max Test measures maximal strength: the performer performs one maximal lift of a specific exercise (e.g. bench press or squat) — the heaviest weight lifted with correct technique is the score.

Key Fact

Test names by component: agility → Illinois Agility Test; balance → Stork Stand; cardiovascular endurance → Multi-Stage Fitness Test; coordination → Wall Toss; flexibility → Sit and Reach; power → Vertical Jump; reaction time → Ruler Drop; speed → 30 Metre Sprint; strength → Handgrip Dynamometer or One Rep Max.

Quantitative and Qualitative Data

Fitness test results are mostly quantitative data — numbers such as time in seconds, distance in centimetres, or force in kilograms. This numerical data can be compared against national norm tables to see whether a performer is “excellent”, “above average”, “average”, “below average” or “poor” for their age and sex. Qualitative data deals with descriptions rather than numbers — for example, a coach observing that a player “looks sluggish in the second half” is collecting qualitative data.

Fitness tests are a useful guide but have significant limitations. First, most are not sport-specific: the Illinois Agility Test measures agility in a straight-line cone pattern — it does not replicate the unpredictable direction changes of a football match. Second, tests do not replicate competitive conditions: a laboratory Multi-Stage Fitness Test does not replicate the decision-making, adrenaline and contact of a real game. Third, many tests are sub-maximal, meaning the performer is not pushed to their true maximum, so results may under-represent actual capacity. Fourth, motivation affects results: a performer who is uninterested may not try fully on a Ruler Drop or Stork Stand. Fifth, some tests require careful protocol to be valid — the Sit and Reach result is meaningless if the performer has not warmed up their hamstrings first. These limitations must be acknowledged when drawing conclusions from test data.

Validity refers to whether a test actually measures the component it claims to measure. The Ruler Drop Test is valid for reaction time because catching a falling ruler directly requires a fast neural response. However, it may have lower validity for sports that require reactive movements of the whole body (e.g. a goalkeeper’s dive). Reliability refers to consistency: if the same test is repeated under the same conditions, does it produce the same result? To improve reliability, standardise the conditions — same time of day, same warm-up, same equipment, same instructions — and take multiple trials.
human-body-and-movement.exam_tip_html: On “interpret data” questions, students commonly copy numbers from the table without commenting on what they mean. Always: (1) make a comparison between two values, (2) quote the specific figure, and (3) explain what it tells you about the performer’s fitness. For example: “The performer improved their Multi-Stage Fitness Test score from level 8.4 to level 10.2 over six weeks, suggesting a significant increase in cardiovascular endurance.” On “analyse” or “evaluate” questions about fitness testing, do not just list limitations — explain how each limitation affects the usefulness of the data for a specific sport or performer.
human-body-and-movement.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Each of the ten components of fitness has a named standard test; knowing the component measured and the basic procedure for each test is essential.
  • Fitness test data is mostly quantitative and can be compared against national norms, but tests have real limitations: they are often not sport-specific, do not replicate competitive conditions, and results can be affected by motivation and incorrect protocol.
  • Validity means the test measures what it claims to; reliability means results are consistent when the test is repeated under the same conditions.

practice_questions.text: Identify the fitness test used to measure cardiovascular endurance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: the Multi-Stage Fitness Test (accept: bleep test or 20-metre shuttle run test).

practice_questions.text: State two limitations of using fitness tests to assess a performer's ability in their sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two distinct limitations from: tests are not sport-specific / do not replicate movements of the activity / do not replicate competitive conditions / many are sub-maximal (therefore may be inaccurate) / motivation of participant affects results / incorrect procedures reduce validity. Two near-identical answers (e.g. 'not sport-specific' and 'doesn't replicate the sport') score only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the Ruler Drop Test is conducted and what the score indicates about a performer's fitness.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for describing the set-up (partner holds ruler at the 0 cm end; performer places dominant hand around but not touching the ruler); 1 mark for describing the procedure (ruler is dropped without warning; performer catches it as quickly as possible); 1 mark for explaining the scoring (the distance in cm the ruler falls before being caught indicates reaction time — a shorter distance indicates a faster reaction time).

practice_questions.text: Table 1 shows fitness test results for two 16-year-old county-level athletes before and after a 10-week training block. Athlete A: Illinois Agility Test — before 15.8 s, after 14.2 s. Athlete B: Illinois Agility Test — before 16.1 s, after 15.9 s. Using the data, interpret what the results suggest about the effectiveness of training for each athlete.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for comparing Athlete A's before and after scores (improved by 1.6 seconds); 1 mark for making an inference about Athlete A (training was effective / meaningful improvement in agility); 1 mark for comparing Athlete B's before and after scores (improved by only 0.2 seconds, a marginal change); 1 mark for making a contrasting inference about Athlete B (training had little effect on agility / improvement is negligible and may be within measurement error). Note: accept any valid reference to the figures quoted from the table.

practice_questions.text: A school physical education teacher wants to set up a fitness testing programme for her Year 10 GCSE class. She plans to use the Multi-Stage Fitness Test, the Illinois Agility Test and the Sit and Reach Test. Analyse the benefits and limitations of using this selection of tests to assess the overall fitness of her students.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): identifies and explains genuine benefits for at least two of the three tests (e.g. Multi-Stage Fitness Test provides quantitative cardiovascular endurance data that can be compared to national norms, motivating students with a clear score; Illinois Agility Test is practical in a school setting with minimal equipment; Sit and Reach requires only a box and gives a quick flexibility benchmark); identifies specific limitations for at least two tests (e.g. Illinois test does not replicate sport-specific agility patterns in team games; Sit and Reach reliability is affected by hamstring warm-up and whether students fully extend; Multi-Stage Fitness Test requires motivation to reach maximum level); considers the overall coverage (three tests only cover cardiovascular endurance, agility and flexibility — components like strength, power and reaction time are not assessed); sustained analytical discussion with specific reference to the tests and their sporting relevance.

Secure (3-4 marks): identifies benefits and limitations for most tests; some analysis of what the selection does or doesn't cover; generally accurate.

Developing (2 marks): identifies one benefit and one limitation; limited analysis of coverage.

Emerging (1 mark): one relevant point about a test with minimal development.

practice_questions.text: A sports coach argues that fitness testing should form a central part of every athlete's training programme throughout the year, not just at the start of a season. Evaluate this claim, considering the benefits of regular fitness testing and the potential drawbacks of using it too frequently or in inappropriate contexts.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9 marks): evaluates benefits of regular testing (monitors improvement over time and allows training adjustments; motivates athletes by showing progress; identifies when fitness is declining so reversibility can be addressed; provides data to compare against national norms and set goals); evaluates drawbacks of frequent testing (time taken away from actual training; testing fatigue if done too often; results can be demotivating if improvement plateaus; many tests are not sport-specific so results do not directly translate to competitive performance); evaluates context and timing (testing most appropriate at start and end of training blocks; during competition season, maintaining performance is the priority and repeated testing may disrupt preparation); provides a balanced conclusion (regular testing has value when spaced appropriately and limitations are understood; blind reliance on test scores without contextualising them is a mistake); consistent sporting examples throughout.

Secure (6-7 marks): identifies benefits and drawbacks with sporting examples; some consideration of context or timing; generally balanced.

Developing (3-5 marks): some benefits and at least one drawback; limited sporting application.

Emerging (1-2 marks): one relevant point about fitness testing with minimal evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which fitness test measures power (explosive strength)?
What does 'validity' mean in the context of fitness testing?
options: Whether the test produces consistent results each time
Whether the test accurately measures what it claims to measure
Whether the test is completed safely

human-body-and-movement.title: Principles of Training: SPORT and FITT
human-body-and-movement.description: Specificity, progressive overload, reversibility, tedium and the FITT principles applied to programmes.
human-body-and-movement.content_html:
Why Principles Matter

Elite athletes do not train randomly. Their programmes are built on scientific principles that ensure each session causes the right adaptations without injury, boredom or wasted effort. Two frameworks summarise these principles: SPORT (Specificity, Progressive Overload, Reversibility, Tedium) and FITT (Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type). Together they provide a blueprint for designing any training programme, from a beginner’s fitness plan to an international athlete’s competition preparation.

SPORT: The Four Principles

Specificity — training must be designed to match the specific demands of the sport and the individual. A sprinter must train the fast-twitch muscle fibres and anaerobic energy systems used in a 100m race; continuous low-intensity jogging would not develop the right adaptations. A swimmer should train in the water to develop sport-specific cardiovascular and muscular endurance rather than only running. If the training is not specific to the sport, the gains will not transfer to performance.

Progressive overload — the body adapts to the demands placed upon it. Once it has adapted, the same training stimulus produces no further improvement. To keep progressing, the training load must be gradually and continuously increased — using the FITT variables. A weight trainer who always lifts the same weight will plateau; they must add weight, more sets or more repetitions to continue building strength. The progression must be gradual: too-rapid increases lead to injury.

Reversibility — fitness adaptations are not permanent. When training stops or is significantly reduced — due to injury, illness or a long break — the body returns towards its pre-training state. Cardiovascular adaptations (such as a lower resting heart rate and larger stroke volume) reverse relatively quickly, often within a few weeks. Muscle mass is lost more slowly. This principle underlines why consistent, year-round training is more effective than intense bursts followed by long rest periods.

Tedium — if a training programme is repetitive and boring, motivation will decline and the performer may train at lower intensity or drop out altogether. Introducing variety — different training methods, different environments, different partners, mixed session structures — maintains psychological engagement and ensures the performer continues to train at the required intensity. This is sometimes written as “avoiding tedium” in the spec.

Key Fact

SPORT: Specificity (match training to sport demands), Progressive Overload (gradually increase load to keep adapting), Reversibility (gains are lost if you stop training), Tedium (vary training to avoid boredom). Note: the spec uses “Tedium” — not “Thresholds” or “Time”.

SPORT and FITT are complementary but distinct. SPORT gives the overarching principles — the “why” and “what” of training design (should training be specific? yes; should load progress? yes). FITT gives the four variables you can actually manipulate to achieve those principles — the “how.” For example, applying progressive overload (a SPORT principle) is achieved by increasing frequency, intensity or time (all FITT variables). Understanding this relationship is often tested in the exam through questions asking you to “apply the FITT principles to achieve progressive overload for a specific athlete”.

FITT: The Four Training Variables

Frequency — how often a person trains per week. A beginner might train twice a week to allow full recovery; an elite endurance athlete may train twice a day. Frequency must be balanced against recovery: too many sessions without rest leads to overtraining and injury, too few limits adaptation.

Intensity — how hard the training is. Intensity can be expressed as a percentage of maximum heart rate (for cardiovascular training), a percentage of one rep max (for weight training), or by effort level or speed. Training zones and thresholds relate directly to intensity: the aerobic training zone is 60–80% of maximum heart rate; the anaerobic zone is 80–90%. Choosing the right intensity ensures the correct energy system is stressed.

Time — the duration of a training session or individual exercise bout. A continuous run lasting 30 minutes will primarily stress the aerobic system; interval sprint sessions of 10 seconds each stress the anaerobic system. For flexibility, a static stretch should be held for up to 30 seconds.

Type — the method of training used. Type must align with the principle of specificity: a long-distance runner should use continuous training; a boxer should use circuit training with punching drills and HIIT; a gymnast needing flexibility should use static stretching sessions. Choosing the wrong type of training may improve a general component of fitness without translating to sport-specific performance gains.

Key Fact

FITT: Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard — linked to training zones and heart rate %), Time (how long), Type (which training method). All four can be increased to apply progressive overload. Intensity links directly to training thresholds (aerobic 60–80% max HR; anaerobic 80–90% max HR).

A county-level 400m freestyle swimmer applies the principles as follows. Specificity: all endurance sessions are in the pool using freestyle technique, not on a running track. Progressive overload: over 12 weeks the swimmer increases weekly distance by 10% and gradually shortens rest intervals between repetitions. Reversibility: during the off-season the swimmer maintains 50% of their training volume with twice-weekly pool sessions so that cardiovascular adaptations are not lost. Tedium: sessions alternate between long continuous swims, interval sets, technique drills and open-water training to maintain motivation. For FITT: frequency moves from 4 to 6 sessions per week over the training block; intensity is set at 70% of max HR for aerobic sets and 85% for lactate-threshold sets; time per session increases from 60 to 90 minutes; type rotates between continuous, fartlek and interval training in the pool.

Applying SPORT and FITT Together

The most effective training programmes use both frameworks simultaneously. Specificity determines the training type; progressive overload is achieved by manipulating frequency, intensity and time over weeks and months; reversibility reminds the coach to maintain a training stimulus during breaks; and tedium reminds the programme designer to vary the type of session. When a student is asked to “design a training programme” or “evaluate the effectiveness of a training plan”, they should check whether all four SPORT principles and all four FITT variables are appropriately applied.
human-body-and-movement.exam_tip_html: On a “9-mark Evaluate” question about training principles or a training programme, the most common error is writing a one-sided answer: listing only benefits or only limitations. Mark schemes reward a balanced argument with sporting examples on both sides. Structure your answer: state the principle and its benefit for performance, then consider a limitation or a sport where the principle is harder to apply, and link each point to a named sport or athlete scenario. For shorter “define” or “describe” questions, precision matters: “progressive overload” must include the idea that the training load is gradually increased over time, not just that you train harder — one-word answers lose the second mark. Also check: the spec uses “Tedium” as the fourth SPORT principle, not “Thresholds” — this is a common confusion.
human-body-and-movement.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • SPORT stands for Specificity, Progressive Overload, Reversibility and Tedium — these are the overarching principles that should underpin any training programme.
  • FITT stands for Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type — these are the four variables that can be adjusted to implement progressive overload and ensure specificity.
  • SPORT and FITT work together: SPORT explains why changes should be made; FITT explains how to make them in practice.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the FITT principles can be applied to help a club-level tennis player improve their cardiovascular endurance during pre-season.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark each for applying any three of the four FITT variables to the scenario with specific detail. Frequency example: train 4 times a week rather than twice, as cardiovascular gains require more sessions. Intensity example: set sessions at 70-80% of maximum heart rate to work in the aerobic training zone. Time example: sessions of 45-60 minutes to ensure sustained aerobic demand. Type example: use continuous training (e.g. cycling, running on court) to develop cardiovascular endurance specifically. Each answer must include the variable name and a specific application.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a coach can use the principle of specificity when designing a training programme for a 400m track cyclist.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining specificity (training must match the demands of the sport/activity); 1 mark for explaining the specific energy system demands of 400m track cycling (high-intensity anaerobic effort over approximately 40-50 seconds, with significant lactic acid production); 1 mark for explaining how training type should reflect this (interval training or HIIT on the bike, not long-distance continuous running); 1 mark for explaining how muscle specificity applies (training the quadriceps, gluteals and hip flexors through cycling-specific movements rather than gym exercises that do not replicate the cycling action).

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old club-level distance runner has been following the same 10km running programme for three months with no improvement in race times. Analyse how the SPORT and FITT principles could be used to redesign the programme so that it leads to further performance improvements.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): identifies that the lack of improvement is explained by the principle of progressive overload — the body has adapted to the current stimulus; applies at least three FITT variables specifically (e.g. increase frequency from 3 to 5 sessions per week; increase intensity by introducing 80-85% max HR threshold runs; increase time of long runs by 10% per week); identifies specificity as supporting continued running-based sessions rather than switching to a different sport; raises reversibility to advise against abrupt rest periods; avoids tedium by introducing fartlek training alongside continuous sessions; provides a coherent analysis of how these changes would lead to further cardiovascular and muscular endurance adaptation. Sporting context maintained throughout.

Secure (3-4 marks): identifies progressive overload as the issue; applies two or more FITT variables with some specificity; some reference to sport context.

Developing (2 marks): identifies that training needs to be harder or more varied; limited use of SPORT/FITT terminology.

Emerging (1 mark): one relevant principle mentioned with minimal development.

practice_questions.text: A school sports coach is designing an annual training programme for a Year 11 football squad. Evaluate how effectively the SPORT principles can be applied to team sport training compared to individual sport training, considering both the benefits and the challenges for a football coach.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9 marks): evaluates each SPORT principle with a two-sided argument. Specificity: in individual sports (e.g. marathon running) specificity is straightforward — one performer, one event; in football, specificity is harder because different positions require different fitness profiles (a goalkeeper needs different components from a midfielder), so a whole-squad programme may not be fully specific for every player. Progressive overload: easy to apply individually; harder in team training because players start from different fitness baselines — a blanket 10% increase in session intensity may overload some players while under-loading others. Reversibility: applies equally to both; coaches of both individual and team sport must plan for off-season maintenance. Tedium: team sport naturally provides variety through small-sided games, drills and positional training; individual sport coaches must work harder to introduce variety. Evaluates the overall effectiveness (SPORT principles work well in team sport but require differentiation and group management strategies that individual sport coaches do not face). Balanced argument, naming specific football examples and contrasting with individual sport examples throughout.

Secure (6-7 marks): all four SPORT principles covered with some two-sided argument; mostly applied to football with some comparison to individual sport; generally accurate.

Developing (3-5 marks): at least two SPORT principles covered; limited balance; some sporting application.

Emerging (1-2 marks): basic reference to one or two principles with minimal analysis.
