human-body-and-movement.title: Methods of Training
human-body-and-movement.description: Seven training methods matched to fitness aims, with work:rest ratios explained.
human-body-and-movement.content_html:
Why Choose the Right Training Method?

Not all training is created equal. A marathon runner who only does heavy weight training will not improve her aerobic endurance; a sprinter who only plods along at a slow jog will never develop the explosive power he needs off the blocks. Training must be specific to the demands of the sport — this is the principle of specificity in action. Choosing the correct training method is therefore the first and most important decision a coach or athlete makes when designing a programme.

Continuous Training

Continuous training involves exercising at a steady pace for a minimum of 20 minutes without any rest breaks. Activities such as running, cycling, swimming and rowing are all commonly used. Because the intensity remains constant and the body has a continuous oxygen supply, continuous training primarily develops cardiovascular endurance. It is well suited to distance runners, rowers and cyclists.

The main advantage is that it is simple, low-cost and easy to monitor — a runner simply keeps going at a steady pace within their aerobic training zone (60–80% of maximum heart rate). A disadvantage is that it can become repetitive and may not replicate the varied demands of team sports, which involve bursts of speed interspersed with periods of lower intensity.

Fartlek Training

Fartlek training takes its name from the Swedish for “speed play”. Unlike standard continuous training, fartlek deliberately mixes periods of higher intensity effort with periods of slower recovery running, all without stopping. A footballer might jog steadily for two minutes, then sprint for 30 seconds, then stride at half-pace for a minute, then repeat. Because the performer decides when to change pace, it replicates the unpredictable demands of many team sports.

Key Fact

Fartlek means “speed play” in Swedish. It varies speed and terrain continuously, making it ideal for team-sport athletes whose games combine aerobic and anaerobic demands — such as footballers, rugby players and hockey players.

Interval Training and HIIT

Interval training uses a planned work:rest ratio — a set period of hard effort followed by a set period of rest or low-intensity recovery. The athlete repeats this pattern for a fixed number of sets. For example, a 400 m track athlete might run 200 m at race pace, rest for 90 seconds, and repeat six times. By controlling the work:rest ratio, the coach can target either aerobic or anaerobic systems: longer work periods with short rests challenge the aerobic system, while very short, maximal sprints with longer rests target the anaerobic system.

High-intensity interval training (HIIT) is a specific form of interval training where the work periods are performed at near-maximal intensity (typically above 80% of maximum heart rate, within the anaerobic training zone) and rest periods are short. A typical HIIT session might involve 20 seconds of all-out effort followed by 10 seconds of rest, repeated eight times (the Tabata protocol). HIIT is time-efficient and produces improvements in both aerobic capacity and anaerobic power, making it popular with athletes who are pressed for time.

Many students assume interval training is always anaerobic because of the repeated high-intensity efforts. In fact, the energy system targeted depends entirely on the work:rest ratio and intensity. A 3-minute effort at 65% maximum heart rate, with 1 minute of walking recovery, repeated five times, is aerobic interval training. Anaerobic interval training requires efforts above 80% of maximum heart rate with longer recovery periods. Always identify the intensity and duration to justify which energy system is being stressed — this is exactly the justification examiners look for.

Circuit Training

Circuit training involves moving around a series of stations, performing a specific exercise at each one before moving on to the next. A coach designing a circuit must consider: the space and equipment available, the number of stations, the work:rest ratio at each station, and the type of exercise at each station. The beauty of circuit training is its flexibility — by changing the exercises, the number of stations, the time at each station and the rest periods, the same circuit format can be adapted to develop cardiovascular endurance, muscular endurance, strength or power.

For example, a muscular endurance circuit might include press-ups, sit-ups, squat jumps, tricep dips and step-ups, each performed for 45 seconds with 15 seconds to move to the next station. To make the same circuit develop strength instead, the coach would add resistance (using dumbbells or weighted vests), reduce the repetitions per station and increase the rest periods.

Weight Training

Weight training uses free weights, machines or bodyweight exercises with added resistance to develop muscular strength, power or muscular endurance. The fitness aim determines the weight and repetitions used. For strength and power, athletes use a high weight (above 70% of one rep max) and a low number of repetitions — approximately three sets of four to eight repetitions. For muscular endurance, athletes use a lower weight (below 70% of one rep max) with a high number of repetitions — approximately three sets of 12 to 15 repetitions.

Safe practice is non-negotiable: correct lifting technique prevents injury, appropriate weight selection avoids overloading, and a spotter should be present when performing heavy lifts such as the bench press or squat. The back should remain straight during deadlifts and squats to protect the lumbar vertebrae.

Key Fact

Strength/power training: above 70% of one rep max, approximately 3 sets of 4–8 reps. Muscular endurance training: below 70% of one rep max, approximately 3 sets of 12–15 reps. The fitness aim determines the weight and rep range.

Plyometric Training

Plyometric training develops explosive power. The physiological basis is the stretch-shortening cycle: the muscle first undergoes a rapid eccentric (lengthening) contraction as the athlete lands or prepares, storing elastic energy in the muscle and tendon; this is immediately followed by a powerful concentric (shortening) contraction as the athlete jumps, bounds or throws. The faster the transition between these two phases, the greater the power output. Exercises include bounding, depth jumping, box jumps and medicine-ball throws. Plyometrics is well suited to sprinters, high jumpers, basketball players and volleyball players — any athlete who needs explosive leg or upper-body power.

Static Stretching

Static stretching involves slowly lengthening a muscle to the point of mild discomfort and holding the position for up to 30 seconds. Because the muscle is held in an isometric contraction (no movement, no change in length), this method is categorised as isometric in nature. Static stretching improves flexibility by gradually lengthening the muscle fibres and their surrounding connective tissue over time. It is advisable to avoid bouncing during stretches (ballistic stretching), as this activates the stretch reflex and risks muscle strains. Static stretching is most effective as part of a cool-down rather than immediately before explosive exercise.

Consider a county-level basketball player with a 10-week pre-season. Her coach wants to improve cardiovascular endurance, muscular power and flexibility. An appropriate programme might combine: (1) fartlek training twice a week to mirror the stop-start aerobic and anaerobic demands of a basketball game; (2) plyometric training twice a week (depth jumps and bounding) to improve explosive jumping power for rebounds and lay-ups; (3) static stretching at the end of each session to improve hip and hamstring flexibility, reducing injury risk. Continuous training alone would be insufficient because it would not develop the anaerobic power the sport demands.
human-body-and-movement.exam_tip_html: On a 9-mark ‘Evaluate’ question about training methods, the most common error is producing a one-sided answer — for example, only listing advantages of a method without weighing its disadvantages or comparing it to an alternative. Examiners reward a balanced argument: present the benefits with a sporting example, then consider the limitations or when another method might be more appropriate. Use a “For X… However Y…” structure throughout and anchor every point to a named sport or named athlete type. For 2-mark ‘State Two’ questions, make sure your two answers are genuinely different — saying “it improves aerobic fitness” and “it improves cardiovascular endurance” is the same point and will only earn one mark.
human-body-and-movement.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Each training method has a primary fitness focus: continuous and fartlek develop cardiovascular endurance; interval and HIIT target aerobic and anaerobic capacity depending on the work:rest ratio; weight training develops strength or muscular endurance depending on the load and rep range; plyometrics develops explosive power; static stretching improves flexibility.
  • The work:rest ratio is the key variable in interval and circuit training — shorter rests and longer work periods stress the aerobic system, while shorter work periods at maximal intensity with longer rests stress the anaerobic system.
  • Training must always be matched to the demands of the sport (specificity) and the fitness aim of the athlete. Evaluating a method means weighing its advantages and disadvantages in the context of a specific sport and performer.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes HIIT?
A) Sustained exercise at a constant pace for at least 20 minutes
B) Short bursts of near-maximal effort alternated with brief rest periods
C) Moving around a series of exercise stations with different fitness aims
D) Stretching a muscle and holding the position for up to 30 seconds
practice_questions.marks: B) Short bursts of near-maximal effort alternated with brief rest periods [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of circuit training compared to continuous training.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each of two distinct advantages, for example:
- It can target multiple components of fitness in one session (1)
- It can be adapted by changing stations, rest periods or resistance (1)
- It can replicate movements specific to a sport (1)
- It provides variety, reducing tedium (1)
Note: responses must be qualitatively different to earn both marks. 'It improves fitness' and 'it makes you fitter' count as the same point.

practice_questions.text: Describe how plyometric training develops muscular power.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
- The muscle undergoes a rapid eccentric (lengthening) contraction first (1)
- Elastic energy is stored in the muscle and tendon during this phase (1)
- This is immediately followed by a powerful concentric (shortening) contraction (1)
- The rapid transition between phases (the stretch-shortening cycle) produces a greater power output than a concentric contraction alone (1)
Any three of the above points, clearly described. Credit 'eccentric then concentric' and 'stretch-shortening cycle' as trigger phrases.

practice_questions.text: Explain why fartlek training is more appropriate for a football player than continuous training.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks:
- Fartlek varies speed and intensity throughout the session, including bursts of high-intensity effort (1)
- This mirrors the intermittent demands of football, where players alternate between jogging, sprinting and walking (1)
- Continuous training maintains a steady pace and develops aerobic endurance only (1)
- Football requires both aerobic and anaerobic capacity, and fartlek training stresses both energy systems (1)
Full credit requires both an explanation of what fartlek does AND why this is more appropriate for football than continuous training.

practice_questions.text:
A 17-year-old club-level long jumper wants to increase her explosive leg power over a 12-week training block.

Evaluate the use of plyometric training and weight training as methods she could use to achieve this goal.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9 marks): A balanced evaluation of both methods. Identifies advantages and disadvantages of each, consistently applies them to a long jumper's specific needs (take-off power, sprint speed, injury risk), and reaches a justified conclusion about which method or combination is most appropriate. Uses accurate terminology throughout (eccentric/concentric, one rep max, stretch-shortening cycle, sets/reps).

Secure (5-7 marks): Discusses both methods with some application to the long jump. Advantages and disadvantages present for at least one method. Some sporting application but may be inconsistent. Generally accurate terminology.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points about one or both methods but limited development. May only list advantages without considering limitations, or may apply the points to sport only superficially.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic identification of one method's feature. Little or no application to a specific sporting context. Descriptive rather than evaluative.

practice_questions.text: A sprint coach is designing an interval training session for a 100 m sprinter. Explain how the work:rest ratio should be set to ensure the anaerobic energy system is targeted, and why this is important for the sprinter's performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks:
- The work period should be short and at maximal intensity (above 80% max HR / all-out sprint) (1)
- The rest period should be longer than the work period to allow ATP-PCr and anaerobic stores to partially recover (1)
- For example, a 10-second maximal sprint followed by 50–60 seconds of rest would target the ATP-PCr (anaerobic) system (1)
- This is important because a 100 m sprint is entirely anaerobic — the race lasts under 12 seconds and the intensity is too high for aerobic respiration to meet the energy demand (1)

human-body-and-movement.title: Optimising Training and Preventing Injury
human-body-and-movement.description: Heart rate zones, one rep max, altitude training, training seasons and injury prevention.
human-body-and-movement.content_html:
Making Every Session Count

Training harder is not always the same as training smarter. A swimmer who pushes too hard every day risks injury and burnout; one who never challenges the aerobic system will plateau. Optimising training means identifying the right intensity, at the right time of year, with the right safeguards in place. The tools for doing this — heart rate zones, one rep max calculations, seasonal planning and injury prevention strategies — turn a vague exercise routine into a precision programme.

Maximum Heart Rate and Training Zones

Before setting a training intensity, a coach needs to know the athlete’s maximum heart rate. The formula is straightforward: maximum heart rate = 220 − age. For a 16-year-old student, the calculation gives 220 − 16 = 204 beats per minute (bpm).

Training intensity is then expressed as a percentage of maximum heart rate. The aerobic training zone sits between 60 and 80% of maximum heart rate. Using the same 16-year-old: the aerobic zone runs from 0.60 × 204 = 122 bpm to 0.80 × 204 = 163 bpm. Working within this zone is sufficient to stress the aerobic system without overloading it.

For more intense work, the anaerobic training zone spans 80 to 90% of maximum heart rate. For our 16-year-old this is 163 bpm to 184 bpm. Above this threshold, the body is working too hard for aerobic respiration to supply all the energy, so anaerobic respiration (producing lactic acid) contributes increasingly. The training threshold is the minimum intensity needed to produce a training effect — broadly, this is the lower boundary of the aerobic training zone (60% of maximum heart rate).

Key Fact

Maximum heart rate = 220 − age. Aerobic zone: 60–80% of maximum HR. Anaerobic zone: 80–90% of maximum HR. Always show your working and include units (bpm).

One Repetition Maximum

In weight training, the one rep max is the heaviest weight a performer can lift just once with correct technique. Once known, it is used to set the training intensity for a specific fitness aim. For strength and power, the athlete trains at above 70% of their one rep max, using approximately three sets of four to eight repetitions. For muscular endurance, they train at below 70% of their one rep max, using approximately three sets of 12 to 15 repetitions.

If a rugby player’s one rep max for the bench press is 80 kg, a strength session would use a minimum of 56 kg (70% of 80 kg = 56 kg) for three sets of six repetitions. A muscular endurance session for the same player would use a maximum of 56 kg for three sets of 14 repetitions. These boundaries ensure the correct physiological stress is applied rather than guesswork.

A 17-year-old swimmer has a one rep max of 60 kg on the shoulder press. Her coach wants to programme one strength session and one muscular endurance session per week.

Strength session: 70% of 60 kg = 42 kg. She should use at least 42 kg, performing 3 sets of 4–8 reps (e.g. 45 kg for 3 × 6).

Muscular endurance session: below 70% of 60 kg = below 42 kg. She should use less than 42 kg, performing 3 sets of 12–15 reps (e.g. 30 kg for 3 × 14).

Note: in the exam, always show the formula, the substitution, the answer and the unit (kg, bpm, %, seconds). Showing working earns method marks even if the final answer is wrong.

Altitude Training

At high altitude, the air contains less oxygen per breath — the partial pressure of oxygen is lower than at sea level. This means the body’s oxygen-carrying capacity is initially reduced when an athlete trains at altitude. The body responds to this physiological stress by producing more red blood cells, increasing the volume of haemoglobin available to transport oxygen around the body. When the athlete returns to sea level, they temporarily have a higher concentration of red blood cells, which improves their aerobic performance.

Altitude training is particularly beneficial for endurance events: marathon runners, cyclists, rowers and long-distance swimmers all use altitude camps. Mo Farah famously used altitude training camps in Font Romeu and Addis Ababa as part of his preparation for world championship and Olympic events. However, altitude training has limitations: it is expensive to travel to and stay at altitude; some athletes suffer altitude sickness (nausea, headaches, fatigue) when they first arrive; and the benefits begin to reverse within a few weeks of returning to sea level. There is also the risk of over-training at altitude because the reduced oxygen makes even moderate efforts feel much harder.

Key Fact

At altitude, reduced oxygen triggers the body to produce more red blood cells. On returning to sea level, the athlete has increased oxygen-carrying capacity, improving aerobic endurance. This benefit is temporary and begins to reverse after a few weeks.

Seasonal Training Periods

Most competitive sports divide the year into three training seasons, allowing athletes to peak at the right time and avoid year-round fatigue.

The pre-season (preparation phase) takes place before competition begins. The emphasis is on building general aerobic fitness through higher-volume, lower-intensity work, alongside sport-specific fitness and technique work. A football player in pre-season might focus on cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength and basic skills before the league begins.

During the competition season (peak or playing season), the goal shifts from developing fitness to maintaining fitness levels and working on the specific skills and tactics needed for matches and competitions. Training volume typically decreases while intensity is maintained. A sprinter in their competition season focuses on race-pace running and technical refinement rather than heavy strength blocks.

After the season ends, the post-season (transition phase) provides the body with active recovery. Athletes engage in rest and light aerobic training to maintain a basic level of general fitness without placing stress on the musculoskeletal system. This phase prevents the worst effects of reversibility and allows physical and psychological recovery before pre-season begins again.

Preventing Injury

Injury prevention is built into every aspect of a well-designed training programme. Key strategies include: completing a thorough warm-up before exercise to increase body temperature, muscle pliability and range of movement; avoiding over-training by selecting an appropriate weight or intensity and including adequate rest between sessions; wearing appropriate clothing and footwear that supports the joints being used; using taping or bracing to support previously injured or vulnerable joints; and maintaining hydration throughout, as dehydration thickens the blood and reduces performance.

Technique matters enormously: using correct lifting technique in weight training (neutral spine, controlled descent, knees tracking over toes in squats) prevents both acute and overuse injuries. Stretches should be eased into slowly and held — never bounced — to avoid activating the stretch reflex and risking muscle tears. Finally, training type and intensity must match the training purpose: a swimmer preparing for a long-distance event should not spend every session in the anaerobic zone.

For a marathon runner, altitude training is highly beneficial: it directly increases red blood cell production, improving the oxygen supply to muscles during a race that relies entirely on aerobic respiration for 26.2 miles. The investment in travel and accommodation is justified by the performance gains. For a 100 m sprinter, altitude training offers far less benefit: the race lasts under 12 seconds and relies almost entirely on the anaerobic ATP-PCr system, not on oxygen delivery. The sprinter would be better served by plyometric training and sprint-specific interval work at sea level. This comparison shows that the same intervention can have very different values depending on the energy system demands of the sport.
human-body-and-movement.exam_tip_html: Calculation questions on heart rate training zones require three things to earn full marks: (1) the correct formula written out, (2) the numbers substituted correctly, and (3) the answer with its unit (bpm). Students frequently forget the unit or give an answer without showing working. On a 3-mark calculate question, working can earn method marks even if the final figure is slightly off. For a 6-mark ‘Analyse’ question about altitude training, go beyond listing benefits — each point should be developed with a physiological reason and applied to a specific type of athlete. Bullet-point lists without development do not reach the higher mark band.
human-body-and-movement.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Maximum heart rate = 220 − age. The aerobic training zone is 60–80% of maximum HR; the anaerobic zone is 80–90%. These boundaries allow training intensity to be set with precision rather than guesswork.
  • One rep max determines weight training intensity: above 70% for strength (4–8 reps), below 70% for muscular endurance (12–15 reps). Altitude training boosts red blood cell production and benefits aerobic endurance athletes most.
  • Injury prevention relies on warm-up, correct technique, appropriate load selection, taping, hydration and rest. Training is structured across three seasons: pre-season (build fitness), competition (maintain and refine), post-season (rest and recovery).

practice_questions.text: Identify the formula used to calculate maximum heart rate.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for: maximum heart rate = 220 minus age (or 220 - age) [1 mark]
Do not accept answers that state only '220' without the subtraction of age.

practice_questions.text: A club-level cyclist is 18 years old. Calculate her aerobic training zone. Show your working and include units.
practice_questions.marks:
Max HR = 220 - 18 = 202 bpm (working must be shown)
Aerobic zone: 60% of 202 = 121.2 bpm (accept 121 bpm) to 80% of 202 = 161.6 bpm (accept 162 bpm)
1 mark for correct calculation of maximum HR (202 bpm)
1 mark for correctly calculating both boundaries of the aerobic zone with units (bpm)
Note: if the candidate states max HR incorrectly but applies 60% and 80% consistently, award the method mark but not the accuracy mark.

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows a 16-year-old rugby player's heart rate at three points during a training session.

Rest: 65 bpm | End of warm-up: 118 bpm | Peak (during sprint drills): 178 bpm

His maximum heart rate is 204 bpm. Using the data, calculate his heart rate as a percentage of his maximum heart rate during the sprint drills. State whether this places him in the aerobic or anaerobic training zone.
practice_questions.marks:
Working: 178 ÷ 204 × 100 = 87.3% (accept 87%)
1 mark for correct formula or method (peak HR ÷ max HR × 100)
1 mark for the correct percentage (87% / 87.3%), with units shown
1 mark for correctly identifying this as the anaerobic training zone (80-90% of max HR)
Note: if the candidate uses a wrong percentage threshold to identify the zone, they lose the final mark only. Accept 'above the aerobic zone threshold' as equivalent.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which altitude training improves aerobic performance when an athlete returns to sea level.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks (2 marks per way):
Way 1: At altitude, reduced oxygen availability triggers the body to produce more red blood cells (1); this increases the volume of haemoglobin, improving the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity when the athlete competes at sea level (1)
Way 2: The increased red blood cell concentration means more oxygen can be delivered to the working muscles per beat of the heart (1); this delays fatigue and improves performance in aerobic events such as the marathon or long-distance cycling (1)
Alternative Way 2: The training effect is physiological and lasts for several weeks after returning to sea level (1); athletes therefore time altitude camps carefully to peak for a major competition (1)

practice_questions.text:
A 17-year-old county-level middle-distance runner is planning her training year. She has a major regional championship in July.

Analyse how the seasonal aspects of training should be structured across the year to ensure she peaks in July.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (6 marks): Accurately describes all three phases (pre-season, competition, post-season), links each phase to specific training characteristics (volume, intensity, type), and applies each to the runner's context (e.g. pre-season starts high-volume base fitness work, competition phase shifts to race-specific interval training at or above the anaerobic threshold, post-season allows physiological recovery). Uses appropriate terminology throughout (reversibility, progressive overload, training zones, peaking).

Secure (4-5 marks): Identifies two or three phases with accurate descriptions. Training characteristics mostly correct. Application to a runner present but may lack depth for one phase.

Developing (2-3 marks): Names the phases but description of training characteristics is limited or partially inaccurate. Limited application to the runner's specific event.

Emerging (1 mark): Names one phase or makes a basic true statement about seasonal training. No development or sporting application.

practice_questions.text: Explain three factors an athlete should consider to prevent injury during a weight training session.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each of three distinct, developed factors, for example:
- Complete a thorough warm-up to increase muscle temperature and pliability, reducing the risk of strains (1)
- Use correct lifting technique throughout (e.g. neutral spine in deadlifts, knees tracking toes in squats) to prevent acute and overuse injuries (1)
- Select an appropriate weight that does not cause failure of technique, avoiding over-training (1)
- Use a spotter when performing heavy compound lifts such as the bench press (1)
- Wear appropriate footwear to provide joint support and stability (1)
- Maintain hydration to prevent blood thickening and maintain muscle function (1)
Any three distinct points, each explained with a reason for how it prevents injury.

human-body-and-movement.title: Warm Up and Cool Down
human-body-and-movement.description: Components, physiological benefits and psychological role of warming up and cooling down.
human-body-and-movement.content_html:
Why Warm Up and Cool Down?

Every training session and competitive performance should begin with a structured warm-up and end with a structured cool-down. These are not optional extras or time-fillers — they are physiologically grounded practices that reduce the risk of injury, improve performance quality during the session and accelerate recovery afterwards. Understanding exactly what each component achieves, and why, is essential for any sports performer or coach.

The Components of a Warm-Up

A complete warm-up has four components, each with a distinct purpose.

The first component is a pulse raiser. This involves light aerobic activity — a gentle jog, dynamic movements or easy cycling — that gradually increases the heart rate, raises body temperature and begins redirecting blood flow towards the working muscles through vasodilation. The pace is deliberately modest at the start and builds progressively over several minutes. A flat sprint from cold would risk muscle strains because muscles are stiffer and less pliable at rest.

The second component is stretching. Dynamic stretching — such as leg swings, hip circles and shoulder rotations — is preferred during a warm-up because it maintains movement and keeps the heart rate elevated. The increased body temperature from the pulse raiser means the muscles are already more pliable, allowing a greater range of movement to be achieved safely. Mobility work here ensures that the joints used in the activity ahead are taken through their full range before high-intensity demands are placed on them.

The third component is skill familiarisation (sometimes called skill-based practice). This bridges the gap between the general physical preparation of the pulse raiser and stretching, and the full demands of the sport. A basketball team might include dribbling and shooting drills; a gymnast might rehearse scaled-down versions of her floor routines at moderate intensity. This component ensures the neuromuscular system is primed for the precise movement patterns the sport requires.

The fourth component is mental preparation. This involves focusing attention on the task ahead, rehearsing strategies and visualising successful performance. For a 100 m sprinter, this might mean visualising the starting sequence and the acceleration phase; for a rugby fly-half, it might involve mentally rehearsing decision-making under pressure. Mental preparation reduces anxiety to optimal levels and sharpens concentration before competition begins.

Key Fact

The four warm-up components are: (1) pulse raiser — raises heart rate and body temperature; (2) stretching — increases range of movement and muscle pliability; (3) skill familiarisation — rehearses sport-specific movements; (4) mental preparation — focuses the mind and reduces anxiety.

Physiological Benefits of Warming Up

The physiological benefits of a warm-up are interconnected. Raising body temperature increases the speed at which nerve impulses travel and makes muscle contractions faster and more forceful — both of which directly improve performance. The increased blood flow to working muscles delivers more oxygen and glucose, ensuring the aerobic energy system is ready to function efficiently from the earliest stages of exercise.

The range of movement at joints increases as synovial fluid becomes less viscous and more freely distributed around the joint capsule. Tendons and ligaments also become more elastic at higher temperatures, reducing the likelihood of tears and strains during explosive movements. Gradually increasing the effort to full pace — rather than going from rest to maximal effort instantly — also gives the cardiovascular system time to adjust: cardiac output increases progressively as both heart rate and stroke volume rise, rather than being shocked into sudden high demand.

Recall from lessons on the cardiovascular system and the effects of exercise that cardiac output (Q) = stroke volume × heart rate. During a warm-up, both stroke volume and heart rate begin to rise as the body prepares for activity. Blood is redirected from the digestive organs towards the skeletal muscles through vasodilation in the muscle capillaries and vasoconstriction elsewhere. Recall also the anticipatory rise — heart rate begins to increase even before exercise starts, driven by adrenaline released in response to the prospect of exercise. A warm-up reinforces this anticipatory rise and continues the upward cardiovascular response at a controlled pace.

Psychological Benefits of Warming Up

Beyond the physiological effects, warming up provides important psychological preparation. It gives performers time to practise movement skills through a full range of movement at moderate intensity, building confidence. The mental preparation component specifically addresses arousal levels — a performer who is over-anxious can use the warm-up period to slow breathing and use imagery to regain focus; one who feels flat can use high-energy dynamic activities and motivational cues to raise arousal. Sports psychologists and coaches use warm-up routines as part of a pre-performance ritual that signals to the performer that competition is imminent.

The Components of a Cool-Down

After exercise, an immediate stop is physiologically harmful: blood can pool in the lower limbs when muscular contractions no longer pump it back towards the heart, causing dizziness and slowing the removal of waste products. A structured cool-down prevents this.

The first component of a cool-down is maintaining an elevated breathing rate and heart rate through a gradual reduction in intensity — for example, moving from a sprint to a jog, then from a jog to a brisk walk, then to a gentle stroll. This gradual decrease keeps blood circulating, continuing to supply oxygen to the muscles and carry away lactic acid and carbon dioxide for processing and removal.

The second component is static stretching. After exercise the muscles are warm and pliable — this is the optimal time for static stretching, because the muscle fibres lengthen most easily at elevated temperature. Regular post-exercise stretching helps to maintain and improve flexibility over time. It also reduces the sensation of tightness and stiffness that can set in within hours of a training session.

Key Fact

The three cool-down components are: (1) gradual reduction in intensity (light jog/walk) to keep blood circulating; (2) maintained elevated breathing rate to continue removing lactic acid and CO&sub2;; and (3) static stretching to reduce muscle stiffness and aid flexibility.

Physiological Benefits of Cooling Down

Cooling down allows the body to recover from the physiological demands of exercise. Gradual reduction in intensity keeps the heart rate and breathing rate elevated for a controlled period, maintaining blood flow through the muscles so that lactic acid and other metabolic waste products are transported to the liver and kidneys for processing and removal. This directly reduces the risk of DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness) — the aching that typically peaks 24 to 48 hours after an intense training session. Athletes who cool down consistently report less severe DOMS and are able to return to quality training more quickly.

DOMS is caused by microscopic damage to muscle fibres and the associated inflammatory response, rather than solely by lactic acid build-up as was once thought. However, maintaining blood flow during a cool-down does help remove lactic acid and other metabolic waste products that contribute to the acidic environment in the muscle post-exercise. Static stretching during the cool-down may also help align muscle fibres that have been disrupted by intense activity. The combined effect is a reduction in the severity of post-exercise soreness and a faster return to full training capacity.
human-body-and-movement.exam_tip_html: On a 6-mark ‘Analyse’ question about warm-up or cool-down, avoid simply listing components. Each point should be developed: name the component, describe what it does physiologically, and link it to performance or recovery in a named sport. For example: “The pulse raiser gradually raises body temperature, which reduces the viscosity of synovial fluid at the joints, allowing a greater range of movement — particularly important for a gymnast who needs maximum hip and shoulder mobility from the first routine.” For 2-mark ‘State Two’ questions, ensure your two benefits are genuinely different physiological effects — ‘raises heart rate’ and ‘increases blood flow’ are related but distinct enough to earn two marks, whereas ‘raises heart rate’ and ‘heart rate goes up’ will only earn one.
human-body-and-movement.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A warm-up has four components: pulse raiser (raises heart rate and body temperature), stretching (increases range of movement), skill familiarisation (rehearses sport-specific movements) and mental preparation (focuses the mind). Together they reduce injury risk and optimise performance.
  • The physiological benefits of warming up include increased muscle pliability, greater joint range of movement, improved oxygen delivery to muscles and a gradual cardiovascular response. The psychological benefits include confidence building and optimal arousal.
  • A cool-down maintains elevated heart rate and breathing for a gradual recovery, removes lactic acid and CO&sub2; via sustained blood flow, and uses static stretching to reduce muscle stiffness and the severity of DOMS.

practice_questions.text: State two physiological benefits of completing a warm-up before exercise.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each of two distinct physiological benefits, for example:
- Increased body temperature makes muscles more pliable, reducing the risk of strains (1)
- Increased range of movement at joints as synovial fluid becomes less viscous (1)

Note: two answers must be physiologically distinct to earn both marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe how cooling down helps the body recover from intense exercise. Include reference to lactic acid in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
- Gradual reduction in intensity maintains elevated heart rate and blood flow to the muscles (1)
- Sustained blood flow transports lactic acid away from the muscles to the liver and kidneys for processing and removal (1)
- This reduces the acidity in the muscles and helps prevent or minimise DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness) (1)
- Static stretching during the cool-down helps maintain muscle flexibility and reduce post-exercise tightness (1)
Any three of the above, with lactic acid specifically referenced for at least one mark.

practice_questions.text: Explain why skill familiarisation is included in a warm-up, and how it differs from the pulse raiser.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks:
- Skill familiarisation involves sport-specific drills and movements at moderate intensity (1)
- It prepares the neuromuscular system by rehearsing the precise movement patterns required in the activity (1)
- It builds confidence and bridges the gap between general preparation and full competition demands (1)
- The pulse raiser is non-specific (general aerobic activity such as jogging) and focuses on raising heart rate and body temperature rather than rehearsing skills (1)
Full marks require both an explanation of skill familiarisation's purpose AND a clear distinction from the pulse raiser.

practice_questions.text:
A Year-12 county-level netball team has 20 minutes before a regional quarter-final. Their coach is planning the warm-up.

Analyse the importance of each component of an effective warm-up for the netball players before this match.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (6 marks): All four components identified and each clearly linked to a physiological or psychological benefit specific to netball. For example: pulse raiser raises body temperature and increases blood flow to muscles needed for explosive movement and change of direction; stretching increases joint range of movement particularly at the hip and shoulder, needed for shooting and defensive reaching; skill familiarisation with passing drills and footwork patterns activates the neuromuscular pathways specific to netball decision-making; mental preparation reduces pre-match anxiety and sharpens decision-making under pressure. Uses accurate physiological terminology throughout.

Secure (4-5 marks): Three or four components described with correct benefits. At least two benefits applied to netball specifically. Generally accurate terminology.

Developing (2-3 marks): Two components identified and described. Limited sporting application. One or more physiological effects correctly stated.

Emerging (1 mark): Names one component or states one general benefit of warming up without development or application.

practice_questions.text: State two benefits of including static stretching in a cool-down.

- Helps maintain or improve flexibility over time as muscles are warm and pliable after exercise (1)
- Reduces post-exercise muscle stiffness and tightness (1)
- Helps reduce the severity of DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness) (1)
- Allows muscle fibres to return towards their resting length after sustained contraction (1)

Sport-specific drills and exercises performed during a warm-up to rehearse the movement patterns required in the activity ahead.
A waste product of anaerobic respiration that accumulates in the muscles and blood during intense exercise, causing fatigue and a burning sensation.
Holding a stretched position for up to 30 seconds during a cool-down to maintain or gradually increase flexibility and reduce post-exercise muscle stiffness.
Muscle soreness and stiffness experienced 24-48 hours after unaccustomed or intense exercise, caused by microscopic damage to muscle fibres.

human-body-and-movement.title: Using Data in Physical Activity and Sport
human-body-and-movement.description: Collecting, presenting and interpreting qualitative and quantitative data from sport and training.
human-body-and-movement.content_html:
Why Data Matters in Sport

Modern sport is driven by data. Premier League clubs analyse thousands of data points per match to inform selection and tactics. Olympic coaches monitor heart rate, lactate thresholds and power outputs to fine-tune training loads. Even at school level, recording fitness test results and tracking progress over time transforms vague feelings of “getting fitter” into evidence-based decisions. Understanding how to collect, present and interpret data is therefore a core skill for any sports performer, coach or analyst.

Qualitative and Quantitative Data

All data in sport falls into one of two broad categories. Quantitative data deals with numbers and measurements. Heart rate in beats per minute, sprint time in seconds, vertical jump height in centimetres, percentage body fat — all of these are quantitative because they give a numerical value that can be compared against norms or tracked over time. Quantitative data collected during fitness testing can be compared to national averages or previous personal bests.

Qualitative data, by contrast, deals with descriptions, opinions and observations that cannot be reduced to a simple number. A coach’s detailed notes on a gymnast’s technique, a performer’s own feelings about their confidence levels before a competition, or an analyst’s description of a team’s defensive structure — all of these are qualitative because they describe quality rather than quantity.

Key Fact

Quantitative data = numbers (heart rate, time, distance, score). Qualitative data = descriptions and observations (technique notes, confidence ratings, tactical observations). Quantitative data can be compared to national norms; qualitative data provides context and depth that numbers alone cannot capture.

Methods for Collecting Quantitative Data

Quantitative data is typically gathered using structured tools that produce numerical outputs. Questionnaires and surveys are common methods. In a sporting context, a questionnaire might ask participants to rate their enjoyment of different activities on a scale of 1 to 10, or to record how many hours per week they spend in physical activity. Because the responses are numerical or categorical, the data can be totalled, averaged and compared across groups. For example, a school might survey all Year 10 students to find out participation rates in different sports, producing a dataset that can be displayed in a bar chart or pie chart.

Methods for Collecting Qualitative Data

Qualitative data requires methods that allow the depth of a person’s experience or a coach’s expert judgement to be captured. Interviews provide rich, detailed responses: a sports psychologist might interview an athlete about their pre-competition anxiety in depth, exploring triggers, coping strategies and past experiences in a way that a questionnaire could never capture. Observations involve a coach or analyst watching a performer and making detailed notes about technique, decision-making or movement patterns. Video analysis is a form of observation widely used in elite sport.

A key distinction is that qualitative methods are open-ended: the researcher cannot predict all possible responses in advance, and the richness of the data is its strength. The limitation is that qualitative data is harder to compare statistically. Two coaches observing the same performance might write different notes, making it difficult to draw objective conclusions across large groups.

Presenting Data: Tables, Bar Charts and Line Graphs

Raw data — a long list of numbers — is rarely informative on its own. Presenting it visually reveals patterns and trends that would otherwise be buried in a table of figures. The choice of chart type depends on what the data is and what you are trying to show.

A table organises data in rows and columns, making it easy to read off individual values. Tables are useful when precision matters — a coach tracking an athlete’s one rep max over 10 weeks needs to see exact figures, not an approximation from a chart. A bar chart uses rectangular bars of different heights to compare categories — for example, comparing the average number of students participating in five different sports at one school. The y-axis shows the quantity (e.g. number of students) and the x-axis shows the categories (e.g. sport). Both axes must be clearly labelled with the variable name and units.

A line graph shows how a variable changes over time and is ideal for displaying trends. A coach might plot an athlete’s resting heart rate across 12 weeks of training on a line graph: the downward trend over time provides clear visual evidence of a bradycardia adaptation (lower resting heart rate as the heart becomes stronger and more efficient). Pie charts are used to show proportions — for example, the percentage split of students choosing different activity categories in a survey.

Key Fact

Bar chart = comparing categories at one point in time (e.g. participation in sport A vs sport B). Line graph = showing change over time (e.g. resting heart rate across a training programme). Pie chart = showing proportions of a whole (e.g. % of students doing each sport). All graphs must have labelled axes with units.

Interpreting and Analysing Data

Reading a value from a chart is only the first step. Genuine data interpretation means making a comparison, quoting a specific figure, and explaining what that figure means in the sporting context. A student who writes “the data shows heart rate went up” has described the data. A student who writes “heart rate increased from 68 bpm at rest to 172 bpm at peak exercise, a rise of 104 bpm, indicating the performer was working well within the anaerobic training zone (80–90% of maximum heart rate for a 16-year-old)” has interpreted the data.

Quantitative analysis includes calculating the mean (add all values and divide by the number of values), the range (highest value minus lowest value), and percentage changes. To calculate a percentage change: subtract the old value from the new value, divide by the old value and multiply by 100. For example, if a student’s 30 m sprint time improves from 5.2 seconds to 4.9 seconds: change = 0.3 s; percentage change = (0.3 ÷ 5.2) × 100 = 5.8% improvement.

The most frequent error on data interpretation questions is copying numbers from the table without saying what they show. Always make a comparison, quote one specific figure, then explain the sporting implication. A second common error is forgetting to include units in calculations — an answer of “104” is incomplete; “104 bpm” is correct. A third error is confusing the mean with the range: the mean tells you the average performance level; the range tells you how consistent (or inconsistent) the results are. Wide range = inconsistent; narrow range = consistent.

Table: Javid’s Illinois Agility Test scores (seconds) over 5 attempts: 16.4, 15.9, 15.7, 16.1, 15.3.

Mean: (16.4 + 15.9 + 15.7 + 16.1 + 15.3) ÷ 5 = 79.4 ÷ 5 = 15.88 seconds.

Range: 16.4 − 15.3 = 1.1 seconds. This suggests moderate consistency — Javid’s results varied by just over a second across five attempts.

Percentage change (first to last): (16.4 − 15.3) ÷ 16.4 × 100 = 1.1 ÷ 16.4 × 100 = 6.7% improvement. Always show the formula, the substitution, the answer and the unit.
human-body-and-movement.exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark ‘Interpret Data’ question, the single biggest mark-losing error is restating numbers without explaining what they mean. Always follow this structure: (1) quote a specific figure from the data, (2) make a comparison (e.g. ‘this is higher than…’ or ‘this represents a change of…’), and (3) explain the sporting implication (e.g. ‘this indicates the performer was working in the anaerobic training zone’). For calculation questions, show every step: formula, substitution, answer with unit. Missing the unit costs the final mark. On 6-mark ‘Analyse’ questions about data methods, develop each point — don’t just list ‘questionnaire, interview, observation’; explain what type of data each produces and when each would be the most appropriate method.
human-body-and-movement.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Quantitative data uses numbers (collected via questionnaires and surveys); qualitative data uses descriptions (collected via interviews and observations). Quantitative data can be compared statistically; qualitative data provides depth and context.
  • Data is presented in tables (for precise values), bar charts (for comparing categories), line graphs (for trends over time) and pie charts (for proportions). All graphs must have clearly labelled axes with units.
  • Data interpretation means comparing figures, quoting specific values and explaining sporting implications — not merely describing what the data shows. Quantitative analysis uses mean (average), range (highest minus lowest) and percentage change.

practice_questions.text: Identify the type of data produced when a coach times a swimmer's 50 m length and records it in seconds.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for: quantitative data [1 mark]
Do not accept 'numerical' alone without the term 'quantitative', unless the explanation makes clear it is measurable/countable data.

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows the number of students participating in four sports at Redmoor Academy during one lunchtime session.

Netball: 22 students | Football: 38 students | Badminton: 14 students | Athletics: 16 students

Calculate the mean number of students participating across the four sports.
practice_questions.marks:
Working: (22 + 38 + 14 + 16) = 90 ÷ 4 = 22.5 students
1 mark for correct addition and division method shown (90 ÷ 4)
1 mark for the correct answer: 22.5 students (accept 22-23 if rounded, but deduct final mark if no working shown)
Note: units (students) should be included. Award 1 mark only if no working is shown but the answer is correct.

practice_questions.text:
Table 2 shows three Year-10 students' sit-and-reach test scores (cm) at the start and end of a 10-week flexibility training programme.

Student A: Start 18 cm, End 24 cm
Student B: Start 14 cm, End 17 cm
Student C: Start 21 cm, End 28 cm

Calculate Student C's percentage improvement in flexibility. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Working: change = 28 - 21 = 7 cm; percentage change = 7 ÷ 21 × 100 = 33.3%
1 mark for correctly identifying the change (28 - 21 = 7 cm)
1 mark for applying the correct percentage change formula (7 ÷ 21 × 100)
1 mark for the correct answer with units: 33.3% (accept 33% or 33.3%)
Always show the formula and substitution. Correct answer without working scores 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text:
Bar Chart 1 shows weekly participation rates (% of registered members) in three sports at a local sports centre across a 4-week period.

Week 1: swimming 45%, fitness suite 62%, team sports 28%
Week 2: swimming 48%, fitness suite 65%, team sports 31%
Week 3: swimming 47%, fitness suite 70%, team sports 29%
Week 4: swimming 44%, fitness suite 74%, team sports 30%

Interpret what the data shows about participation trends at this sports centre.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. Responses must compare figures (not just describe one figure), quote a specific value, and explain the implication:
- Fitness suite participation shows a consistent upward trend from 62% in week 1 to 74% in week 4, a rise of 12 percentage points, suggesting growing engagement with gym-based exercise (1 mark for comparison + implication)
- Swimming participation remained relatively stable (range 44-48%), suggesting a steady core user group with little growth or decline (1)
- Team sports participation was consistently the lowest across all four weeks (range 28-31%), which may indicate barriers to participation in team activities compared to individual exercise options (1)
- The gap between fitness suite and team sports participation widened from 34 percentage points in week 1 to 44 in week 4, suggesting individual exercise formats are growing in popularity relative to team sports (1)
Award marks for any four distinct, developed interpretations with specific data references.

practice_questions.text:
A sports scientist is studying the effects of a 12-week cardiovascular training programme on three Year-11 students. She wants to collect both quantitative and qualitative data.

Analyse the advantages and disadvantages of using interviews compared to fitness tests to collect data for this study.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (6 marks): Clearly identifies both methods, accurately explains the type of data each produces (qualitative vs quantitative), and develops both advantages and disadvantages of each in the context of this specific study. For example: fitness tests produce quantitative data (e.g. multi-stage fitness test score) that can be compared to national norms and tracked statistically across 12 weeks, providing objective evidence of improvement; however, they may not reflect how the students feel about their progress or engagement, which matters for long-term adherence. Interviews produce qualitative data (rich descriptions of experience and motivation), but results are harder to compare between students and may be influenced by social desirability (students say what the researcher wants to hear). Reaches a justified conclusion about when each is most appropriate.

Secure (4-5 marks): Identifies both methods with correct data types. Advantages and disadvantages present for at least one method. Some application to the study. Generally accurate.

Developing (2-3 marks): Describes one method accurately, or mentions both with limited development. Limited application to the study.

Emerging (1 mark): Names a method or correctly identifies quantitative or qualitative without development.

practice_questions.text:
A coach records the following resting heart rate data for an athlete across a 6-week training programme: Week 1: 72 bpm, Week 2: 70 bpm, Week 3: 69 bpm, Week 4: 67 bpm, Week 5: 65 bpm, Week 6: 63 bpm.

Calculate the range of the data set and explain what it suggests about the athlete's adaptation to training.
practice_questions.marks:
Working: range = 72 - 63 = 9 bpm
1 mark for correct calculation: highest (72) - lowest (63) = 9 bpm (unit required)
1 mark for identifying the trend: resting heart rate decreased consistently over 6 weeks
1 mark for explaining the adaptation: this is bradycardia, the long-term effect of cardiovascular training, where the heart becomes stronger and pumps more blood per beat (increased stroke volume), so it needs to beat less often at rest

knowledge_checks.q: A coach makes detailed notes about a player's movement patterns during a match. What type of data is this?

The _____ is calculated by adding all values in a data set and dividing by the number of values.
Surveys and questionnaires are methods used to collect _____ data because they produce numerical responses.
Match each data collection method to the type of data it produces.
right: Qualitative — detailed personal descriptions
Quantitative — numerical scores that can be averaged
Qualitative — descriptive written judgements

glossary_terms.definition: Data expressed in numbers that can be measured, counted and compared statistically.
Data expressed in descriptions, observations or opinions rather than numbers.
A set of written questions with fixed-choice or numerical-scale responses used to collect measurable data from a sample of participants.
A structured tool, often administered digitally or in writing, used to gather numerical data from a group of people about their habits, participation or opinions.
A spoken or written conversation between a researcher and participant, used to gather detailed personal views, feelings or experiences.
Watching and recording what performers do in a training or competitive environment, without direct questioning.
A way of organising data into labelled rows and columns so that individual values can be read quickly and comparisons made.
The average of a set of values, calculated by adding all values together and dividing by the number of values.
The difference between the highest and lowest values in a data set.

socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.title: Skill, Ability and the Classification of Skills
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.description: Skill versus ability, the four classification continuums and sporting examples.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.content_html:
Skill and Ability — Two Different Things

In everyday conversation, people use “skill” and “ability” as if they mean the same thing. In physical education, they do not. Skill is something you develop through practice. It is learned, purposeful and can be refined over time. A novice swimmer performing front crawl for the first time is displaying very little skill; an Olympic swimmer performing the same stroke is highly skilled because years of deliberate practice have made the action consistent, efficient and well-controlled.

Ability, by contrast, is something you are born with. It is a stable, largely unchangeable trait that sets the upper limit of what you can potentially achieve. Abilities include things like reaction time, balance, limb coordination and explosive power. You cannot teach someone better reaction time the way you can teach them better technique — genetic endowment places a ceiling on these qualities. A sprinter like Dina Asher-Smith had natural fast-twitch muscle fibre capacity (an ability) long before she had refined sprint technique (a skill). The skill was developed through coaching; the ability was always there.

Key Fact

Skill is learned and can be improved through practice. Ability is innate (natural, inherited) and sets the performer’s potential ceiling. A talented young gymnast may have excellent natural balance (ability) but still needs years of practice to execute a beam routine without error (skill).

The Four Classification Continuums

Skills are not simply “good” or “bad” — they vary across four dimensions. Each dimension is best understood as a continuum rather than a binary choice, because most skills fall somewhere between the two extremes. Examiners expect you to place a skill on the continuum and justify your choice, not just label it.

1. Basic — Complex

A basic skill demands very little from the performer in terms of decision-making or perceptual processing. Walking, running in a straight line, or a simple underarm throw all sit towards the basic end. A complex skill, at the other end, involves many sub-routines to be coordinated simultaneously, a wide range of possible responses, and heavy attentional demands. A tennis serve — which requires ball toss timing, racket path, weight transfer, wrist snap and ball placement all to be synchronised — sits towards the complex end. A basketball lay-up sits between the two: it has a set pattern (making it less random) but requires coordination of running, jumping and release angle (making it more demanding than a simple catch).

2. Open — Closed

This is one of the most frequently confused continuums. Open and closed refer to the predictability of the environment, not to whether the skill is simple or difficult. An open skill takes place in an unstable environment. A football pass under pressure from a defender is an open skill because the environment — positions of teammates, defenders, ball bounce — changes from moment to moment and the performer must constantly adapt. In contrast, a closed skill takes place in a stable environment. A gymnast performing a floor routine performs each move in a predictable, unchanging space; a swimmer at the start of a race dives into the same lane each time. Because the environment is stable, the movement pattern can be pre-planned and repeated identically.

Many students write that a skill is “open because it is difficult” or “closed because it is simple” — this is wrong and will lose marks. A highly complex gymnastics routine is a closed skill because the environment is predictable. A simple one-touch pass in football is an open skill because defenders and teammates are moving and the performer must react to them. Always base your answer on whether the environment is changing and unpredictable (open) or stable and predictable (closed).

3. Self-Paced — Externally Paced

This continuum refers to who controls the timing of the skill. In a self-paced skill, the performer chooses when to start and how fast to execute. A golfer selecting their moment to drive, a gymnast deciding when to begin her vault run-up, or a footballer taking a penalty all control their own timing. In an externally paced skill, external factors dictate when the performer must respond. A cricket batsman facing a delivery must time their shot to the ball, not to their own preference. A hockey player receiving a pass must react to the arriving ball. The more an athlete must react to something outside their control, the further towards the externally paced end the skill sits.

4. Gross — Fine

The gross — fine continuum is about the muscles involved and the precision required. A gross skill uses large muscle groups: running, jumping, throwing, swimming. The movements are powerful and whole-body. A fine skill requires delicate coordination of small muscle groups — the hands, fingers and wrists. A snooker player potting a ball, an archer releasing the bowstring with a relaxed grip, or a dart player aiming at the treble 20 all involve fine skills. Note that fine skills do not have to be low effort — a surgeon’s instrument control is fine but intense. Fine skills also typically demand precision that gross skills do not.

Key Fact

The four continuums — basic/complex, open/closed, self-paced/externally paced, gross/fine — allow you to describe and compare ANY skill systematically. Most skills sit between the extremes. A cricket batting stroke, for example, is towards the complex, open, externally paced and gross end of each continuum.

A tennis serve can be placed on all four continuums:

Basic — Complex: Towards the complex end. The serve involves multiple sub-routines — ball toss, stance, backswing, contact point, follow-through — all of which must be coordinated precisely.

Open — Closed: Towards the closed end when serving first. The server controls the environment: the court is always the same dimensions, the ball is stationary in their hand, and the serve begins when they choose. However, for the returner, receiving a serve is an open skill because the ball direction and speed are unpredictable.

Self-Paced — Externally Paced: Self-paced. The server decides exactly when to toss the ball and begin the swing. No external factor dictates their timing.

Gross — Fine: Towards the gross end. The serve uses large muscle groups of the legs, torso, shoulder and arm. However, the final wrist snap and precise contact point add a fine element, placing it slightly towards the middle.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.exam_tip_html: On ‘explain’ and ‘analyse’ questions about skill classification, the most common error is stating a classification without justifying it. A marker will not credit “it is an open skill” alone — you must say why using the continuum definition (e.g. “it is an open skill because the environment is unpredictable — defenders are moving and the performer must adapt continuously”). For a 6-mark analyse question, select at least two of the four continuums, place the skill precisely, and give a sporting example for each. Avoid writing “this skill is open because it is complex” — these are separate continuums and must be justified separately. On multiple-choice and identify questions, re-read the continuum labels carefully: self-paced means the performer controls timing, not that the skill is easy.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Skill is learned through practice; ability is innate and sets the performer’s potential ceiling — a key distinction the spec tests with definition questions.
  • Skills are classified on four continuums: basic/complex (decisions and sub-routines), open/closed (predictability of environment), self-paced/externally paced (who controls timing), and gross/fine (muscles used and precision required).
  • Most skills sit between the extremes of each continuum. Always justify your classification using the definition of the continuum, not just the label.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the best example of a closed skill?
A) A football player receiving a through pass from a teammate
B) A gymnast performing a cartwheel on the floor exercise mat
C) A hockey player hitting a moving ball past a goalkeeper
D) A basketball player taking a free throw during a fast break
practice_questions.marks: B) A gymnast performing a cartwheel on the floor exercise mat [1 mark]. The environment is stable and predictable; the movement can be planned and repeated identically. All other options involve unpredictable, changing environments (open skills).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'ability' in the context of sport and physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the core idea: ability is an innate / natural / inherited characteristic. 1 mark for development: it is stable and largely unchangeable; it underpins a performer's potential to learn and perform skills (accept: it sets a ceiling on what a performer can achieve). Do not credit definitions that describe ability as learned or practised.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a swimming coach could use the four skill classification continuums to analyse a performer's front crawl stroke.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for each continuum correctly applied with a brief justification (max 3 continuums credited). Examples: Basic/complex — complex, because it requires simultaneous coordination of arm pull, leg kick, breathing pattern and head position (1). Open/closed — closed, because the pool environment is stable and the performer moves through predictable conditions (1). Self-paced/externally paced — self-paced, because the swimmer decides their own stroke rate and turn timing (1). Gross/fine — gross, because large muscle groups of the arms, shoulders, core and legs produce the movement (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a basketball player taking a free throw is classified differently on the open/closed continuum compared to the same player making a lay-up during open play. Use the definitions of open and closed skills in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a free throw is a closed skill. 1 mark for justification: the environment is stable and predictable; the player stands at the same spot, no defenders can challenge, and the timing is self-controlled. 1 mark for identifying that a lay-up in open play is an open skill (or further towards the open end). 1 mark for justification: the environment is unpredictable; defenders are moving, teammates are repositioning, and the player must adapt their movement and timing to the changing situation.

practice_questions.text: A Year-10 PE teacher is designing classification tasks for two groups: one group will practise hitting a stationary ball on a tee, the other will practise hitting a ball bowled at them by a partner. Analyse how the four continuums differ between these two tasks.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses all four continuums, clearly differentiating both tasks on each, with precise definitions and specific justifications rooted in the scenario. Points might include: basic/complex — hitting a stationary ball is more basic (fewer decisions, simpler movement), while hitting a bowled ball is more complex (timing judgement, footwork, range of shots possible); open/closed — stationary ball is closed (environment controlled, ball position fixed), bowled ball is open (ball direction, speed, bounce variable); self-paced/externally paced — tee hit is self-paced (performer starts when ready), bowled ball is externally paced (bowler dictates timing); gross/fine — both are gross skills (large muscle groups driving the shot) but the tee hit may be slightly more fine near the point of contact. Consistent reference to both tasks throughout.

Secure: Correctly analyses at least three continuums, with most justifications accurate. Generally applies to both tasks but may be less precise on one or two.

Developing: Names and partially explains two or three continuums. May label without justifying, or analyse only one task.

Emerging: Names one or two continuums; limited or no justification; may confuse continuum definitions.

practice_questions.text: A 15-year-old club athlete competes in both archery and rugby union. Evaluate the view that classifying skills on the four continuums helps coaches plan training more effectively than simply labelling skills as 'easy' or 'hard'. Use examples from both sports in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced, well-developed evaluation with a range of points on each side, each applied to specific sporting examples from archery and/or rugby, with a clear and justified conclusion. Arguments in support: the four continuums reveal specific training needs — knowing an archery shot is closed, self-paced and fine tells a coach to prioritise consistency of technique and mental routine rather than reaction speed or physical power; classifying a rugby tackle as open, externally paced and gross directs training towards reactive drills and contact conditioning rather than technical precision; using continuums prevents coaches from applying the wrong training prescription, e.g. drilling a rugby player in closed-skill repetition when open-skill adaptability is what match performance demands; continuums allow comparison of a performer's current skill level to the demands of the full game situation. Arguments against or limitations: classifying skills is time-consuming and most coaches work intuitively from experience; the four continuums may oversimplify — many skills shift along continuums depending on context (a tennis serve is closed when initiating but the rally is open); beginners may benefit more from straightforward 'easy/hard' progression than from theoretical classification. Justified conclusion: the four continuums are most useful when planning training progression, especially when designing drills that match real competition demands.

Secure: Two or three points on each side, mostly applied to both sports, with a reasonable conclusion.

Developing: Points on both sides but limited development; sporting context present but thin or one-sport only.

Emerging: One-sided or very basic response; little or no sporting application.

knowledge_checks.q: A footballer dribbling past defenders in a match is performing which type of skill on the open/closed continuum?
options: Closed, because the ball is always round
Open, because the environment is unpredictable and changing
Self-paced, because the footballer can stop when they like
Fine, because the footballer uses precise footwork

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is an example of an innate ability rather than a learned skill?
A snooker player potting a ball uses small muscle groups and high precision. This places it towards the _____ end of the gross-to-fine continuum.
A skill where the performer decides when to begin and controls the rate of movement is called a _____ skill.
Match each continuum to its correct defining feature:
right: Whether the environment is predictable or changing
Who controls the timing of the movement
The number of decisions and sub-routines involved
