socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.title: Personality, Aggression and Motivation
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.description: Introvert and extrovert types, direct and indirect aggression, intrinsic and extrinsic motivation.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.content_html:
Personality Types in Sport

Personality shapes how athletes prefer to practise, how they respond to pressure and which sporting environments suit them best. The specification focuses on two broad personality types: the introvert and the extrovert. These are not rigid categories but opposite ends of a continuum — most people sit somewhere between the two extremes, and personality alone does not determine athletic success.

Introverts are typically shy or quiet, enjoy their own company, prefer to think carefully before acting, and become drained by excessive social interaction. In sport, introverts tend to gravitate towards individual sports that require sustained concentration, low social interaction and precision — activities such as archery, long-distance swimming, cycling, or singles tennis. These sports demand the kind of focused, deliberate mental state that introverts find comfortable. Introverts also require less external stimulation to reach their optimal arousal level, which you explored in the previous lesson on the inverted-U theory — their optimal arousal peak sits towards the lower end of the arousal axis.

Extroverts, by contrast, are sociable, talkative and enthusiastic. They are energised by interaction with others and become restless or bored when isolated. In sport, extroverts are drawn to team sports with a fast pace and high levels of social interaction — rugby, football, basketball and volleyball all provide the external stimulation they need. The gross skill demands of these sports suit extroverts well. They thrive on crowd noise, team energy and the unpredictability of open-skill environments. Their optimal arousal point sits higher on the arousal axis — they need more activation to perform at their best.

Key Fact

Introvert: shy, thoughtful, enjoys solitude, prefers individual precision sports (e.g. archery, swimming), requires low arousal. Extrovert: sociable, enthusiastic, prone to boredom in isolation, prefers team sports with fast pace and gross skills (e.g. rugby, football), requires high arousal.

Aggression in Sport

Aggression in sport is not simply “playing hard” or “being competitive”. The specification defines it as behaviour intended to harm or gain an advantage over an opponent, and distinguishes two forms: direct and indirect. Understanding this distinction is important because it maps onto different sports and different types of contact.

Direct aggression involves physical contact with another performer. A rugby tackle, a basketball box-out, a martial arts throw and a hard shoulder barge in football are all examples of direct aggression — regardless of whether they fall within the rules of the game. Direct aggression is therefore not inherently illegal: a correctly executed shoulder charge in football is direct aggression within the rules. However, a late tackle intended to injure an opponent is also direct aggression — now clearly outside the rules and potentially criminal.

Indirect aggression involves force directed at an object rather than at another person. A fast bowler in cricket bouncing the ball at a batsman’s head is a classic example — the aggression is real and intentional, but the ball is the intermediary. Other examples include a powerful smash in badminton aimed at the opponent’s body, a hard drive in hockey, or a forceful serve in tennis. The key distinction: direct = physical contact with the opponent; indirect = force through an object or the environment.

Students frequently describe all physical or forceful actions as aggression. The specification defines aggression specifically as behaviour intended to harm or gain advantage. A cricketer bowling fast with full effort is not necessarily aggressive — it is skilled play. But the same bowler aiming a short-pitched ball at the batsman’s head with the intent to intimidate is indirect aggression. Similarly, a rugby tackle executed within the laws of the game is direct aggression that is permitted — but a punch thrown at an opponent is direct aggression that is prohibited. The intent and the target matter, not just the force involved.

Motivation: Intrinsic and Extrinsic

Motivation is what drives a performer to participate, train and persist through difficulty. The specification separates motivation into two sources: intrinsic motivation and extrinsic motivation.

Intrinsic motivation arises from the activity itself: the pleasure of mastering a skill, the satisfaction of a personal best, the sense of achievement after a tough training session, or simply the enjoyment of the game. A club runner who continues training through winter because she loves the feeling of a well-paced long run is intrinsically motivated. Intrinsically motivated performers are generally more resilient — they will continue training even when external rewards are absent because the activity itself is the reward. Research consistently shows that intrinsic motivation is more reliably associated with long-term participation and sustained effort than extrinsic motivation.

Extrinsic motivation comes from outside the performer. The specification distinguishes two subtypes. Tangible extrinsic rewards are physical objects: medals, trophies, certificates, prize money, and performance bonuses. They are visible, memorable and socially valued. Intangible extrinsic rewards are non-physical: a coach’s praise, a team’s applause, positive feedback from a crowd, public recognition, or social media approval. Both types of extrinsic motivation can boost performance in the short term, but their effects differ in depth and duration.

Key Fact

Extrinsic motivation: tangible = physical rewards (medals, trophies, prize money). Intangible = non-physical rewards (praise, applause, recognition). Intrinsic motivation is more effective long-term: the performer is motivated by the activity itself, not reliant on external rewards.

Evaluating Intrinsic vs Extrinsic Motivation

The specification requires you to evaluate the merits of both types of motivation. Intrinsic motivation is generally considered more powerful and sustainable. A performer driven by genuine enjoyment and self-improvement is less likely to drop out when results are poor or when coaches change, because their satisfaction is not contingent on external approval. It also leads to a deeper engagement with practice: intrinsically motivated athletes are more likely to seek out deliberate practice, to problem-solve independently and to self-regulate their training.

Extrinsic motivation has real but limited value. Used well — particularly with beginners and young performers — extrinsic rewards provide a short-term boost that keeps participants engaged until intrinsic motivation develops. A sticker chart for a Year 7 swimmer or a certificate at a junior athletics event costs little but keeps the child coming back. The danger comes from overuse: when extrinsic rewards become the primary driver, the performer can become dependent on them. Research in sports psychology shows that if a reward is then removed or reduced, motivation — and participation — can drop sharply. Some theorists describe this as the “overjustification effect”: the external reward effectively replaces the internal enjoyment, rather than supplementing it. Extrinsic rewards may still result in feelings of pride and self-satisfaction, but they are less reliable long-term anchors for participation than intrinsic love of the activity.

The three topics in this lesson connect directly. An introvert in an individual sport may be predominantly intrinsically motivated — they compete for personal challenge and precise self-improvement, not for crowd recognition. Their lower optimal arousal threshold means calm training environments serve them well. An extrovert in a team sport may respond more to extrinsic, intangible rewards such as crowd praise and team recognition, and may actually perform better in front of a large crowd (higher arousal, which suits their higher optimal arousal threshold). Understanding that personality, arousal management and motivation interact helps coaches design environments and reward structures that genuinely engage each individual athlete, rather than applying one approach to all.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.exam_tip_html: For a 2 marks — Define question on intrinsic or extrinsic motivation, you need the source and the mechanism: intrinsic = from within the performer / personal satisfaction; extrinsic = from an external source / rewards or recognition. Simply writing “intrinsic means wanting to do it” earns one mark at best. For direct vs indirect aggression, always anchor your answer to whether physical contact with the opponent is involved — that is the single deciding factor the mark scheme uses. On a 9 marks — Evaluate question about extrinsic motivation, students routinely produce one-sided answers praising extrinsic rewards without acknowledging the overjustification risk. Full marks require a balanced argument: benefits of extrinsic motivation (short-term boost, useful for beginners) against its limitations (dependency, undermines intrinsic motivation if overused), with sporting examples for each side and a justified conclusion.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Introverts prefer individual precision sports requiring low arousal; extroverts prefer team sports with high stimulation and gross skills. Neither type is superior — the right sporting environment enhances each.
  • Direct aggression involves physical contact with an opponent; indirect aggression channels force through an object (e.g. a bat, ball or racket) without physical contact with the opponent.
  • Intrinsic motivation (from within) is more durable and leads to long-term participation. Extrinsic motivation (tangible rewards such as medals; intangible rewards such as praise) provides short-term boosts but can undermine intrinsic motivation if it becomes the dominant driver.

Arguments against: intrinsic motivation is more durable because it is not dependent on external provision; overuse of extrinsic rewards risks dependency — if removed, motivation drops sharply (overjustification effect); performers motivated intrinsically are more resilient when results are poor. socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.title: Engagement Patterns and Social Groups
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.description: How gender, age, race, religion, family and disability shape participation in physical activity.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.content_html:
What Are Engagement Patterns?

Engagement patterns describe who participates in physical activity, how often, and in which activities. They vary significantly across different social groups — not because of differences in ability, but because of the social, cultural, economic and practical factors that shape people’s lives. Understanding why participation differs between groups is central to this topic, because the goal of sport policy and education is to remove barriers and make physical activity genuinely accessible to all.

The specification identifies five social groups whose engagement patterns merit specific study: gender, race and religion (including culture), age, family and friends (peers), and people with a disability. For each group, a range of factors can either promote or discourage participation. These factors are not mutually exclusive — a person’s engagement is typically shaped by a combination of several simultaneously.

Gender and Engagement Patterns

Despite significant progress in recent decades, engagement patterns in the UK still differ between men and women. Women and girls historically face additional barriers that reduce their participation rates in many formal and competitive sports. Sexism and stereotyping play a documented role: cultural assumptions that sport is a male domain discourage participation, particularly at secondary school age when peer opinion carries heavy social weight. Media coverage is a powerful amplifier: women’s sport receives a fraction of broadcast time compared to men’s sport in most disciplines, which limits the visibility of female role models and reduces the perceived status of women’s sport.

Role models matter enormously to engagement. When Beth Mead scored a hat-trick in England’s opening game of the 2022 UEFA Women’s Euros, junior girls’ football club registrations spiked across England. Similarly, Dame Sarah Storey’s Paralympic cycling gold medals have been credited with increasing female disability sport participation. The absence of visible female role models in a sport creates a self-reinforcing cycle: girls don’t see women competing, so they don’t believe the sport is for them. Family commitments also fall disproportionately on women across all age groups, reducing available leisure time. Socio-economic factors intersect here too: lower-income households, where women are statistically over-represented, may have less disposable income to spend on sport memberships, equipment and travel.

Key Fact

Key factors limiting female engagement: sexism and stereotyping (cultural assumptions about suitability), limited media coverage (reduces role model visibility), family commitments (reduces available leisure time), and socio-economic factors (lower disposable income, fewer facilities in lower-income areas). Positive role models such as Beth Mead and Dame Sarah Storey have demonstrably increased participation.

Race, Religion and Culture

Engagement patterns can differ significantly between ethnic and religious groups. Race-based discrimination in sport — from unconscious bias in recruitment to overt racist behaviour from crowds — creates hostile environments that deter participation. In football, cricket and athletics, governing bodies have run high-profile campaigns to address racism, acknowledging that even elite sport is not free from this barrier.

Religion and culture add further dimensions. Religious festivals, prayer times and dietary requirements can create scheduling conflicts with training and competition. A Muslim athlete observing Ramadan fasts may find the energy demands of high-intensity training during that period challenging, requiring coaches and clubs to show flexibility. Cultural norms within some communities restrict female participation in mixed-sex sport or sport where clothing requirements conflict with modesty expectations. Familiarity also matters: if a sport has no visible presence within a particular cultural community, members of that community may not encounter it, learn its rules or perceive it as accessible. Education and community outreach can address this, but change is slow.

Age

Participation patterns change across the life course. Young people tend to participate at higher rates when physical education is compulsory, activity is part of the school day and peer social groups are built around sport. After leaving school, participation often drops sharply — a phenomenon described in research as the “dropout cliff” — as competing demands of higher education, work and family life reduce available leisure time and physical activity becomes optional rather than compulsory.

Older adults face different barriers: declining physical capacity, increased risk of injury, fewer accessible facilities, and reduced social networks following retirement or bereavement. However, accessible and appropriate activities — such as walking football, seated yoga, aqua aerobics and bowls — can sustain engagement among older populations. Attitudes towards ageing also matter: negative stereotypes around older people and sport discourage participation and undermine the confidence of individuals who might otherwise be active. The role of attitudes — both the individual’s own and those of those around them — is a consistent theme across all groups.

Family is one of the strongest predictors of physical activity in children. Children whose parents participate in sport are significantly more likely to be active themselves — parents model behaviour, provide transport, pay fees, and signal through their own choices that sport is worthwhile. Conversely, family commitments can be the biggest barrier to adult female participation in particular, as childcare and caring responsibilities disproportionately reduce available leisure time for women.

Peers carry enormous influence in adolescence: young people are more likely to participate if their friendship group is active, and more likely to drop out if sport is not part of their social identity. Socio-economic factors cut across all groups: socio-economic factors such as disposable income determine whether a family can afford club memberships, specialist equipment, coaching fees and travel. Free or low-cost community sport programmes are therefore critical to equitable access, particularly for young people in lower-income households.

Disability

People with physical or intellectual disabilities historically face some of the most significant barriers to participation in sport. These fall into physical and attitudinal categories. Physical barriers include inaccessible facilities (steps rather than ramps, no accessible changing rooms, pools without hoist equipment), lack of adapted equipment, and absence of disability-specific sessions or coaching. Attitudinal barriers are often harder to address: negative stereotypes assume that people with disabilities are not interested in or capable of sport at competitive level, despite extensive evidence to the contrary. Dame Sarah Storey’s 17 Paralympic gold medals, Jonnie Peacock’s 100 m sprint title at London 2012 and the growth of wheelchair basketball as a spectator sport all challenge these assumptions.

Adaptability and inclusiveness of facilities and activities are therefore key factors. Where clubs, leisure centres and governing bodies have invested in adaptive provision — deaf-friendly coaching, wheelchair-accessible courts, sitting volleyball, boccia, goalball — participation among disabled groups has increased. The relationship between disability and engagement underlines the broader principle: removing practical barriers and challenging negative attitudes are the twin levers for improving engagement patterns across all under-represented groups.

Key Fact

Barriers for disabled people: physical (inaccessible facilities, no adapted equipment, no disability sessions) and attitudinal (stereotyping, negative assumptions about capability and interest). Adaptability and inclusiveness of provision are the key solutions. Role models like Dame Sarah Storey and Jonnie Peacock challenge stereotypes and raise visibility.

Several factors appear as barriers across multiple groups, not just one. Role models: absence of visible, relatable role models reduces aspirational engagement for any under-represented group. Media coverage: low media coverage limits the perceived legitimacy and interest of a group’s participation. Accessibility: physical access to facilities matters across gender, age, disability and socio-economic status. Attitudes: both the individual’s own attitudes and the attitudes of coaches, clubs and institutions affect whether individuals feel welcome. Education: schools and community programmes that introduce diverse young people to a wide range of activities early build habits of participation that often persist into adulthood. Recognising these cross-cutting factors helps answer exam questions that ask you to explain multiple barriers or evaluate strategies to increase engagement.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.exam_tip_html: On a 4 marks — Interpret Data question about engagement patterns, you must do three things: quote a specific figure from the data, make a comparison, and explain what it means in a sporting context. Simply reading a number off a table earns nothing by itself — the mark scheme rewards the inference. For example: “School B has 27% participation compared to School A’s 18% — a difference of 9 percentage points — suggesting School B has more inclusive provision or stronger role model visibility.” On a 9 marks — Evaluate question about factors affecting engagement, a common error is listing only one group’s barriers. Full marks require multiple factors applied across different groups, with balanced points (both barriers and enabling factors), sporting examples and a justified conclusion. Use the cross-cutting factors (role models, media, socio-economic access) as a framework to structure a balanced answer.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Engagement patterns measure who participates in physical activity and why. They differ between social groups because of social, cultural, economic and practical barriers, not inherent differences in ability or interest.
  • Key groups with documented lower engagement include women (sexism, stereotyping, less media coverage, family commitments), ethnic and religious minorities (discrimination, cultural and scheduling conflicts), older adults (physical decline, stereotypes, fewer accessible activities), and people with disabilities (inaccessible facilities, attitudinal barriers).
  • Cross-cutting solutions include positive role models, improved media coverage of under-represented groups, accessible and inclusive facilities, removal of socio-economic barriers, and education that introduces a wide range of activities to young people early.

practice_questions.text: Identify one factor related to media coverage that could reduce female participation in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any valid response linking media coverage to reduced female participation, e.g.: women's sport receives less broadcast time than men's sport, reducing the visibility of female role models; lack of media coverage means female sport is perceived as less important or prestigious; girls are less likely to see women competing and therefore less likely to aspire to participate.

practice_questions.text: State two factors related to disability that can reduce a person's participation in physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per valid factor, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: inaccessible facilities (e.g. no ramps, no hoist equipment in pools); lack of adapted equipment; absence of disability-specific coaching sessions; negative stereotyping by coaches or institutions; attitudinal barriers (assumptions that disabled people are not interested in or capable of sport); lack of role models in disability sport.

practice_questions.text: Describe how socio-economic factors can affect engagement patterns in physical activity. Give an example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining or explaining what socio-economic factors are (related to income, social class, occupation — factors that affect disposable income and available leisure time); 1 mark for explaining the mechanism — lower income means less money for club memberships, equipment, transport or specialist coaching, making sport less accessible; 1 mark for a specific example (e.g. a family with limited income cannot afford football club fees, sports kit or travel to away fixtures; free-to-use community sport programmes are therefore critical).

Group | Participation rate
Male students | 68%

practice_questions.text: Analyse the factors that explain why engagement patterns in physical activity differ between older adults (aged 60+) and young adults (aged 18–30).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies and explains at least three contrasting factors across both age groups, applying each specifically to the age group. For older adults: physical decline (reduced strength, flexibility, cardiovascular endurance, increased injury risk), fewer social networks, reduced available provision, negative stereotypes about ageing and sport, reduced leisure time in pre-retirement years. For young adults: transition out of compulsory education removes structured activity, competing demands of work and family reduce leisure time, dropout cliff phenomenon as sport becomes optional. Recognises enabling factors for older adults (walking football, aqua aerobics, adapted provision). Developed prose with sporting examples.

Secure: Addresses both age groups with at least two factors per group and some explanation of mechanism. Sporting application present. May lack full balance or detailed development.

Developing: Identifies relevant factors but treats them superficially. May focus on only one age group or list without explanation. Sporting context limited.

Emerging: Basic points only. Little age-specific application.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which role models are the most important factor in improving engagement patterns among under-represented groups in sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation with well-developed points on both sides. Arguments in support: positive role models give under-represented groups aspirational figures who look like them, demonstrating that sport is possible (e.g. Beth Mead and women's football registrations, Dame Sarah Storey and disability sport); they increase media coverage indirectly by making their sport more commercially attractive; they challenge stereotypes that deter participation. Arguments against or limitations: role models alone cannot overcome structural barriers such as inaccessible facilities, socio-economic cost, scheduling conflicts related to religion or family, or institutionalised discrimination; media coverage and accessibility are arguably more systemic levers; without affordable, accessible provision, a role model's inspiration cannot translate into actual participation. Justified conclusion reached, e.g. role models are necessary but insufficient — they must be accompanied by structural changes in access and provision. Sporting examples throughout.

Secure: Both sides with some development. At least one limitation of relying solely on role models identified. Conclusion present. Examples used.

Developing: Mostly one-sided. Some relevant points but limited development. Sporting application limited.

Emerging: Basic, largely descriptive. No meaningful balance or evaluation.

socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.title: Commercialisation: Sponsorship and the Media
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.description: The golden triangle of sport, sponsorship and media, and impacts on performers.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.content_html:
What is Commercialisation?

Commercialisation is the process by which sport is bought and sold as a product. Sport generates enormous revenue through ticket sales, television rights, merchandise and sponsorship deals. As sport became a global entertainment industry, businesses saw it as a powerful vehicle for reaching audiences and building brand recognition. The result is that money now flows into sport from commercial partners at every level — from grassroots clubs to elite international events.

The Golden Triangle

The relationship between sport, sponsorship and the media is described as the “golden triangle.” Each corner of the triangle supports and benefits the other two. Sport needs funding; sponsors need audiences; the media needs content to attract viewers and readers. These three parties are mutually dependent. For example, a major football tournament attracts millions of television viewers, so broadcasters pay billions for the rights to show it. Those viewing figures attract sponsors who pay to have their logos seen. The tournament organisation uses the income to fund prize money and infrastructure, which raises the quality of competition, which attracts more viewers — and the cycle continues.

Key Fact

The golden triangle links sport, sponsorship and the media in a mutually reinforcing relationship. Sport provides content, the media provides an audience, and sponsors provide money in return for visibility with that audience.

Types of Sponsorship

Sponsorship takes three main forms. Financial sponsorship involves a company paying an athlete, team or event directly in return for advertising exposure — for instance, a bank sponsoring a tennis player so its logo appears on their clothing. Clothing and equipment sponsorship means a manufacturer provides kit, footwear or specialist equipment. A sprinter may wear a named brand’s spikes and appear in their advertising campaigns. Facility sponsorship involves a company paying for the naming rights or upkeep of a venue — a stadium bearing a corporate name is a common example. In every case, the sponsor’s goal is to increase brand awareness and sales by associating with a popular or prestigious sporting figure or event.

Types of Media

The media takes several forms, each with its own relationship to sport. Television provides the largest audiences and the highest revenue; live broadcasting rights to major leagues and tournaments are worth hundreds of millions of pounds. Radio offers commentary and discussion but cannot show action. The press (newspapers and magazines) provides analysis and in-depth reporting. The internet allows fans to access highlights, statistics and analysis at any time. Social media has transformed sport by allowing direct communication between athletes and fans, instant highlights sharing and viral marketing — an athlete’s Instagram post can reach tens of millions of followers within minutes.

Before social media, fans learned about athletes almost exclusively through television, newspapers and official club channels. An athlete’s public image was tightly controlled by PR teams. Social media disrupted this entirely. Athletes like Dina Asher-Smith and Marcus Rashford use their platforms to communicate directly with fans, comment on social issues and build personal brands that attract sponsors independently of their governing bodies. This gives athletes greater power but also greater exposure to criticism. A single post can generate positive or negative coverage almost instantaneously, and a viral moment can be more commercially valuable than a traditional advertising campaign.

Impacts on Performers

Commercialisation has significant positive and negative effects on performers. On the positive side, sponsorship income allows elite athletes to train full-time without financial worry, access cutting-edge equipment and coaching, and reach audiences through media exposure that raises their public profile. A sponsored athlete can achieve financial security that would have been impossible in an amateur era. On the negative side, the pressure to perform for commercial partners can be intense. Athletes may feel obligated to compete when injured, adjust their playing style to suit television schedules, or act as brand ambassadors in ways that feel inauthentic. High-profile athletes are also subjected to intense media scrutiny of their personal lives, which can affect mental wellbeing.

Key Fact

Commercialisation benefits performers through financial security and increased profile, but creates pressures including media scrutiny, pressure to perform while injured, and obligations to commercial partners.

Impacts on Sport

For sport as a whole, commercialisation has raised standards at the elite level through increased investment in facilities, coaching and performance science. Broadcast revenue funds leagues, which fund academies, which develop future talent. However, commercial priorities can distort sport: kick-off times may be changed to suit overseas television audiences, traditional competition formats may be altered to create more commercially attractive spectacles, and less commercially viable sports may struggle to attract any sponsorship at all, leaving them under-resourced compared to football or tennis.

Impacts on Officials, Audiences and Sponsors

Officials face increased pressure under the commercial spotlight — errors are replayed in slow motion by broadcasters and scrutinised by millions of viewers. This pressure can affect decision-making. For audiences, commercialisation has made elite sport more accessible than ever through extensive broadcast coverage, but rising ticket prices driven by commercial revenue can price out traditional working-class fans from attending matches in person. For sponsors, associating with a successful sport or athlete is highly valuable — but a high-profile scandal or poor performance can damage the brand by association.

Many students argue that commercial money is purely positive for sport. This is too one-sided. While funding raises standards, commercial interests can prioritise profit over sporting values. For example, some competitions have been rescheduled to times inconvenient for home fans to suit international television markets. Grassroots sports with smaller audiences often receive little or no commercial support despite their importance for public health and community. A strong 9-mark answer must acknowledge both positive and negative effects on each group: performers, sport itself, officials, audiences and sponsors.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.exam_tip_html: On a 6-mark ‘Analyse’ question about commercialisation, list-style answers score poorly. Each point should follow a three-step structure: state the impact, link it to how it affects a specific group (performer, sport, audience), and give a real or plausible example. On a 9-mark ‘Evaluate’ question, you must discuss both positive and negative impacts. A common error is writing only positives or only negatives — the mark scheme rewards a balanced argument. Use a ‘For X… However Y…’ structure and anchor each side to a sporting context. For example: “Sponsorship income allows elite athletes to train full-time [positive]. However, commercial pressure can force athletes to compete while injured to meet contractual obligations [negative].”
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The golden triangle links sport, sponsorship and the media in a mutually reinforcing cycle — each corner depends on and supports the other two.
  • Commercialisation has positive impacts (financial security for performers, higher standards, wider audiences) and negative impacts (pressure on athletes, distortion of scheduling, exclusion of less commercial sports).
  • Extended-response questions on this topic demand balanced arguments covering multiple groups: performers, sport, officials, audiences and sponsors.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the golden triangle in sport?
A) The three phases of athletic training: strength, endurance and speed
B) The mutually reinforcing relationship between sport, sponsorship and the media
C) The three main types of sports facilities: indoor, outdoor and aquatic
D) The three tiers of sports governance: local, national and international
practice_questions.marks: B) The mutually reinforcing relationship between sport, sponsorship and the media [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'commercialisation' in the context of sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic definition indicating that sport is treated as a product/business; 1 mark for linking this to financial gain or profit, or to the involvement of sponsors, media or businesses. Example full-mark answer: 'Commercialisation is the process by which sport is treated as a commercial product, with businesses investing in it to generate profit through sponsorship, media rights and merchandise sales.'

practice_questions.text: Explain two positive impacts and two negative impacts of sponsorship on performers in sport.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for any of the following, up to 4 marks total (must cover both positives and negatives for full marks):
Positive: financial security allowing full-time training (1); access to high-quality equipment and coaching (1); increased public profile through media exposure (1).
Negative: pressure to compete while injured to meet commercial obligations (1); loss of control over personal image as a brand ambassador (1); intense media scrutiny of personal life (1).

practice_questions.text: A county-level hockey club has recently attracted a regional sports retailer as a kit sponsor. Analyse the impact of this sponsorship arrangement on the club, its players and the sponsoring company.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Discusses impacts on all three parties (club, players and sponsor) with developed points and specific examples. Considers both positive and negative implications. Uses accurate commercial vocabulary (sponsorship, branding, profile, obligations). Answers read as continuous analysis, not a list.
Secure: Covers at least two of the three parties with developed points; mostly accurate; some sporting application.
Developing: Relevant points but limited development; may address only one or two parties; minimal sporting application.
Emerging: Basic or vague points; no development; may only state that sponsorship provides money without exploring implications.

Acceptable points include: Club gains kit/equipment costs covered and may attract better players (positive); club may face pressure to display sponsor logos prominently or associate with the brand (limitation); players gain professional-quality kit and raised local profile (positive); players may feel obligated to represent the brand positively off the pitch (negative); sponsor gains brand visibility at matches and through players wearing their kit (positive); sponsor risks reputational damage if players behave badly (negative); sponsor reaches a targeted local audience of sports participants (positive).

practice_questions.text: A young county-level sprinter has been offered a significant sponsorship deal by a national sportswear company. Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of accepting this deal for both the sprinter and for athletics as a sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sides for both the sprinter and the sport of athletics. Consistent use of sporting examples. Reaches a reasoned conclusion. Uses precise vocabulary (sponsorship, commercialisation, media exposure, obligations). Balanced argument throughout.
Secure: Covers advantages and disadvantages for the sprinter; some reference to the sport of athletics; generally accurate; mostly applied to a sporting context.
Developing: Mostly one-sided or focused only on the sprinter; limited reference to athletics as a sport; some relevant points but underdeveloped.
Emerging: Basic points about money being good or bad; no sporting application; descriptive rather than evaluative.

Acceptable points:
For the sprinter (advantages): financial security enabling full-time training; access to high-quality kit at no cost; raised public profile and media opportunities; pathway to further commercial deals.
For the sprinter (disadvantages): pressure to perform when injured to protect commercial value; obligations to represent the brand in specific ways; intense media scrutiny; risk of being dropped if performance declines.
For athletics (advantages): sponsorship raises the profile of the sport; funds available to invest in facilities or grassroots development; successful sponsored athletes act as role models.
For athletics (disadvantages): commercial interests may lead to scheduling being altered for broadcast convenience; focus on elite performers may divert resources from grassroots; smaller events without commercial appeal may be marginalised.

practice_questions.text: State two types of sponsorship that a professional sports club might receive.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two distinct types: financial sponsorship (1); clothing and equipment sponsorship (1); facility/venue sponsorship (1). Answers must be qualitatively different — two examples of money-based sponsorship would score only 1 mark.

socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.title: Technology in Sport
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.description: How technology affects performers, officials, audiences and the integrity of sport.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.content_html:
Technology’s Growing Role in Sport

Technology has transformed every aspect of modern sport, from how athletes train and compete to how officials make decisions and how audiences watch events. Advances in performance analysis technology mean that a sprint coach can examine a runner’s biomechanics frame-by-frame, identifying tiny inefficiencies in technique that would be invisible to the naked eye. Meanwhile, officiating technology has given referees, umpires and judges access to replays and data that make certain decisions far more accurate. These changes bring clear benefits but also raise important questions about fairness, the integrity of sport and the human element of competition.

Benefits of Technology for Performers

Athletes benefit from technology in training, recovery and competition. Wearable heart rate monitors, GPS trackers and lactate testing devices allow coaches to track an athlete’s workload with precision, reducing the risk of overtraining and injury. Video analysis software allows performers to review their own technique immediately after practice, a form of knowledge of performance feedback that was once available only through a coach’s spoken description. In competition, swimwear developed using fluid dynamics research reduces drag in the water, and running shoes engineered with carbon-fibre plates return more energy to the foot with each stride. These advances have contributed to significant improvements in world records across multiple disciplines.

Key Fact

Technology benefits performers through more precise training monitoring (wearables, GPS, video analysis), improved equipment design (swimwear, running shoes) and faster feedback on technique. These advantages can improve performance and reduce injury risk.

Drawbacks of Technology for Performers

Not all technological impacts on performers are positive. Athletes from wealthier nations or better-funded clubs have access to far more advanced technology than those from less affluent backgrounds, creating an uneven playing field at both national and international level. There is also the risk of technology dependency: a performer who relies entirely on data feedback from devices may find it harder to develop intrinsic awareness of their own body. Additionally, innovations in equipment — such as advanced swimwear that was later banned by governing bodies — can blur the line between technological advantage and performance-enhancing equipment, raising ethical questions about fairness.

Technology and Officials

Officiating technology has had a profound effect on decision accuracy. Systems that track ball position, player movements and contact points allow officials to review contentious decisions with high precision. Positive outcomes include fewer incorrect decisions affecting match results and reduced pressure on officials in the most high-stakes moments. However, technology also changes the rhythm of competition: reviews and interventions can disrupt the flow of a game, frustrate players and reduce the spontaneity that makes sport exciting. There is also a philosophical concern that removing uncertainty from officiating changes the nature of sport, which has always involved a human element on both sides of the white line.

Students often assume that more technology automatically means fairer officiating. This oversimplifies the issue. Officiating systems rely on the accuracy of their sensors and the interpretation of rules by those reviewing footage. A marginal decision that the system rules on may still be disputed because the technology has tolerances and thresholds. Furthermore, only sports and events with sufficient funding can afford the technology in the first place, meaning high-level competitions may have access to review systems that lower leagues do not — raising questions about consistency of standards across the sport. A strong analysis question answer must consider these limitations alongside the benefits.

Technology and Audiences

Technology has transformed the experience for audiences. High-definition television broadcasting, multiple camera angles, instant replays, slow-motion footage and statistical overlays have made watching sport at home a richer experience than ever before. Streaming services allow audiences to watch events on mobile devices anywhere in the world, expanding global fanbases. Social media integration means fans can discuss events in real time, creating a sense of community even among geographically dispersed supporters. On the negative side, the shift to subscription-based streaming means that some audiences, particularly those with lower incomes, may be priced out of watching major events that were previously available on free-to-air television.

Key Fact

Technology impacts audiences positively through high-definition broadcasts, multiple camera angles and global streaming; negatively through paywalls that may exclude lower-income fans from watching major events on free-to-air television.

Technology and Sponsors

For sponsors and commercial partners, technology has opened new opportunities. Digital advertising boards in stadia can be customised for different broadcast markets, showing different sponsors’ logos to television audiences in different countries simultaneously. Social media analytics allow sponsors to measure the exact reach and engagement generated by their association with athletes or events, providing data to justify investment. However, the rise of streaming means that viewing audiences are more fragmented across platforms than they were when everyone watched on the same free-to-air channel, which can make it harder for sponsors to guarantee the mass audience exposure they once received.

Technology and the Integrity of Sport

One of the deepest debates around technology concerns sport’s integrity. When equipment advances produce significant performance gains, governing bodies must decide whether such technology provides a legal advantage that is open to all, or whether it constitutes a form of technological doping. Similarly, the use of data analysis systems to study an opponent’s patterns in minute detail raises questions about whether preparation based on technology reduces the creativity and adaptability that make individual sports captivating. These are not straightforward questions, and students who can articulate both sides of the argument — with specific sporting examples — will score well on extended-response questions.

Broadcasting technology has opened sport to genuinely global audiences. Events like the Olympic Games are watched by billions of people across multiple continents, and modern broadcast infrastructure — including satellite uplinks, fibre optic cables and compression technology — makes it possible to deliver high-quality live footage anywhere with an internet connection. The coverage of the Paralympic Games has grown dramatically as broadcast technology improved, helping to challenge perceptions of disability and inspire new participation. For sponsors, a global broadcast audience represents an extraordinarily valuable commercial opportunity; for athletes, it brings both opportunity and obligation. This expansion of audiences has also driven investment in previously marginalised sports and diversified the range of sporting content available to viewers.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.exam_tip_html: On a 6-mark ‘Analyse’ question about technology in sport, a common error is describing what technology does without explaining the impact. The mark scheme rewards analysis: state the technology, describe its effect, explain who benefits or loses out, and give a sporting example. Avoid vague statements such as “technology is good for sport” — be specific: “GPS tracking allows coaches to monitor a player’s sprint distance in training, enabling workload to be adjusted to reduce injury risk.” For 9-mark ‘Evaluate’ questions, always consider technology’s impact on multiple groups (performers, officials, audiences, sponsors) and ensure your argument addresses both benefits and drawbacks. One-sided answers are capped at the Developing band.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Technology benefits performers (wearables, video analysis, improved equipment), officials (greater accuracy in decisions) and audiences (HD broadcasting, streaming, multiple camera angles).
  • Technology also carries drawbacks: inequalities in access, disruption to the flow of competition, paywalled content excluding lower-income fans, and questions about fairness when equipment advances are not universally available.
  • Extended-response answers on technology must evaluate impacts across multiple groups and consider both positive and negative consequences to reach a balanced, well-supported conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Identify one way that technology is used to help officials in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any valid example of officiating technology, such as: video review/replay systems (1); sensor-based line-call or tracking systems (1); goal-line technology (1).

practice_questions.text: State two negative impacts of technology on audiences who watch sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct negative impacts: subscription/paywalled streaming pricing out lower-income fans (1); breaks in play due to technology reviews disrupting viewing experience (1); fragmentation of audiences across multiple platforms reducing shared viewing experience (1). Two near-identical points (e.g. 'it costs money' and 'it is expensive') earn only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways technology can improve the experience of watching sport for a television audience.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying the technology; 1 mark for explaining how it improves the viewer experience. Up to 4 marks (2 ways × 2 marks each).
Example points: High-definition and multi-angle cameras allow viewers to see detail they could not see in person (identification 1; explanation 1); instant slow-motion replays allow audiences to review controversial moments and understand decisions better (identification 1; explanation 1); statistical overlays and graphics provide additional context such as player speeds, distances and tactical patterns (identification 1; explanation 1).

practice_questions.text: A club-level rugby union team has recently been given access to a GPS tracking system for training sessions. The head coach wants to use the data to reduce injuries and improve conditioning. Analyse the impact this technology might have on the players and on the coaching staff.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis of impacts on both players and coaching staff. Points are developed with specific examples. Both positive and negative consequences are explored. Accurate sport-science vocabulary used throughout.
Secure: Impacts on both groups covered; mostly accurate; mostly applied to a sporting context; some development of points.
Developing: Relevant points present but limited development; may focus predominantly on one group; minimal sporting application.
Emerging: Basic observations that GPS provides data or tells coaches things; no development or application to the scenario.

Acceptable points:
For players: more precise workload management may reduce injury risk (positive); data can motivate players by showing objective progress (positive); some players may feel over-monitored or anxious about being judged on data metrics (negative); performance data could lead to unfair selection decisions if taken out of context (negative).
For coaching staff: precise training load data enables more evidence-based decisions about intensity and recovery (positive); ability to identify players at elevated injury risk before injury occurs (positive); large volumes of data require time and expertise to interpret correctly (limitation); technology cost and training to use it may be a barrier for smaller clubs (limitation).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the impact of technology on the integrity and fairness of sport, considering both its benefits and its potential to undermine what makes sport valuable.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation exploring multiple dimensions of fairness and integrity. Considers performers, officials and sport as a whole. Uses specific sporting examples. Reaches a reasoned, balanced conclusion. Precise vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Addresses benefits and drawbacks of technology for fairness and/or integrity; mostly accurate; mostly applied to a sporting context; generally balanced.
Developing: Mostly one-sided or vague; relevant points present but underdeveloped; limited sporting context.
Emerging: Basic statements about technology being helpful or harmful with no development or sporting application.

Acceptable points:
For integrity/fairness (benefits): officiating technology reduces incorrect decisions that affect match outcomes; drug-testing technology makes it harder for athletes to use banned substances; performance data levels the playing field by giving coaches objective information; Paralympic broadcasting technology has changed perceptions of disability sport.
Against integrity/fairness (drawbacks): unequal access to technology creates a new form of inequality between well-funded and under-resourced teams; advanced equipment innovations may give wealthy nations a technological edge; video review systems interrupt play and can reduce spontaneity; reliance on technology may erode coaches' and athletes' intrinsic knowledge and intuition; some equipment innovations have been banned after providing unfair advantages, suggesting regulation lags behind technology.

practice_questions.text: State two ways technology has changed how sports are broadcast to audiences.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct points: high-definition/multi-camera broadcasts (1); live streaming to mobile or internet-connected devices (1); instant slow-motion replay (1); statistical graphics and overlays during broadcasts (1). Two near-identical answers earn only 1 mark.

socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.title: Conduct of Performers in Sport
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.description: Etiquette, sportsmanship, gamesmanship and the contract to compete in modern sport.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.content_html:
How Performers Are Expected to Behave

Sport is governed not only by written rules but by unwritten codes of conduct that define how athletes are expected to treat opponents, officials and the spirit of competition itself. These codes range from formal agreements to cultural customs, and they are often tested most severely when the pressure to win is at its greatest. Understanding the difference between behaviour that upholds sporting values and behaviour that exploits or undermines them is central to sport’s identity as more than a simple contest of skill.

Etiquette

Etiquette refers to the unwritten rules of conduct in sport — customs that participants are expected to follow even though they are not written into the official rule book. In tennis, it is considered etiquette to acknowledge a lucky net cord with a gesture to your opponent. In golf, players are expected to repair divots, rake bunkers and maintain silence when others are playing. In cricket, a fielding side traditionally applauds a departing batsman who has played well. None of these behaviours are compulsory under the laws of the game, but failing to observe them draws social disapproval and signals a disrespect for the sport’s traditions.

Sportsmanship

Sportsmanship describes behaviour that embodies fair play, respect and generosity in competition. A sportsmanlike act might include a footballer kicking the ball out of play when an opponent is injured so they can receive treatment, despite there being no rule requiring it. It includes shaking hands with opponents after a match, accepting officials’ decisions without complaint, and refusing to take advantage of an opponent’s misfortune. Sportsmanship is widely seen as a moral standard to which all competitors should aspire, regardless of the stakes.

Key Fact

Etiquette is the unwritten code of conduct in a sport (customs and traditions). Sportsmanship is the attitude and behaviour of fair play, respect and generosity towards opponents and officials. Both go beyond the written rules.

Gamesmanship

Gamesmanship sits at the opposite end of the conduct spectrum from sportsmanship. It involves using strategies that are technically within the rules but deliberately break their spirit to gain an unfair advantage. Examples include: a tennis player bouncing the ball an excessive number of times before serving in order to disrupt an opponent’s concentration; a rugby player deliberately slowing down play by lying on the wrong side of a ruck for as long as the referee will allow; or a batsman calling for a new bat or changing their gloves when the bowling side is building momentum, purely to break their rhythm. Gamesmanship is legal but widely considered unsporting.

Gamesmanship is distinguishable from outright cheating because it stays within the formal rules. Cheating — such as deliberately handling the ball in football or falsifying a time in athletics — breaks the written rules and can result in disqualification. Gamesmanship breaks the spirit but not the letter of the law. However, the boundary is contested. At what point does prolonged time-wasting become a cynical act that undermines the sport? At what point does sledging (verbal distraction) in cricket cross from psychological contest into intimidation? These questions have no simple answers, which is precisely why they generate rich material for extended-response questions.

The Contract to Compete

The contract to compete is the implicit agreement that all participants enter when they take part in a sporting contest. By agreeing to compete, athletes commit to abiding by the rules, respecting the spirit of the competition and giving their opponents a fair chance to succeed. The contract to compete underpins concepts of fair play — without it, sport would be reduced to a simple contest in which any tactic, no matter how unethical, was acceptable as long as it helped you win. A performer who deliberately injures an opponent, uses performance-enhancing drugs or engages in aggressive gamesmanship to the point of intimidation could be said to be breaking the contract to compete.

Key Fact

The contract to compete is the implicit agreement all competitors enter when they take part in sport. It requires them to abide by the rules, respect opponents and the spirit of the game, and give all participants a fair chance to succeed.

Why These Concepts Matter

These concepts matter beyond individual events. Sport’s social and cultural value rests partly on its reputation as an arena in which effort, skill and fair competition determine outcomes. When gamesmanship becomes widespread, public trust in sport erodes. When sportsmanship is absent, sport loses its role as a model of positive values for young participants. Research into youth sport suggests that the conduct of elite athletes influences the attitudes and behaviours of young people who aspire to perform at a high level. Athletes who model sportsmanship — acknowledging good play by opponents, respecting officials and competing without cynicism — provide a more powerful form of role model influence than those who win by any means necessary.

Students often use etiquette and sportsmanship interchangeably, but they are distinct concepts. Etiquette is about customs and traditions specific to a sport (how you are expected to behave in that sporting context). Sportsmanship is a broader moral attitude about how you treat opponents and the spirit of competition regardless of the sport. In a 6-mark question asking you to describe the conduct expected of performers, you should use both terms accurately: describe the etiquette of a specific sport (e.g. kicking the ball out in football when an opponent is injured) and describe sportsmanship as a general value (e.g. shaking hands after the match and accepting the official’s decision). Using both terms correctly with specific sporting examples will earn full credit.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.exam_tip_html: For a 3-mark ‘Describe’ question on conduct, students often give one-word answers like “etiquette means respect.” To earn 3 marks, describe the concept fully (what it is), give a specific sporting example, and explain why it matters. For a 6-mark ‘Analyse’ question, avoid listing definitions. Instead, analyse how each type of conduct shapes the experience of sport for different groups — performers, officials, spectators and young participants. A common error is treating gamesmanship as identical to cheating; be clear that gamesmanship is within the rules but against their spirit, which is a meaningful distinction worth developing in your answer.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Etiquette is the unwritten code of conduct in a sport (customs and traditions); sportsmanship is the broader moral attitude of fair play, respect and generosity towards opponents and officials.
  • Gamesmanship exploits loopholes within the rules to gain a psychological or tactical advantage — it is legal but widely considered unsporting and damaging to the spirit of competition.
  • The contract to compete is the implicit agreement all participants enter: to abide by the rules, respect the spirit of the sport and give opponents a fair chance — the foundation of fair play in all sport.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes gamesmanship?
A) Behaviour that involves physically harming an opponent to gain advantage
B) Strategies that break the formal rules of the sport to achieve a result
C) Actions that are within the rules but deliberately violate the spirit of competition
D) Behaviour that shows respect and generosity towards opponents
practice_questions.marks: C) Actions that are within the rules but deliberately violate the spirit of competition [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'sportsmanship' in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic definition identifying fair play, respect or generosity; 1 mark for linking this to treatment of opponents, officials or the rules of the sport. Example full-mark answer: 'Sportsmanship is behaviour that shows fair play, respect and generosity towards opponents, officials and the rules of the sport, placing the spirit of competition above personal gain.'

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'etiquette' in sport and give one specific sporting example.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying etiquette as unwritten rules or informal codes of conduct (not part of the official rule book); 1 mark for explaining that etiquette involves customs or traditions expected of participants; 1 mark for a valid sporting example (e.g. tennis player acknowledging a net cord; golfer repairing divots; cricketer applauding a departing batsman). Example full-mark answer: 'Etiquette is the unwritten code of conduct expected of performers in sport (1). It consists of customs and traditions that are not part of the official rules but that participants are expected to follow to show respect for the sport (1). For example, in tennis it is expected that a player will gesture to acknowledge a lucky net cord, even though there is no rule requiring this (1).'

practice_questions.text: Explain why the contract to compete is important for maintaining fair play in sport. Use a sporting example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for defining the contract to compete as an implicit agreement to abide by the rules and spirit of the sport; 1 mark for explaining that it requires competitors to give opponents a fair chance; 1 mark for explaining what happens when the contract is broken (erosion of trust, unfair outcomes); 1 mark for a valid sporting example where the contract was upheld or broken. Example: 'The contract to compete is the implicit agreement all competitors enter when they take part in sport (1). It requires athletes to follow the rules and give opponents a fair chance to succeed (1). When it is broken — for instance, if a performer uses excessive gamesmanship to intimidate an opponent or deliberately injures a rival — the principle of fair competition is undermined and public trust in the sport is damaged (1). In cricket, the contract to compete means batsmen should not use excessive time-wasting tactics to break a bowler’s rhythm if it goes beyond legitimate play (1).'

practice_questions.text: A year-10 county football player has noticed that their team’s opponents regularly engage in gamesmanship during matches, including excessive time-wasting, feigning injury and making loud comments designed to distract players during set pieces. Analyse the impact this behaviour might have on the match, the performers involved and the wider sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis across all three areas (match, performers, wider sport). Points are developed with specific examples. The distinction between gamesmanship and cheating is maintained throughout. Uses accurate vocabulary (etiquette, sportsmanship, contract to compete, spirit of sport). Continuous analytical prose rather than a list.
Secure: Covers at least two of the three areas with developed points; mostly accurate; mostly applied to a football context.
Developing: Relevant points present but limited development; may address only one area; minimal sporting context.
Emerging: Basic observations that gamesmanship is bad or unfair; no development or sporting application.

Acceptable points:
On the match: time-wasting reduces the quality of play and the time available for genuine competition (negative); it may frustrate the opposition into making errors or receiving cautions from the referee (tactical gain for gamesmanship team).
On the performers: players on the receiving end may feel demoralised, distracted or become aggressive in response (negative); players using gamesmanship may lose focus on their own technique and game plan (risk); young performers may normalise gamesmanship as acceptable behaviour (wider harm).
On the wider sport: frequent gamesmanship erodes the spectator experience (negative); it damages sport’s reputation as a model of positive values for young people (negative); officials face greater difficulty managing the game (increased pressure on officials); if gamesmanship becomes culturally accepted, the contract to compete and the spirit of the sport are undermined (structural harm to sport).

practice_questions.text: State two examples of etiquette from different sports.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct examples from different sports (any sport is acceptable). Examples: tennis player acknowledging a net cord to their opponent (1); golfer repairing a divot or raking a bunker (1); cricketer applauding a well-played innings by an opposition batsman (1); rugby player helping an opponent to their feet after a tackle (1); footballer kicking the ball into touch when an opponent is injured (1). Two examples from the same sport earn only 1 mark if they refer to the same type of behaviour.
