socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.title: Performance Enhancing Drugs and Blood Doping
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.description: Prohibited substances, blood doping and the advantages and disadvantages for performers.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.content_html:
Performance-Enhancing Drugs in Sport

Performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) are substances that athletes take to improve their physical or psychological output in training or competition. Most PEDs are prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and the governing bodies of individual sports. The use of prohibited substances is considered cheating because it undermines the principle of fair competition and often poses serious health risks to the performer. Despite this, doping remains a persistent problem across numerous sports at elite level. Understanding which categories of PED exist, why performers use them and the consequences they carry is essential both for the exam and for understanding the ethical landscape of modern sport.

Stimulants

Stimulants are substances that increase alertness, reduce the sensation of fatigue and heighten aggression and competitiveness. They can improve reaction time and allow a performer to sustain high-intensity effort for longer. Sports such as sprint cycling or combat sports, where aggression and alertness are direct performance assets, have seen stimulant abuse. Side effects include elevated heart rate, anxiety, insomnia and in severe cases heart attack. Stimulants are banned in competition by most governing bodies.

Narcotic Analgesics

Narcotic analgesics are powerful painkillers that reduce or eliminate the sensation of pain. Performers who have sustained injuries, or who train at a very high volume (which inevitably produces chronic discomfort), may be tempted to use narcotic analgesics to continue competing. The critical danger is that pain is the body’s warning signal. A performer who cannot feel pain is at serious risk of worsening an existing injury, potentially causing long-term damage to tendons, ligaments or bones. Side effects include dependency, nausea and loss of coordination.

Anabolic Agents

Anabolic agents, commonly called anabolic steroids, are synthetic hormones that accelerate the development of muscle mass and reduce recovery time between training sessions. They are most commonly associated with power-based sports such as weightlifting, shot put or rugby, where muscle mass is a direct determinant of performance. By allowing performers to train harder and recover faster, anabolic agents provide a substantial competitive advantage. Side effects include liver damage, cardiovascular disease, hormonal disruption (including in secondary sexual characteristics) and, in adolescent users, premature closure of growth plates, which can permanently reduce height.

Key Fact

Five main categories of prohibited substance: stimulants (alertness, reduce fatigue — sprint/combat sports); narcotic analgesics (mask pain — injury management); anabolic agents (muscle mass — power sports); diuretics (weight loss — weight-category sports); peptide hormones such as EPO (oxygen-carrying capacity — endurance sports).

Diuretics

Diuretics accelerate fluid loss through urine production. In weight-category sports such as boxing, judo or weightlifting, an athlete might use a diuretic in the days before weigh-in to shed enough fluid to compete in a lower weight category, gaining a size and strength advantage against smaller opponents. Diuretics are also sometimes misused to dilute urine samples, reducing the concentration of other banned substances and making them harder to detect. Side effects include dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, muscle cramps and, in severe cases, cardiac arrhythmia.

Peptide Hormones and EPO

Erythropoietin (EPO) is the most widely known peptide hormone misused in sport. Normally produced naturally by the kidneys in response to low oxygen levels (such as at altitude), EPO stimulates the production of red blood cells. More red blood cells means a greater capacity to carry oxygen to working muscles, which directly improves aerobic endurance performance. EPO has been widely associated with endurance cycling, cross-country skiing and distance running. Side effects include dangerous thickening of the blood (increased viscosity), which slows blood flow and increases the risk of blood clots, stroke and heart attack — particularly during sleep, when heart rate is low and blood flows slowly.

Blood doping achieves the same outcome as EPO — increased red blood cell count — through a different mechanism. An athlete removes a quantity of their own blood several weeks before competition. The body naturally replaces it. The stored blood is then frozen and re-infused just before the competition begins, producing an artificially elevated red blood cell count and enhanced oxygen-carrying capacity. The benefits are the same as EPO: improved aerobic endurance performance. The side effects are significant: the blood thickens after re-infusion (increased viscosity), which raises the risk of heart attack and stroke. There is also a serious risk of infection from contaminated equipment and the risk of an embolism (a blockage of a blood vessel by a clot or air bubble), which can be fatal.

Beta Blockers

Beta blockers are a distinct category of substance that are permitted in most sports but are restricted in a small number where fine motor control is critical to performance. They reduce heart rate, lower muscle tension and decrease blood pressure by blocking the effects of adrenaline. In sports requiring extreme precision — such as archery, shooting or snooker — a reduced heart rate and steadier hand provides a direct performance advantage. Side effects include nausea, weakness and potentially dangerous cardiac problems. Beta blockers should only be used under medical prescription; athletes using them without medical need in restricted sports face sanctions.

Key Fact

Blood doping and EPO both increase red blood cell count and oxygen-carrying capacity. Both cause dangerous thickening of the blood (increased viscosity), raising the risk of heart attack, stroke and embolism. Blood doping additionally carries risks of infection and embolism from the transfusion process.

Advantages and Disadvantages for Performers

The spec requires students to evaluate both sides of PED use from the performer’s perspective. The potential advantages include: an increased chance of winning; access to fame and financial rewards that success brings; and, where many competitors are doping, a perceived level playing field. The disadvantages are substantial and wide-ranging. Health risks range from liver damage to cardiac arrest and addiction. Detection leads to bans, fines and career destruction. Reputational damage can be permanent and extends to sponsors, national associations and fellow competitors who competed cleanly. For sport as a whole, high-profile doping scandals damage credibility and can reduce spectator interest and commercial revenue over time.

Some athletes have argued that if everyone is doping, using PEDs simply restores a level playing field. Students should be able to challenge this reasoning. First, not all athletes dope — those who refuse to do so are placed at a systematic disadvantage, which is not a level playing field. Second, access to the most effective and safest doping protocols depends on resources, meaning wealthier athletes and nations dope more safely and effectively than poorer ones — an inequality within the inequality. Third, the argument normalises a race to ever-higher levels of doping that accelerates health risks for all. A strong 9-mark answer will recognise the argument, acknowledge why it holds superficial appeal to performers, and then dismantle it with these counter-points.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.exam_tip_html: On a 3-mark ‘Describe’ question about a specific PED category, give three distinct pieces of information: what the substance does, which type of performer might use it and why, and one side effect. Avoid the common error of repeating the same point in different words — for example, “it increases muscle mass” and “it helps muscles grow” are the same point and will only earn 1 mark. For a 9-mark ‘Evaluate’ question on whether PED use can ever be justified, you must present genuine arguments on both sides and reach a conclusion. A response that only condemns PED use without engaging with the arguments athletes make for using them will be capped at the Developing band. Use the ‘For X… However Y…’ structure with a specific sporting type anchored to each side.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Five prohibited categories: stimulants (alertness), narcotic analgesics (pain), anabolic agents (muscle mass), diuretics (weight loss), peptide hormones including EPO (oxygen-carrying capacity). Blood doping achieves the same effect as EPO via transfusion. Beta blockers are restricted, not banned outright.
  • EPO and blood doping both thicken the blood (increased viscosity), raising the risk of heart attack, stroke and embolism — potentially fatal side effects that apply to both methods.
  • Advantages for performers include potential success, fame and wealth; disadvantages include severe health risks, bans, fines, reputational damage and long-term career destruction.

practice_questions.text: Identify the category of performance-enhancing drug most likely to be used by a powerlifter who wants to increase muscle mass rapidly.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: anabolic agents (1) or anabolic steroids (1).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'blood doping' in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that blood doping involves removing and re-infusing blood to increase red blood cell count; 1 mark for linking this to an improvement in oxygen-carrying capacity or endurance performance. Example full-mark answer: 'Blood doping is a prohibited method in which an athlete removes a quantity of their own blood weeks before competition, stores it, and re-infuses it just before competing in order to artificially increase red blood cell count and oxygen-carrying capacity.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the effects and side effects of using EPO as a performance-enhancing substance.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying that EPO increases red blood cell production; 1 mark for explaining that this increases oxygen-carrying capacity and benefits endurance performance; 1 mark for a valid side effect (blood thickening/increased viscosity; risk of heart attack or stroke; risk of blood clot/embolism). Example full-mark answer: 'EPO stimulates the production of red blood cells in the body (1). More red blood cells increase the blood’s ability to carry oxygen to working muscles, improving aerobic endurance performance (1). A dangerous side effect is that EPO thickens the blood, increasing viscosity, which can lead to blood clots, heart attack or stroke (1).'

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why a performer might choose to use anabolic agents, and two reasons why this decision could have serious negative consequences for them.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks (2 reasons for + 2 consequences): must cover both sides for full marks.
Reasons for using (up to 2 marks): increased muscle mass improving strength and power performance (1); faster recovery from training enabling greater training volume (1); increased chance of competition success leading to financial reward and recognition (1).
Negative consequences (up to 2 marks): risk of liver damage and cardiovascular disease (1); hormonal disruption, including in secondary sexual characteristics (1); risk of ban, fine and permanent reputational damage if detected (1); permanent growth plate damage in adolescent users (1).

practice_questions.text: A club-level distance runner has been told by a teammate that EPO is undetectable and that many top competitors use it anyway. Evaluate the arguments for and against the runner using EPO, and reach a conclusion about whether such arguments can be justified.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation presenting genuine arguments on both sides. Challenges the ‘level playing field’ reasoning with counter-arguments. Uses accurate physiological vocabulary (red blood cells, oxygen-carrying capacity, viscosity). Reaches a reasoned, balanced conclusion. Consistent sporting application throughout.
Secure: Covers arguments for and against EPO use; mostly accurate physiological understanding; mostly applied to an endurance sporting context; generally balanced.
Developing: Mostly one-sided or acknowledges both sides without developing either; some relevant points but underdeveloped; limited sporting application.
Emerging: Basic statements that EPO is wrong or helpful without physiological explanation; no balanced argument; descriptive rather than evaluative.

Acceptable arguments for using EPO: increased red blood cells improve oxygen delivery to muscles, directly improving endurance performance; may be perceived as levelling the field if others are doping; potential for greater competition success, fame and financial reward; if truly undetectable, perceived risk of sanction is low.
Arguments against using EPO: blood thickening significantly raises risk of heart attack, stroke and embolism — particularly dangerous during sleep when heart rate is low; the ‘level playing field’ argument is flawed because many competitors do not dope; wealthier competitors access safer protocols creating new inequalities; if detected, consequences include lengthy ban, loss of results, fines and career-ending reputational damage; the use violates the contract to compete and the ethical foundations of sport; the sport of distance running suffers credibility damage from doping scandals, reducing sponsorship and audience engagement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two side effects of blood doping for a performer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark each for any three distinct side effects, or 1 mark for identifying the mechanism and 1 mark for explaining the consequence. Acceptable side effects: thickening of blood/increased viscosity (1); risk of heart attack (1); risk of stroke/embolism/blockage of a blood vessel (1); potential infection from contaminated equipment (1); risk from the transfusion process itself (1). Example 3-mark answer: 'Blood doping causes the blood to thicken as red blood cell count increases (1). This increased viscosity slows blood flow and raises the risk of a heart attack (1). There is also a risk of embolism — a blockage of a blood vessel — which can be fatal (1).'

glossary_terms.definition: Substances taken by performers to gain an advantage in competition or training, most of which are prohibited by sporting governing bodies.
Drugs that increase alertness, reduce fatigue and heighten competitiveness, prohibited in most sports during competition.
Painkilling drugs that mask the sensation of pain, allowing performers to train or compete through injuries that would otherwise prevent participation.
Synthetic hormones that promote muscle growth and increase lean body mass, used illegally by power and strength athletes to accelerate training adaptations.
Substances that increase the rate of urine production, used to achieve rapid weight loss in weight-category sports or to dilute the concentration of other prohibited substances.

A naturally occurring hormone produced by the kidneys that stimulates red blood cell production; synthetic EPO is a prohibited peptide hormone used to boost oxygen-carrying capacity in endurance athletes.
A prohibited method in which an athlete removes, stores and later re-infuses their own blood to increase red blood cell count before competition.

socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.title: Spectator Behaviour and Hooliganism
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.description: The positive and negative effects of crowds and the strategies used to combat hooliganism.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.content_html:
Spectators: A Force for Good and Ill

Sporting events exist, in large part, because of spectators. The roar of a packed stadium, the wave of noise that greets a home goal, the nervous hush before a penalty — all of these are products of crowd presence. Yet that same crowd can become a source of danger, intimidation and reputational damage if behaviour breaks down. Understanding the dual nature of spectator influence is essential for any student of sport.

Home advantage is one of the clearest positive effects of a crowd. Research in English football consistently shows that home teams win more often than away teams. The reasons are several: players feed off crowd energy, officials may be subconsciously influenced by the home crowd’s reactions, and away teams carry the psychological burden of hostile noise. In athletics, a partisan stadium crowd can lift a 400-metre runner through the final bend in a way that an empty track simply cannot replicate.

Key Fact

Spectators generate atmosphere and can provide a significant home advantage. However, they can also create excessive pressure, trigger crowd trouble and pose safety risks — all of which can harm both performance and the wider reputation of a sport.

Positive Effects of Spectators

Beyond home advantage, spectators contribute to the financial sustainability of sport. Gate receipts, broadcast rights and sponsorship are all driven by audience size. A full stadium signals a healthy, commercially attractive sport. For young performers in particular, crowd support can be a powerful intrinsic motivator: seeing others invest emotion in your performance reinforces a sense of belonging and purpose. High-profile events broadcast to millions can also inspire young people to take up a sport, widening engagement patterns in the population.

Negative Effects of Spectators

The negative effects of spectators are equally significant. Crowd noise and hostile atmosphere can increase a performer’s arousal beyond the optimal level, tipping them into over-arousal and a deterioration in performance — a concept explored in the inverted-U theory covered in Lesson 10. An away goalkeeper pelted with abuse before a penalty shoot-out is being subjected to deliberate psychological disruption. Even without overt hostility, the weight of a large crowd’s expectations can cause anxiety and choking in performers who struggle to manage their mental state.

More seriously, spectators who move beyond verbal hostility into physical confrontation create a public order crisis. Hooliganism is the collective term for this behaviour, and it has been a significant problem in English football since at least the 1960s. Hooliganism causes direct harm to individuals, destroys the spectator experience for law-abiding fans, generates enormous policing costs and has led to English clubs being banned from European competition (following the Heysel stadium disaster of 1985). The knock-on effect for grassroots participation is real: younger players and families are deterred from attending or playing if they associate the sport with violence.

Hooliganism rarely has a single cause. The spec identifies a range of overlapping factors:

  • Rivalries: historic or local rivalries (city derbies, regional contests) intensify emotional investment to the point where hostility feels justified.
  • Hype: media build-up can manufacture a sense of occasion that encourages aggressive group identity.
  • Alcohol and drugs: disinhibit behaviour and reduce the individual’s risk calculation.
  • Frustration: poor refereeing decisions or a losing scoreline can trigger reactive aggression in crowd members already emotionally primed.
  • Gang culture: for some groups, attending a match is a vehicle for pre-organised violence unconnected to the sport itself.
  • Display of masculinity: sociological research suggests that for certain subcultures, hooliganism functions as a performance of toughness, with crowd disorder reinforcing group identity and status.

Understanding these causes is important because the effectiveness of control strategies depends on which causes they address. Alcohol restrictions tackle disinhibition; education campaigns tackle culture; banning orders target repeat offenders regardless of cause.

Strategies to Combat Hooliganism

Authorities have introduced numerous strategies to reduce hooliganism, and you need to be able to evaluate how effective each one is:

All-seater stadia: following the Taylor Report (1990), English top-flight grounds converted to all-seater venues. Seating reduces the anonymity of standing crowds, makes identification of offenders easier and creates a calmer physical environment. Critics argue that it has reduced atmosphere without fully eliminating disorder, and that it has priced out working-class supporters.

Segregation of fans: away supporters are allocated separate sections with barriers between them. This physically prevents the kind of confrontation between rival groups that sparks disorder. It is highly effective at the ground but displaces the problem to the streets before and after matches.

Alcohol restrictions: alcohol cannot be consumed in view of the pitch at English Football League grounds. Some high-risk matches have total alcohol bans or enforce dry trains. Alcohol is strongly correlated with disinhibited behaviour, so restrictions have a measurable effect, though determined individuals can pre-load before arriving at the stadium.

Early kick-offs: scheduling games for 12:00 or 12:30 reduces the time available for pre-match drinking, particularly for away supporters who travel by train. This is a cost-effective measure that requires no additional infrastructure.

Improved security and CCTV: increased steward numbers, police presence and extensive CCTV coverage deter disorder through visibility and the certainty of identification. CCTV also allows retrospective prosecution, contributing to successful banning order applications.

Banning orders are now the primary tool for managing persistent offenders. Courts issue them following convictions or civil applications by police. Individuals subject to a banning order must report to a police station during international matches, preventing travel abroad. Since their introduction, banning orders have reduced the number of known England hooligan offenders travelling to tournaments significantly.

Travel restrictions complement banning orders by limiting access to fixtures for away supporters in high-risk categories. Ticket-only travel schemes on official coaches reduce the number of unaccounted individuals in transit.

Education and campaigns: initiatives such as “Kick It Out” and football club community programmes aim at cultural change over the longer term. High-profile endorsements by respected athletes and ex-players carry credibility with young fans. This is the most sustainable strategy but the slowest to produce results and the hardest to evaluate with data.

Arrest statistics at English football matches have fallen substantially since the early 1990s. Compared to the period when standing terraces and minimal segregation were the norm, English football today is dramatically safer for spectators. The combination of structural changes (all-seater stadia, segregation) with legal tools (banning orders) and cultural programmes has produced genuine progress.

However, there are costs and limitations. All-seater stadia require significant capital investment — a barrier for lower-league clubs. Security staffing is expensive and is often passed on to supporters through ticket prices. Banning orders require police resource to monitor and enforce. Critics also point out that online abuse and discriminatory chanting remain difficult to prosecute and represent a continuation of spectator harm in a different form. The safest honest assessment is that physical violence has been substantially reduced but the underlying attitudes that cause it have not been fully addressed.

Key Fact

The seven main anti-hooliganism strategies are: all-seater stadia, segregation, alcohol restrictions, early kick-offs, improved security/CCTV, banning orders and education/campaigns. In an extended-response question, evaluate each on effectiveness, cost and whether it addresses the root cause or just the symptom.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.exam_tip_html: For a 9-mark evaluate question on spectator behaviour, the most common error is to list strategies without evaluating them. A Mastering-band answer does three things: (1) gives a range of strategies and causes, (2) argues which are most effective and why, and (3) acknowledges limitations or counter-arguments before a clear concluding judgement. Use the “For X… However Y…” structure for each strategy. For example: “Banning orders are effective because they prevent known offenders attending fixtures; however, they require police resource to monitor, which is costly.” For 4-mark explain questions on this topic, name a strategy, explain how it works, then say why it reduces hooliganism — three linked points, not three separate lists.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Spectators generate positive effects (atmosphere, home advantage, financial sustainability) but can cause harm through excessive pressure on performers and the risk of crowd trouble and hooliganism.
  • Hooliganism arises from multiple causes including rivalries, alcohol, frustration, gang culture and displays of masculinity — no single strategy eliminates all of them.
  • Seven main strategies combat hooliganism: all-seater stadia, segregation, alcohol restrictions, early kick-offs, improved security, banning orders and education. The most effective responses combine structural, legal and cultural measures.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a positive effect of spectators on a sporting performance?
A) Increased risk of crowd disorder
B) Excessive pressure leading to over-arousal
C) Creation of a home advantage for the home team
D) Higher security costs for the event organiser
practice_questions.marks: C) Creation of a home advantage for the home team [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why hooliganism occurs at sporting events.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of two different reasons from: rivalries between teams or fan groups; hype and media build-up; alcohol or drug use; frustration at decisions or results; gang culture; display of masculinity. Answers must be qualitatively different — 'fuelled by alcohol' and 'drug use' count as one point.

practice_questions.text: Explain how banning orders are used to combat hooliganism in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying banning orders as a legal tool (civil order issued by a court). 1 mark for explaining what they prohibit (attending specified fixtures or all football matches in the country). 1 mark for explaining how they are enforced for international fixtures (offender must surrender passport or report to a police station). 1 mark for explaining why they are effective (targets repeat offenders; removes known troublemakers; reduces incidents at high-risk matches).

practice_questions.text: Analyse the effectiveness of alcohol restrictions as a strategy for reducing hooliganism at football matches.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): identifies the strategy clearly (alcohol cannot be consumed in view of the pitch; some matches enforce total bans); analyses how it reduces hooliganism (alcohol is linked to disinhibition, reducing rational decision-making; restricting it lowers the likelihood of impulsive aggressive behaviour); acknowledges a significant limitation (pre-loading before arrival is not prevented; restriction at the ground does not control consumption during travel); reaches a developed analytical conclusion — for example, alcohol restrictions are effective within the stadium but have limited impact on disorder in surrounding streets. Uses sporting context throughout.
Secure (3–4 marks): describes the strategy and gives at least one developed analysis point with a partial limitation.
Developing (2 marks): identifies the strategy with a simple reason why it helps, but limited development or no limitation.
Emerging (1 mark): basic identification of alcohol restrictions with minimal development.

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old county-level rugby player has noticed that her performance drops noticeably when playing away fixtures in front of large, hostile crowds. Evaluate the extent to which spectators have a negative rather than positive impact on a performer's experience of sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): presents a balanced evaluation of both positive and negative spectator impacts; applies points consistently to a sporting context; covers at least three negative impacts (over-arousal, hostile atmosphere, deterrence of young participants, safety risks) and at least two positive impacts (atmosphere, home advantage, inspiration, financial support); reaches a clear justified conclusion about which outweighs the other, with a reasoned basis.
Secure (5–7 marks): covers both sides, mostly applied to sport; at least two negative and one positive point; some development beyond a list.
Developing (3–4 marks): relevant points on both sides but limited development; sporting context present but not always linked to the analysis.
Emerging (1–2 marks): basic points, mainly descriptive; one-sided or no sporting application.

practice_questions.text: A table shows annual football-related arrest figures at English grounds over five years: Year 1: 3,200; Year 2: 2,950; Year 3: 2,700; Year 4: 2,480; Year 5: 2,310. practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct calculation: 3,200 minus 2,310 = 890 arrests. 1 mark for quoting both figures and stating the unit (arrests). 1 mark for a valid inference: arrests fell by 890 over five years, suggesting anti-hooliganism strategies (such as banning orders, all-seater stadia or increased security) have been increasingly effective at reducing violent spectator behaviour.

socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.title: Physical, Emotional and Social Wellbeing
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.description: How participation in sport supports physical health, mental health and social wellbeing.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.content_html:
What Do We Mean by Health and Wellbeing?

Health is not simply the absence of illness. The World Health Organisation defines it as a state of complete physical, mental and social wellbeing — a definition that has shaped how GCSE PE approaches this topic. A person can be physically fit (able to run five kilometres without stopping) yet struggle with anxiety, loneliness or low self-worth. True wellbeing is multi-dimensional, and physical activity affects all three dimensions simultaneously, which is what makes it one of the most powerful public health tools available.

This lesson examines each dimension in turn: physical health, mental health and social health. Each is an equal component of overall wellbeing, and a physically active lifestyle improves all three.

Key Fact

Participation in physical activity improves health across three dimensions: physical (heart function, body systems, disease prevention), mental (stress reduction, hormone release, emotional control) and social (friendships, teamwork, community). These three dimensions are interconnected — improving one often improves the others.

Physical Health and Wellbeing

The physical benefits of regular exercise are the most visible and the most extensively researched. Regular aerobic activity — whether swimming, cycling, running or team sport — strengthens the heart muscle, increases stroke volume (the amount of blood ejected with each heartbeat) and reduces resting heart rate. The result is a more efficient cardiovascular system that can deliver oxygen to working muscles more effectively during exercise and recover more quickly afterwards. Athletes who train consistently over years develop bradycardia, a resting heart rate well below the population average of 70 beats per minute.

Beyond the heart, regular exercise improves the efficiency of the respiratory system, the musculoskeletal system and the immune system. The lungs become more efficient at gas exchange; muscles grow stronger and more fatigue-resistant; bones maintain their density and reduce the risk of osteoporosis in later life. These systemic benefits mean a physically active person is better equipped to perform everyday tasks (carrying shopping, climbing stairs, walking to work) and is less likely to suffer from a range of chronic diseases including type 2 diabetes, certain cancers and hypertension.

One of the clearest population-level physical benefits of exercise is its role in weight management. Regular activity burns calories, maintains muscle mass and supports a healthy body composition. This helps avoid obesity, which is itself a risk factor for heart disease, diabetes and reduced mobility. The physical and the social are already beginning to connect: an individual who maintains a healthy weight through sport is also likely to have the physical capacity to engage with others in activity, creating a positive feedback loop.

Mental Health and Wellbeing

The mental health benefits of exercise are now backed by a substantial body of clinical research and are increasingly recognised by healthcare systems as a legitimate treatment for mild-to-moderate anxiety and depression. The mechanisms are both biochemical and psychological.

At the biochemical level, moderate to vigorous exercise triggers the release of serotonin, a neurotransmitter linked to feelings of happiness and calm. It also promotes the release of endorphins — natural pain-relieving chemicals that produce the so-called “runner’s high” familiar to distance athletes. The neurological effect of these hormones is a measurable reduction in perceived stress and anxiety. For many individuals, a vigorous training session or team sport match functions as a reliable, accessible and side-effect-free stress management tool.

Beyond hormones, physical activity provides psychological benefits through mastery and control. Setting a personal best, learning a new skill or winning a team competition builds self-efficacy — the belief in one’s own capacity to succeed. This is particularly powerful for young people, for whom sporting achievement can become a foundation for confidence in other areas of life. The ability to control emotions during competition (remain calm under pressure, manage frustration after a mistake) transfers directly to emotional regulation in daily life. These mental benefits are why sport is used therapeutically in programmes for young people experiencing mental health difficulties.

Stress is the body’s physiological response to a perceived threat or challenge. When stressed, the hypothalamus activates the adrenal glands to release adrenaline and cortisol. These hormones raise heart rate, blood pressure and blood glucose, preparing the body for action. In short bursts this is useful; chronically elevated stress hormones damage the cardiovascular system, suppress immunity and impair sleep.

Exercise provides the body with a “legitimate outlet” for the physiological state stress creates. A run or a football training session allows the body to use the elevated heart rate and glucose productively. After exercise, serotonin and endorphin levels remain elevated for hours, creating a period of improved mood and reduced anxiety. Over time, regular exercisers show lower baseline cortisol levels and a faster physiological return to calm after stressful events. This is why mental health professionals increasingly recommend structured physical activity as a first-line intervention for mild anxiety.

Social Health and Wellbeing

Humans are social animals. The sense of belonging to a group, having friends and being valued by a community are fundamental psychological needs. Sport and physical activity are remarkably powerful vehicles for meeting these needs, which is why social health is a genuine and distinct category in the wellbeing framework.

Team sports in particular demand cooperation and teamwork. Playing in a netball team, a cricket XI or a rowing eight requires communication, trust, shared responsibility and collective problem-solving. These are not merely sporting skills: they are life skills transferable to workplaces, families and communities. Young people who participate in team sport regularly develop stronger interpersonal skills and a better understanding of how to negotiate conflict constructively.

Participation also creates opportunities to socialise and make friends. For individuals who are isolated — whether through geography, disability, mental health difficulties or life transitions such as moving to a new school — joining a sports club can be the single most effective intervention for reducing loneliness. Sport provides a structured social context with shared purpose, which lowers the social anxiety of unstructured socialisation. Community sport clubs also play a direct role in meeting basic social needs by connecting individuals to wider networks of mutual support.

Students sometimes assume that wellbeing benefits require competitive, high-intensity sport. This is not what the spec says, and it is not supported by the evidence. The physical, mental and social benefits of physical activity are available across a spectrum from gentle recreational walking through to elite competition. What matters is regular participation, not intensity or competitive context.

Indeed, for some individuals — particularly those recovering from mental health difficulties, or older adults entering exercise for the first time — low-intensity, non-competitive activity (yoga, social swimming, walking groups) may produce greater wellbeing gains precisely because it is accessible, enjoyable and sustainable. The spec asks you to recognise that physical activity broadly encompasses all forms of movement, not just sport.

Key Fact

For extended-response questions on wellbeing, make sure you address all three dimensions with a sporting example for each. A common error is to write only about physical benefits. Mental (serotonin, stress, emotional control) and social (teamwork, cooperation, socialisation) benefits carry equal mark-scheme weight.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark analyse questions on wellbeing, the most frequent error is covering physical benefits thoroughly while barely mentioning mental or social health. Examiners design mark schemes with points spread across all three dimensions. Structure your answer in three clear sections: physical, mental, social. For each, identify a benefit, explain the mechanism (e.g. serotonin for mental; cooperation for social), and anchor it to a sporting example. For 3-mark describe questions (e.g. “Describe how participation in sport improves mental health”), use three distinct points: one for the hormonal/biochemical mechanism, one for psychological benefit (confidence, emotional control), one for the sporting context. Avoid writing the same point twice with slightly different wording — the mark scheme will not credit near-identical answers.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Physical participation improves cardiovascular efficiency, reduces disease risk and supports healthy weight management — all improving physical health and wellbeing.
  • Exercise releases serotonin and endorphins, reduces cortisol levels and builds self-efficacy, delivering substantial and evidence-based mental health benefits.
  • Team sport and group activity foster cooperation, teamwork and socialisation, directly addressing social health needs and reducing loneliness.

practice_questions.text: Identify one mental health benefit of regular participation in physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: reduces stress or tension; release of serotonin/endorphins (feel-good hormones); helps control emotions; reduces anxiety; improves mood. Accept precise physiological answers (serotonin release) or descriptive answers (reduces stress).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'social health'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic definition: the ability to form relationships with others / meet social needs. 1 mark for development: includes the ability to cooperate with others, belong to a community and contribute to group goals; or gives a sporting example (e.g. playing in a team sport provides social contact and a sense of belonging).

practice_questions.text: Describe three ways in which participating in team sport can improve a young person's social wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for three distinct points from: provides opportunities to socialise and make friends; develops cooperation skills (working with others towards a shared goal); develops teamwork (collective effort, shared responsibility); reduces loneliness / combats isolation; connects individuals to a community network; helps develop communication and trust.

practice_questions.text: Explain how regular exercise can improve a person's mental health, referring to at least one biological mechanism.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a benefit (reduces stress / anxiety / improves mood). 1 mark for the biological mechanism (exercise triggers release of serotonin, a neurotransmitter linked to feelings of calm and happiness). 1 mark for a second mechanism or further development (endorphins also released, producing feelings of euphoria; or regular exercise lowers baseline cortisol levels over time). 1 mark for sporting application (a swimmer who trains regularly may find their anxiety levels reduced on school days as a result of consistent serotonin release).

practice_questions.text: A table shows the self-reported wellbeing scores (out of 10) of 40 students before and after a 6-week exercise programme: Physical wellbeing — before 5.2, after 7.1; Mental wellbeing — before 4.8, after 6.9; Social wellbeing — before 5.5, after 7.4. Using the data, calculate the mean improvement across all three dimensions of wellbeing, and explain what this suggests about the value of the programme.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct calculation: improvements are 1.9 (physical), 2.1 (mental), 1.9 (social); mean = (1.9 + 2.1 + 1.9) ÷ 3 = 5.9 ÷ 3 = 1.97 (accept 1.96 to 2.0). 1 mark for showing working and stating the unit (points on the wellbeing scale). 1 mark for a valid inference: the mean improvement of approximately 2 points across all three wellbeing dimensions suggests the programme produced balanced benefits, indicating that physical activity supports physical, mental and social health simultaneously.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how participation in physical activity can improve physical, mental and social wellbeing. Refer to specific mechanisms in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): analyses all three wellbeing dimensions with at least one specific mechanism per dimension; applies each point to a sporting example; links mechanisms to outcomes (e.g. exercise raises serotonin, which reduces anxiety, which improves daily functioning); reaches a developed analytical conclusion about the interconnected nature of the three dimensions.
Secure (3–4 marks): covers at least two dimensions with some development; sporting context mostly present; mechanisms mentioned but not fully explained.
Developing (2 marks): identifies benefits across two or more dimensions but mainly descriptive; limited sporting application.
Emerging (1 mark): one dimension only or very basic points with no sporting context.

socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.title: Sedentary Lifestyle, Obesity and Somatotypes
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.description: Consequences of inactivity, how obesity affects performance, and ectomorph, mesomorph and endomorph body types.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.content_html:
What Is a Sedentary Lifestyle?

A sedentary lifestyle is one defined by prolonged physical inactivity. The word “sedentary” comes from the Latin for “sitting”, and that is its defining feature: large portions of waking hours spent sitting or lying down, with minimal structured exercise. Modern technology has made sedentary living increasingly easy — screen-based entertainment, desk-based work and motorised transport can combine to mean that some individuals complete fewer than 2,000 steps a day.

The consequences of a sedentary lifestyle are cumulative and wide-ranging. They span physical health (weight gain, disease), mental health (depression, low self-esteem) and social health (isolation, withdrawal). Understanding these consequences as distinct but interconnected categories is important for exam answers and for appreciating why public health campaigns consistently promote active living.

Key Fact

The seven consequences of a sedentary lifestyle are: weight gain/obesity, heart disease, hypertension, diabetes, poor sleep, poor self-esteem and lethargy. Obesity itself then creates a secondary cascade of health consequences.

Consequences of a Sedentary Lifestyle

Weight gain and obesity: without regular physical activity to burn calories, energy intake consistently exceeds energy expenditure. The surplus energy is stored as body fat. Over time, this leads to excess body weight and, if severe, to obesity. Unused saturated fat also accumulates in the blood vessels, contributing to the narrowing and hardening of the arteries (atherosclerosis) that underlies much cardiovascular disease.

Heart disease and hypertension: a sedentary heart is a weaker, less efficient heart. Without the regular challenge of aerobic exercise, the heart muscle does not strengthen, cardiac output does not improve and blood vessels lose some of their elasticity. Hypertension (high blood pressure) is strongly associated with physical inactivity and is a major risk factor for heart attacks, strokes and kidney disease. A sedentary lifestyle is one of the most modifiable risk factors for cardiovascular disease.

Diabetes: physical inactivity reduces the body’s sensitivity to insulin, the hormone that regulates blood glucose. When cells become resistant to insulin, blood glucose rises. Over time this can develop into type 2 diabetes, which carries serious long-term complications including nerve damage, vision loss and cardiovascular disease. Regular exercise improves insulin sensitivity, which is why increased physical activity is a first-line recommendation for individuals at risk.

Poor sleep and lethargy: regular exercise improves sleep quality by regulating circadian rhythms and reducing anxiety. A sedentary individual who does not exercise regularly may find it harder to fall asleep and experience less restorative deep sleep. Poor sleep in turn causes lethargy — persistent tiredness and a lack of energy — which makes further activity feel even less appealing, reinforcing the sedentary cycle.

Poor self-esteem: physical inactivity is associated with reduced self-efficacy, weight gain and social withdrawal. Self-esteem — one’s sense of personal worth — is strongly linked to physical self-perception. Individuals who are inactive and overweight often report lower confidence in their bodies and in social situations. This can contribute to depression and further withdrawal from activity, completing a damaging cycle.

Obesity: Definition and Impact on Performance

Obesity is defined medically as an excess accumulation of body fat sufficient to adversely affect health, typically measured by a body mass index (BMI) over 30. For a GCSE student, the key point is that obesity is not simply a cosmetic concern — it has direct, measurable impacts on a person’s ability to perform in physical activity and sport.

Limits cardiovascular endurance: excess body mass increases the oxygen demand on the cardiovascular system during exercise. The heart must work harder to pump blood to a larger body, and the lungs must work harder to supply sufficient oxygen. This means an obese individual reaches their maximum heart rate at lower exercise intensities, runs out of breath sooner and fatigues faster. Stamina (cardiovascular endurance) is significantly impaired.

Limits flexibility: excess fat tissue around joints and the abdomen physically restricts the range of movement at key joints. An obese individual will typically have a reduced ability to flex at the hip, extend the spine and perform movements requiring full range of motion. This makes activities such as gymnastics, martial arts and any sport demanding joint mobility significantly harder.

Limits agility: agility — the ability to change direction quickly and accurately — requires low body mass relative to muscle strength. Excess body fat increases the load that the muscles and joints must move during direction changes, reducing agility and increasing injury risk (particularly to the knees and ankles).

Limits speed and power: speed depends on the ratio of muscular force to body mass. An obese individual carries more mass that must be accelerated by their muscles, directly reducing stride frequency, acceleration and maximum speed. Power output (force × velocity) is similarly compromised when body mass is excessive relative to muscle mass.

Students sometimes confuse being overweight with being obese, or assume that all excess mass is automatically a disadvantage. This is an oversimplification. A professional rugby prop or heavyweight boxer may have a high BMI because of their large muscle mass — they are not medically obese, and their body composition suits their sport. The spec’s discussion of obesity specifically refers to excess body fat, not body mass in general. When evaluating somatotypes and body composition in sport, distinguish between lean body mass (muscle, bone) and fat mass — it is the proportion of fat mass that determines whether obesity is a limiting factor.

Somatotypes: Body Type in Sport

The concept of somatotype was developed in the 1940s by psychologist William Sheldon, who identified three idealised body types. In GCSE PE, somatotypes are used to discuss the relationship between body shape and sporting suitability. Most real people are a blend of all three types, but understanding the extremes is useful for sports science analysis.

The endomorph has a pear-shaped body characterised by wide hips, a high percentage of body fat, relatively narrow shoulders and shorter limbs. Endomorphs tend to have difficulty losing weight but can carry significant muscle mass. In sport, a pure endomorph faces challenges in activities requiring speed, agility and cardiovascular endurance. However, in contact sports where body mass is an advantage (sumo wrestling, certain positions in American football), an endomorphic body type can be beneficial.

The mesomorph is widely regarded as the most versatile sporting body type. Mesomorphs have wide shoulders, a narrow waist, well-defined musculature and a naturally low body fat percentage. They respond quickly to training and gain muscle easily. This body type suits a wide range of sports, including sprinting, gymnastics, swimming and team sports. Athletes like Usain Bolt and Dame Sarah Storey exhibit mesomorphic characteristics, though both also show elements of other somatotypes.

The ectomorph is long, lean and lightly muscled. Ectomorphs have narrow hips and shoulders, long limbs and very little body fat. They may struggle to build muscle mass and can be susceptible to the cold. However, long limbs and low body mass make ectomorphs naturally suited to endurance activities (marathon running, long-distance cycling) and sports where height and reach are advantageous (basketball, volleyball). Paula Radcliffe exemplified many ectomorphic traits that suited elite marathon performance.

The spec asks students to “identify the most suitable body type for particular sports (or positions within a sport) and justify their choice”. This means your answer must include three steps: name the somatotype, describe the relevant physical characteristics, and link those characteristics to specific demands of the sport or position.

Example: “A mesomorph is most suited to gymnastics because their wide shoulders support overhead strength, their low body fat enables the strength-to-weight ratio needed for apparatus work, and their well-defined musculature responds quickly to the explosive power demands of floor and vault routines.” Avoid the error of stating only the body type without the justification — most somatotype questions award the majority of marks for the justified link to sport.

Key Fact

Endomorph: pear-shaped, wide hips, high fat — suited to contact sports requiring mass. Mesomorph: muscular, low fat, wide shoulders — versatile, suited to power and team sports. Ectomorph: lean, long limbs, low mass — suited to endurance and height-dependent sports.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.exam_tip_html: For 9-mark evaluate questions on sedentary lifestyle and obesity, the most common error is listing consequences without evaluating the severity of each or considering whether any consequences are harder to reverse than others. A Mastering-band answer will distinguish between physical, mental and social consequences; will argue which is most significant (with justification); and will consider a counter-argument (e.g. “while physical consequences such as heart disease are serious, they can be addressed through lifestyle change — however, the mental health consequences such as depression are often harder to treat and self-perpetuating”). For somatotype questions, always name the somatotype, give characteristics and justify the link to sport — a one-word answer (“mesomorph”) without justification will not score the marks available. For 6-mark analyse questions on obesity’s effect on performance, use the four performance components (cardiovascular endurance, flexibility, agility, speed/power) as your structure and develop each one.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A sedentary lifestyle causes seven key consequences: weight gain/obesity, heart disease, hypertension, diabetes, poor sleep, poor self-esteem and lethargy — affecting physical, mental and social health.
  • Obesity limits sporting performance across four key areas: cardiovascular endurance, flexibility, agility and speed/power — all arising from excess fat mass increasing the load on the cardiovascular and musculoskeletal systems.
  • The three somatotypes — endomorph (wide hips, high fat), mesomorph (muscular, low fat), ectomorph (lean, long limbs) — each suit different sports, and justifying the link to sporting demands is essential in exam answers.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'sedentary lifestyle'.

practice_questions.text: Describe three consequences of living a sedentary lifestyle.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for three distinct consequences from: weight gain/obesity; heart disease; hypertension (high blood pressure); diabetes (type 2); poor sleep; poor self-esteem; lethargy. Answers that name very similar consequences (e.g. 'heart disease' and 'heart attacks') count as one consequence. Accept physical, mental or social consequences.

practice_questions.text: Explain why obesity limits a performer's ability to participate effectively in team sports.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a performance component limited by obesity (cardiovascular endurance/agility/flexibility/speed). 1 mark for explaining why obesity limits that component (e.g. excess body fat increases the mass the muscles must move, reducing speed; or excess fat restricts range of movement at joints, reducing flexibility and agility). 1 mark for a second performance component and explanation. 1 mark for a sporting application (e.g. in football, an obese player would struggle to maintain the cardiovascular endurance needed for 90 minutes of play and would be slower when accelerating into space).

practice_questions.text: A 15-year-old aspiring marathon runner has been assessed by her coach. She is described as having a lean, slender build, long legs, narrow hips and shoulders, and very low body fat. Analyse the extent to which her somatotype is suited to marathon running and whether it presents any disadvantages.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): correctly identifies the somatotype as ectomorphic; analyses the advantages for marathon running in detail (low body fat reduces mass to be carried, long limbs provide efficient stride length, low mass reduces oxygen demand per kilometre); analyses at least one disadvantage with development (low muscle mass may limit hill climbing power; susceptibility to cold weather in long-distance outdoor racing; increased injury risk from impact forces on slender limbs); reaches a developed analytical conclusion weighing advantages against disadvantages in this specific sport.
Secure (3–4 marks): identifies somatotype, gives at least two advantages with some development and one disadvantage; sporting context mostly present.
Developing (2 marks): identifies somatotype and gives one or two simple points but limited analysis or no disadvantage considered.
Emerging (1 mark): names the somatotype with little or no justification.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether the consequences of a sedentary lifestyle are more serious for physical health than for mental and social health.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): presents a balanced evaluation across all three health dimensions; argues why physical consequences (obesity, heart disease, hypertension, diabetes) may be considered most serious (life-limiting, potentially fatal); argues why mental consequences (depression, poor self-esteem, lethargy creating a self-perpetuating cycle) may be equally or more serious (harder to identify and treat, reinforce the sedentary lifestyle); argues why social consequences (isolation, inability to leave home) compound both; reaches a clear, justified conclusion about which dimension presents the greatest long-term risk, with evidence from the lesson.
Secure (5–7 marks): covers all three dimensions; makes a case for at least one side with development; partial counter-argument; some sporting or health context.
Developing (3–4 marks): covers physical and one other dimension; some development but limited evaluation; conclusion present but not fully justified.
Emerging (1–2 marks): basic list of consequences; one-dimensional; no evaluation of relative severity.

socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.title: Energy, Diet, Nutrition and Hydration
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.description: Daily energy needs, macronutrients, balanced diet ratios and the effects of dehydration on sport.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.content_html:
Energy: The Fuel for Sport and Life

Everything the body does — breathing, thinking, sprinting, lifting — requires energy. That energy is measured in kilocalories (Kcal) and comes entirely from the food we eat. The average adult male requires approximately 2,500 Kcal per day, while the average adult female requires around 2,000 Kcal per day. However, these are only averages — how much energy any individual actually needs depends on four key factors: age, gender, height, and energy expenditure (how much exercise they do). A 16-year-old county-level swimmer training twice a day will have far greater energy needs than a sedentary adult of the same height and gender.

Key Fact

An individual’s daily energy requirement is affected by age, gender, height, and energy expenditure. Average values are 2,500 Kcal/day for males and 2,000 Kcal/day for females — but athletes and highly active individuals need significantly more.

The Balanced Diet: Proportions and Purposes

A balanced diet does not mean eating equal amounts of everything. It means eating the right proportions of different food types to supply the body with all the nutrients it needs. No single food provides every nutrient — variety is essential. Unused energy, particularly from saturated fats, is stored as body fat, which can contribute to obesity over time. The specification requires you to know the approximate percentage breakdown of a balanced diet: 55–60% carbohydrate, 25–30% fat, and 15–20% protein. These proportions reflect the primary roles each macronutrient plays in the body.

Macronutrients: Carbohydrate, Fat and Protein

Carbohydrate is the primary and preferred fuel for all types of exercise, regardless of intensity. Whether a performer is jogging at a comfortable pace or sprinting at maximum effort, carbohydrates are the first fuel the body calls upon. They are broken down into glucose, which is either used immediately or stored as glycogen in the muscles and liver for use during exercise. Elite distance runners such as Dina Asher-Smith prepare for competition partly by ensuring glycogen stores are fully loaded through carbohydrate-rich meals in the days before an event.

Fat provides more energy per gram than carbohydrate, but it can only be used efficiently as a fuel source at low intensity — for example, during a slow, steady-state walk or easy cycle ride. When exercise intensity increases, the body switches back to carbohydrate because fat metabolism is too slow to meet the demand. Fat also has important non-energy roles: it insulates the body, protects organs, and is a carrier for fat-soluble vitamins.

Protein is not a primary energy source. Its main role is the growth and repair of muscle tissue — essential after heavy training when muscle fibres have been broken down by the work they have done. Adam Peaty, for example, follows a protein-rich recovery plan after intense pool sessions to support muscle repair and adaptation. Consuming insufficient protein slows recovery and limits the adaptations (such as hypertrophy) that training is designed to produce.

Vitamins and minerals do not supply energy directly, but they are essential for the efficient working of all body systems. Vitamins support processes from immune function to bone health; minerals such as calcium and iron are vital for bone density and oxygen transport in the blood respectively. The specification does not require you to name specific vitamins or minerals, but you should know that their role is to maintain the efficient working of body systems and general health. A diet lacking in variety will typically be deficient in vitamins and minerals even if its Kcal total looks adequate on paper.

Key Fact

A balanced diet is approximately 55–60% carbohydrate (main energy source), 25–30% fat (energy at low intensity; insulation), 15–20% protein (growth and repair). Carbohydrate is the body’s preferred fuel at all exercise intensities.

Hydration and the Consequences of Dehydration

Water is not just a drink — it is the medium in which almost every chemical reaction in the body takes place. Maintaining water balance (hydration) is critical to performance. Even a 1–2% reduction in body mass through fluid loss can begin to impair sporting performance. Dehydration occurs when the body loses more fluid than it takes in. During intense exercise in warm conditions — such as a cross-country race or a summer football tournament — sweat rates can be high, meaning fluid must be replaced regularly to maintain performance and safety.

Effects of Dehydration on the Body and Performance

Dehydration triggers a series of interconnected physiological problems. As fluid is lost, blood plasma volume falls and the blood becomes thicker. This increase in blood viscosity means the heart must work harder to push blood around the circulatory system, driving up heart rate. Delivery of oxygen and nutrients to muscles slows, accelerating fatigue. In severe cases, heart rhythm may become irregular. Meanwhile, the body’s ability to shed heat through the blood vessels near the skin is compromised, causing core body temperature to rise — increasing the risk of overheating and heat stroke.

Beyond the cardiovascular effects, dehydration also affects the nervous system. Reaction time slows and decision-making deteriorates — a basketball player who is even mildly dehydrated may make slower, poorer decisions on court. Muscle function degrades too: dehydrated muscles fatigue more rapidly and are more prone to cramping, because the electrolyte balance (sodium, potassium) that enables muscle contraction is disrupted. For a sprint cyclist like Geraint Thomas, any cramping or slowing of reaction time in the final kilometre of a race could be decisive.

A common misconception is that hydration simply means “drink lots.” The spec focuses on balance — maintaining appropriate water levels, not overloading with fluids. The assessment reward is for understanding the cascade of effects from dehydration: thicker blood → higher heart rate → slower delivery of oxygen → muscle fatigue/cramp → slower reactions → poorer decisions. Practise writing that chain in order without notes, anchored to a sporting example.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.exam_tip_html:
On “Calculate” and “Calculate from Data” questions involving nutrition, always show your working, state the units (Kcal, %, g) and box your final answer. If asked to calculate the energy from carbohydrate in a diet of 2,400 Kcal, the working is: 2,400 × 0.55 = 1,320 Kcal from carbohydrate (or 2,400 × 0.60 = 1,440 Kcal at the upper end of the range). Missing the unit drops a mark.

On a 6-mark “Analyse” question about dehydration, avoid listing effects without connecting them. Write each effect as a cause-and-effect chain: “Dehydration reduces blood plasma volume, which increases blood viscosity (thickness). The heart must then beat faster to maintain blood flow, leading to earlier fatigue, and reduced oxygen delivery to working muscles.” That single chain earns more credit than five disconnected bullet points.
socio-cultural-influences-and-wellbeing.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Energy is measured in Kcal. Daily needs (avg. 2,500 Kcal male / 2,000 Kcal female) vary with age, gender, height and exercise levels. A balanced diet is 55–60% carbohydrate, 25–30% fat, 15–20% protein — carbohydrate is the body’s preferred fuel at all intensities.
  • Protein’s role is growth and repair of muscle tissue. Fat provides energy only at low intensity and in larger amounts than carbohydrate per gram. Vitamins and minerals maintain efficient body system function.
  • Dehydration increases blood viscosity, raises heart rate, causes overheating, slows reactions, impairs decision-making and causes muscle fatigue and cramps — all of which degrade sporting performance.

practice_questions.text: Identify the macronutrient that the body uses as its main and preferred energy source for all types of exercise.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: carbohydrate (accept carbs / glucose / glycogen — the macronutrient name is the target).

practice_questions.text: A sports nutritionist tells a 16-year-old female athlete that her daily diet provides 2,200 Kcal. Calculate the minimum and maximum amount of energy (in Kcal) that should come from carbohydrate in her balanced diet.
practice_questions.marks: Formula: Kcal from carbohydrate = total Kcal × percentage. Minimum: 2,200 × 0.55 = 1,210 Kcal (1 mark). Maximum: 2,200 × 0.60 = 1,320 Kcal (1 mark). Both values required for full marks; unit (Kcal) must be stated or implied by context.

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows the daily food intake of two junior rugby players during a pre-season training week.

Player | Total daily Kcal | % from carbohydrate | % from protein | % from fat
Jamie  | 3,100 Kcal       | 50%                 | 20%            | 30%
Tyler  | 3,100 Kcal       | 58%                 | 17%            | 25%

Using the data, calculate the number of Kcal that Tyler obtains from carbohydrate each day, and state whether his carbohydrate intake falls within the recommended range for a balanced diet.
practice_questions.marks: Working: 3,100 × 0.58 = 1,798 Kcal from carbohydrate (1 mark for correct working). Final answer: 1,798 Kcal (1 mark). Balanced diet range is 55–60%, so 58% falls within the recommended range (1 mark for correct judgement with reference to the 55–60% figure). Unit (Kcal) must be present.

practice_questions.text:
Table 2 shows the resting and exercising heart rates of two athletes before and after a 90-minute training session in hot conditions. Athlete A drank water throughout; Athlete B drank nothing.

Athlete | Heart rate before session (bpm) | Heart rate at 75 min (bpm)
A       | 68                              | 142
B       | 70                              | 167

Interpret what the data shows about the effect of dehydration on Athlete B's heart rate, and explain why this change occurred.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that Athlete B's heart rate is higher than Athlete A's at 75 minutes (167 bpm vs 142 bpm — a difference of 25 bpm). 1 mark for a comparison that quotes both figures. 1 mark for linking the higher heart rate to dehydration causing increased blood viscosity (thicker blood). 1 mark for explaining the mechanism: the heart must beat faster/work harder to maintain blood flow to muscles when blood is thicker. Quoting figures without making a comparison earns 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: A club-level triathlete has been advised by her coach to increase her protein intake during a 10-week strength-building phase. Analyse how an appropriate increase in protein, alongside sufficient carbohydrate, would support her training adaptations over this period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6 marks): Sustained analysis linking protein's role in muscle repair and hypertrophy to strength adaptations; explains that protein alone is insufficient without carbohydrate to fuel training sessions (carbohydrate = preferred energy source, all intensities); applies correctly to the triathlete context (heavy training, strength-building); may reference recovery between sessions; accurate use of terms (hypertrophy, glycogen, muscle fibre repair). Secure (3–4 marks): Accurate points about protein's role in repair/growth and carbohydrate as fuel; at least one point linked to the athlete's context; some development of each point. Developing (2 marks): Correct function of protein stated (growth and repair); carbohydrate mentioned; limited development or application to sport. Emerging (1 mark): One basic accurate point about protein or carbohydrate in isolation, with little or no sporting application.

practice_questions.text: A Year-11 PE class has been asked whether the government should make sports drinks mandatory for school athletes during competition. Evaluate whether sports drinks are necessary to maintain hydration and performance during school-level sport, considering the consequences of dehydration.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (8–9 marks): Balanced, sustained evaluation with both sides argued; consequences of dehydration cited accurately (increased blood viscosity, raised heart rate, slowed reactions, muscle cramps, impaired decision-making); counter-argument addresses the reality that most school-level sport is short-duration and water is sufficient; may distinguish between low-intensity school sport and high-intensity endurance events; correct use of terminology throughout; sporting examples used to anchor both sides. Secure (5–7 marks): Both sides present; dehydration consequences mostly accurate; sporting application present; some terminology. Developing (3–4 marks): One side argued well; dehydration mentioned but effects may be listed without development; limited balance. Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about hydration being important with little or no balance or application.
